presentation: Acanthosis nigricans in an obese child
stem:
A 13-year-old girl is brought to her GP by her father, who is worried about a brown 'tide mark' on the back of her neck that will not wash off. Over the last 18 months similar patches have appeared in both armpits. The skin is darkened, thickened and feels velvety, with no scaling, itch or redness. She feels well and has no excessive thirst, passing of large volumes of urine or weight loss. Her weight is well above the 99th centile for her age, and her mother has type 2 diabetes.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Arrange a blood glucose test today
options.B: Send skin scrapings for fungal microscopy
options.C: Start a topical retinoid cream
options.D: Refer to dermatology for a skin biopsy
options.E: Reassure and advise more frequent washing

correct_answer: A. Arrange a blood glucose test today
why_correct: Velvety, darkened skin on the neck and in the armpits of an obese child is acanthosis nigricans, a skin marker of insulin resistance, and NICE lists it with obesity and a family history as features pointing towards type 2 diabetes. She therefore needs her blood glucose checked now rather than treatment of the skin; in children diabetes is confirmed on plasma glucose, not HbA1c. If the glucose is raised or diabetes is suspected, she should be discussed with and referred to the paediatric diabetes team the same day. Source: NICE NG18 Diabetes (type 1 and type 2) in children and young people, 2015 (updated 2023); Diabetes UK diagnostic criteria for diabetes.
why_wrong: B. The skin is velvety and not scaly or itchy, so this is not a fungal infection and scrapings miss the metabolic problem. C. A retinoid may soften the skin but treats the sign and leaves possible diabetes uninvestigated. D. Acanthosis nigricans in this setting is a clinical diagnosis and does not need histology. E. The darkening is not dirt, and reassurance alone misses possible type 2 diabetes.
pearl: Acanthosis nigricans in an overweight child is insulin resistance showing on the skin: look for type 2 diabetes.
thinking: Dark velvety skin in neck and armpits  ↓  obese child, mother with type 2 diabetes  ↓  acanthosis nigricans = insulin resistance  ↓  check blood glucose now (plasma glucose, not HbA1c, in children)  ↓  raised or suspected diabetes: same-day paediatric diabetes team
exam_trap: Treating the skin with antifungals, retinoids or hygiene advice instead of looking for the metabolic cause.
takeaway: Acanthosis nigricans in an obese child: check blood glucose now and involve the paediatric diabetes team the same day if diabetes is suspected.
notes: New vignette: 13-year-old girl, father's concern about a 'tide mark', mother with T2DM; options reworded and reordered. Same learning point and key as reviewed MG001 (blood glucose now, no HbA1c option, same-day paediatric diabetes team). Near PLAB item DER048 asks what the sign indicates in an adult with known diabetes (diagnosis), whereas this tests the next step in a child, so not a repeat. NICE NG18 rec 1.1.5 re-checked 8 Oct 2026 (acanthosis nigricans listed as evidence of insulin resistance).

presentation: Rapid-onset acanthosis nigricans with weight loss
stem:
A 68-year-old woman sees her GP because dark, velvety, thickened skin has spread quickly over the past 10 weeks across her armpits, under her breasts and around her neck. The skin of her palms has also become thick, with deep, exaggerated creases. She has had indigestion and has felt full after only a few mouthfuls for 2 months, and her clothes have become loose; she has lost about 7 kg without trying. She is slim, has no history of diabetes and takes no regular medicines. Examination of the abdomen is unremarkable.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Check HbA1c and reassess in three months
options.B: Suspected cancer pathway referral for endoscopy
options.C: Routine referral to the dermatology clinic
options.D: Emollient urea cream and review in six weeks
options.E: Helicobacter pylori breath test and a PPI trial

correct_answer: B. Suspected cancer pathway referral for endoscopy
why_correct: Sudden, widespread acanthosis nigricans in a slim older adult, especially with thickened ridged palms ('tripe palms') and weight loss, suggests malignant acanthosis nigricans, which is most often linked to gastric adenocarcinoma. Independently of the skin, NICE recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral (the UK urgent route for possible cancer) for stomach cancer in people aged 55 or over with weight loss and upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia, so she needs urgent upper GI endoscopy. Source: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (updated 2025).
why_wrong: A. Insulin resistance does not explain florid, rapidly spreading skin change with weight loss in a slim woman, and waiting 3 months is unsafe. C. A routine skin referral delays investigation of a likely internal cancer. D. A keratolytic cream treats only the skin and ignores her red-flag weight loss. E. Test-and-treat for H. pylori is for dyspepsia without alarm features, not dyspepsia with weight loss at 55 or over.
pearl: Acanthosis nigricans that appears suddenly in a thin older adult, particularly with tripe palms, is paraneoplastic until proven otherwise: think stomach.
thinking: Rapid, widespread velvety pigmentation  ↓  tripe palms, slim, no diabetes  ↓  weight loss + early fullness + indigestion, age 68  ↓  malignant acanthosis nigricans, likely gastric cancer  ↓  suspected cancer pathway referral for upper GI endoscopy
exam_trap: Assuming insulin resistance and checking HbA1c, as you would for acanthosis nigricans in an obese patient.
takeaway: Sudden acanthosis nigricans with weight loss in an older adult needs a suspected cancer pathway referral for upper GI endoscopy.
notes: New vignette (68-year-old woman, 10 weeks, sub-mammary spread, early satiety); options reworded and reordered. Key unchanged. The age 55 criterion is kept because it is the NICE referral trigger PLAB relies on; weight loss figure kept as a supporting detail. Near PLAB items DF049/GF017 test upper GI referral for dysphagia, a different scenario. NICE NG12 rec 1.2.7 re-checked 8 Oct 2026.

presentation: Recurrent miscarriage with livedo reticularis
stem:
A 29-year-old woman is seen in the gynaecology clinic after losing three pregnancies in a row, each before 10 weeks. Three years ago she had a pulmonary embolism with no obvious trigger and completed a course of anticoagulation; she takes no medicines now and is not pregnant. She has no rashes on her face, joint symptoms or mouth ulcers. Her legs show a lace-like, purplish mottled pattern over the shins and knees that does not fade when she warms up. Her blood pressure and urinalysis are normal.

Which investigation is most likely to confirm the underlying diagnosis?

options.A: Inherited thrombophilia screen for factor V Leiden
options.B: Antinuclear antibodies with C3 and C4 levels
options.C: Chromosome analysis of her and her partner
options.D: Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies
options.E: Antithrombin, protein C and protein S assays

correct_answer: D. Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies
why_correct: Recurrent early miscarriage, a previous unprovoked venous thromboembolism and persistent livedo reticularis point to antiphospholipid syndrome. RCOG advises testing women with recurrent miscarriage for lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies, with a positive result confirmed on a repeat test at least 12 weeks later. Confirmed antiphospholipid syndrome changes care in a future pregnancy, when aspirin and low-molecular-weight heparin are offered. Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 17 Recurrent Miscarriage, 2023.
why_wrong: A. Inherited thrombophilia testing is not recommended for recurrent first-trimester loss and does not explain livedo reticularis. B. ANA and complement support lupus, which she has no features of, and they do not diagnose antiphospholipid syndrome. C. Parental karyotyping is not routinely recommended and does not explain her thrombosis or skin sign. E. Antithrombin, protein C and protein S are inherited thrombophilia tests that do not fit this pattern.
pearl: Lace-like mottling + clots + early pregnancy losses = antiphospholipid syndrome until the antibodies say otherwise.
thinking: Three losses before 10 weeks  ↓  unprovoked PE  ↓  persistent livedo reticularis  ↓  antiphospholipid syndrome  ↓  lupus anticoagulant + anticardiolipin antibodies, repeat after 12 weeks
exam_trap: Ordering an inherited thrombophilia screen because of the previous clot.
takeaway: Recurrent miscarriage with livedo reticularis or thrombosis: test lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies and repeat at 12 weeks.
notes: New vignette: PE instead of DVT, losses before 10 weeks, gynaecology clinic; not on anticoagulants stated so lupus anticoagulant testing is valid. Anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I kept out of the key as in the reviewed source. Near PLAB RHE019/BX205 ask for the diagnosis once antibodies are known; this asks which test confirms it, so different learning point.

presentation: Pyoderma gangrenosum in Crohn disease
stem:
A 45-year-old man with Crohn disease, currently flaring with abdominal pain and six loose stools a day, is reviewed by the medical team because of an ulcer on the front of his left leg. It started 4 weeks ago as a tender red spot at the site of a minor graze and has rapidly grown to 7 cm, despite a week of oral antibiotics from his GP. The pain is severe. The ulcer has a purple, ragged, overhanging edge and a sloughy base, and a swab grew only normal skin organisms. Last week a practice nurse trimmed the ulcer edge, after which it widened considerably. Foot pulses are easily felt.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Surgical excision of the ulcer and its undermined edge
options.B: Intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.C: Split-skin grafting to close the defect
options.D: Multilayer compression bandaging
options.E: High-dose oral prednisolone

correct_answer: E. High-dose oral prednisolone
why_correct: A rapidly enlarging, very painful ulcer with a purple undermined edge in active inflammatory bowel disease, which worsened after minor trauma (pathergy), is pyoderma gangrenosum. Extensive or rapidly progressive disease needs systemic immunosuppression; in the UK STOP GAP trial oral prednisolone and ciclosporin worked equally well, and prednisolone will also help his Crohn flare, with treatment planned with dermatology and gastroenterology. It is an inflammatory (neutrophilic) ulcer rather than an infection, but it should still be checked for superadded infection, and surgery or debridement is avoided while it is active because trauma extends the ulcer. Source: Ormerod et al, STOP GAP trial, BMJ 2015; DermNet pyoderma gangrenosum.
why_wrong: A. Surgery on an active ulcer triggers pathergy and enlarges it, as the trimming of the edge already showed. B. The ulcer has grown despite antibiotics and the swab shows only skin flora, so more antibiotics will not control the inflammation, although superadded infection should still be looked for. C. Grafting during active disease fails and can create new ulcers at the donor site. D. Compression is for venous ulcers and does nothing for the inflammation.
pearl: An ulcer that gets bigger every time it is cut is pyoderma gangrenosum until proven otherwise: treat the immune system, not the wound.
thinking: Rapidly enlarging, very painful leg ulcer with purple undermined edge  ↓  active Crohn disease, began after a graze  ↓  widened after the edge was trimmed (pathergy)  ↓  pyoderma gangrenosum  ↓  systemic steroid (or ciclosporin), avoid surgery
exam_trap: Treating it as an infected wound that needs more antibiotics or debridement.
takeaway: Pyoderma gangrenosum: systemic immunosuppression such as oral prednisolone, and avoid surgical intervention while it is active.
notes: New vignette: Crohn disease instead of UC, pathergy shown by nurse trimming the edge rather than previous surgical debridement; dose figure removed from the explanation (rule 1). Near PLAB DER054 asks the diagnosis; this asks management, so not a repeat.

presentation: Yellowish atrophic shin plaques
stem:
A 41-year-old man shows his GP two patches on the front of his lower legs that he first noticed 18 months ago and that have slowly grown. Each is an oval, waxy, yellowish plaque with a raised purplish-red border and a glossy, thinned centre through which small blood vessels are easily seen. One patch broke down into a shallow sore after he knocked it on a table. They are painless and do not itch. He has no other skin problems and takes no regular medicines.

Which underlying condition should he be tested for?

options.A: Diabetes mellitus
options.B: Hyperthyroidism due to Graves disease
options.C: Pulmonary sarcoidosis
options.D: Inflammatory bowel disease
options.E: Venous insufficiency of the legs

correct_answer: A. Diabetes mellitus
why_correct: Waxy, yellow-brown, atrophic shin plaques with a purplish rim and visible telangiectasia are necrobiosis lipoidica. It is strongly associated with diabetes mellitus (type 1 and type 2), and many affected people have diabetes or prediabetes, so he should be tested for it. The plaques can ulcerate after minor injury, as happened here. Source: DermNet necrobiosis lipoidica, 2023.
why_wrong: B. Graves disease causes pretibial myxoedema, which gives firm, waxy, orange-peel swellings rather than thin yellow plaques with visible vessels. C. Sarcoidosis causes erythema nodosum (tender red nodules) or lupus pernio, not this picture. D. Inflammatory bowel disease is linked with erythema nodosum and pyoderma gangrenosum on the shins. E. Venous insufficiency causes brown haemosiderin staining and hardened skin around the ankles, with swelling and varicose veins.
pearl: Yellow, shiny, thinned shin plaques with visible vessels = necrobiosis lipoidica = test for diabetes.
thinking: Slowly enlarging shin plaques  ↓  yellow, waxy, atrophic centre, telangiectasia, purplish rim  ↓  necrobiosis lipoidica  ↓  associated with diabetes mellitus  ↓  test for diabetes
exam_trap: Mistaking it for pretibial myxoedema and choosing Graves disease.
takeaway: Necrobiosis lipoidica on the shins should prompt testing for diabetes mellitus.
notes: New vignette: man aged 41, ulceration after minor trauma added; question re-angled from 'most strongly associated' to 'which condition should he be tested for' (same learning point). Sarcoidosis and Crohn distractors broadened to pulmonary sarcoidosis and IBD.

presentation: Black toe with rest pain
stem:
A 69-year-old woman who smokes and has hypertension is seen by her GP because the tip of her right big toe has gone black over the past month. She has had calf pain on walking for a year, and for the past 6 weeks pain in her foot has woken her at night; she now sleeps in a chair with her leg down. The toe tip is black, hard, shrunken and cold, with a sharp line separating it from healthy skin. There is no discharge, swelling or surrounding redness. Pulses cannot be felt below the right groin. She does not have diabetes, and her temperature and heart rate are normal.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Sharp debridement of the black tissue in clinic
options.B: Dry dressing and urgent vascular surgery referral
options.C: Hydrogel dressing to soften and lift the dead tissue
options.D: Oral flucloxacillin and review in one week
options.E: Compression bandaging and a routine vascular referral

correct_answer: B. Dry dressing and urgent vascular surgery referral
why_correct: Night pain relieved by hanging the leg down, absent pulses and a dry, black, sharply demarcated toe mean chronic limb-threatening (critical) ischaemia with dry gangrene. Keep the toe clean and dry: do not debride it and do not apply hydrogel or other moist dressings, because cutting dead tissue from an unperfused foot leaves a wound that cannot heal and moisture can turn dry gangrene wet. She needs urgent assessment by the vascular team, who will image the leg and consider revascularisation before any amputation, because dead tissue in a foot without blood supply will not heal. UK vascular standards expect people with tissue loss to be seen by a specialist within days, not weeks. Source: NICE CG147 Peripheral arterial disease, 2012 (updated 2020); Vascular Society PAD Quality Improvement Framework, 2022.
why_wrong: A. Cutting away dead tissue in an unperfused foot leaves a wound that cannot heal, and any debridement should follow vascular assessment. C. Moist dressings can turn stable dry gangrene into wet, infected gangrene. D. There are no signs of infection, and antibiotics do nothing for the ischaemia. E. Compression is dangerous in an ischaemic leg, and a routine referral is too slow for tissue loss.
pearl: Dry gangrene: keep it dry, keep the scalpel away and get the vascular team to restore blood flow first.
thinking: Claudication progressing to night rest pain  ↓  dry, black, demarcated toe, absent pulses  ↓  chronic limb-threatening ischaemia with dry gangrene  ↓  no infection or sepsis  ↓  keep dry + urgent vascular referral for revascularisation
exam_trap: Debriding the black toe or applying moist dressings before blood flow has been assessed.
takeaway: Dry gangrene from peripheral arterial disease: keep it dry and refer urgently to vascular surgery.
notes: New vignette: woman, big toe, claudication history, sleeps in a chair. Rule 1: '2 working days' standard softened to 'within days'. Near PLAB DR147 (non-healing toe ulcer with rest pain, urgent vascular referral) shares the referral point, but this scenario is dry gangrene and the distinguishing learning point is wound handling (keep dry, no debridement or hydrogel) alongside referral; reviewer may wish to confirm this is acceptable.

presentation: Stable dry gangrene, not for revascularisation
stem:
A 92-year-old man living in a nursing home has a black, dry, shrivelled right second toe with a clear line of demarcation, which has developed over 2 months. He has severe COPD needing home oxygen and is very frail. The vascular multidisciplinary team has assessed him and decided that angioplasty or bypass would not be appropriate; he has capacity and has clearly said he does not want any amputation. The toe has no swelling, discharge, spreading redness or crackling under the skin. He has no fever, his observations are at his usual baseline and his foot pain is controlled with regular analgesia.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Hydrogel dressings to soften and debride the dead toe
options.B: Amputate the toe under local anaesthetic this week
options.C: Long-term oral antibiotics until the toe falls away
options.D: Keep it dry and protected, control pain, plan reviews
options.E: Referral for below-knee amputation to stop it spreading

correct_answer: D. Keep it dry and protected, control pain, plan reviews
why_correct: This is stable, uninfected dry gangrene in a frail man who is not a candidate for revascularisation, after a vascular MDT decision and in line with his own informed wishes, so the plan is individualised conservative (and, as needed, palliative) care: keep the toe clean and dry, offload pressure from the foot, control pain and arrange planned review by the nursing home staff, podiatry and his GP. Staff and the patient should know to seek urgent medical help if swelling, discharge, spreading redness, fever or any systemic illness develops, because these signal conversion to wet gangrene. With this care the dead toe may separate on its own (auto-amputation), whereas surgery on an unperfused foot is unlikely to heal and he has declined it. Source: NICE CG147 Peripheral arterial disease, 2012 (updated 2020); StatPearls Gangrene (NCBI Bookshelf), updated 2025.
why_wrong: A. Moist dressings soften dry gangrene and risk turning it into wet, infected gangrene. B. Without revascularisation the wound is unlikely to heal, and he has declined amputation. C. There is no infection, and prolonged prophylactic antibiotics add side effects and resistance without benefit. E. Stable dry gangrene is not spreading, major amputation needs an MDT decision, and he has capacity and has declined it.
pearl: Stable dry gangrene that cannot be revascularised: keep it dry, offload it, control pain, review it regularly and safety-net for wet change.
thinking: Dry, demarcated toe, no infection, systemically well  ↓  vascular MDT: not suitable for revascularisation  ↓  patient with capacity declines amputation  ↓  conservative care: dry, offloaded, analgesia, planned review  ↓  safety-net for swelling, discharge, redness, fever; toe may separate on its own
exam_trap: Choosing surgical removal of the dead toe when the foot cannot be revascularised and the patient has declined surgery.
takeaway: Stable dry gangrene unsuitable for revascularisation: individualised conservative care with clear safety-netting for wet change, guided by the MDT and the patient's wishes.
notes: New vignette: 92-year-old man with severe COPD instead of heart failure, second toe. Safety-netting and MDT/capacity wording carried over from the reviewed source. No near PLAB item covers conservative care of dry gangrene.

presentation: Dry gangrene turning wet on the ward
stem:
An 81-year-old woman on the vascular surgery ward is waiting for angioplasty for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia of her left leg. When she was admitted, the tip of her left big toe was black, dry and shrunken with a sharp edge. Overnight the front of her foot has become red and swollen, the skin around the toe has broken down and is weeping foul-smelling fluid, and the dusky colour is now creeping up the top of the foot with no clear border. There is no crackling under the skin. The nurse reports she is newly muddled, with a temperature of 38.6°C, heart rate 112 bpm, respiratory rate 24/min and blood pressure 104/62 mmHg.

What is the most likely explanation and the most appropriate action?

options.A: Stable dry gangrene: keep dry and continue to wait
options.B: Cellulitis: oral antibiotics and mark the margin
options.C: Dependent swelling: elevate the leg and review tomorrow
options.D: Wet gangrene: IV antibiotics and call surgeons urgently
options.E: Wound infection: send a swab and wait for sensitivities

correct_answer: D. Wet gangrene: IV antibiotics and call surgeons urgently
why_correct: Dry gangrene is cold, shrivelled and sharply demarcated, with no discharge and little systemic upset. New swelling, skin breakdown, foul discharge, a spreading edge without demarcation, and fever with confusion and tachycardia mean the dead tissue has become infected (wet gangrene), and she has sepsis. This is a surgical emergency needing sepsis management with prompt broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and urgent surgical review for debridement or amputation to control the source, which takes priority over the planned angioplasty. Source: StatPearls Gangrene (NCBI Bookshelf), updated 2025; Vascular Society PAD Quality Improvement Framework, 2022.
why_wrong: A. Swelling, discharge, loss of demarcation and fever show it is no longer stable dry gangrene, and waiting lets infection spread. B. Oral antibiotics for cellulitis ignore the infected dead tissue, which needs IV treatment and surgical source control. C. Swelling from a dependent leg does not cause foul discharge, fever or confusion. E. Waiting for culture results delays treatment that is needed now and will not change the immediate plan.
pearl: Dry gangrene that becomes swollen, wet, smelly and poorly demarcated with a fever has turned wet: call the surgeons now.
thinking: Known dry, demarcated toe gangrene  ↓  new swelling, skin breakdown, foul discharge, edge no longer clear  ↓  fever, tachycardia, new confusion = sepsis  ↓  wet (infected) gangrene  ↓  IV antibiotics + urgent surgical debridement or amputation
exam_trap: Assuming a patient with known dry gangrene is still stable and simply waiting for the planned procedure.
takeaway: Swelling, discharge, a spreading poorly demarcated edge and systemic upset mean wet gangrene: IV antibiotics and urgent surgery.
notes: New vignette: woman, big toe, awaiting angioplasty; question kept as interpretation-plus-action to preserve the recognition point. Inpatient setting kept deliberately: near PLAB DF030 (wet diabetic toe seen in general practice, answer immediate hospital referral) has a different scenario and decision. No crepitus stated to exclude gas gangrene.

presentation: Gas gangrene after a contaminated wound
stem:
A 46-year-old gardener drove a garden fork deep into his right thigh while turning a manure heap. The puncture wound was cleaned and closed with sutures at an urgent treatment centre. Thirty-six hours later he is brought to the emergency department with severe thigh pain that seems far worse than the wound looks. The thigh is tense and swollen, the skin is bronze and purple with dark fluid-filled blisters, and thin, foul-smelling fluid is leaking between the sutures. Crackling can be felt under the skin. His temperature is 39.1°C, heart rate 132 bpm and blood pressure 88/50 mmHg. An X-ray shows gas tracking through the muscles.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: IV antibiotics and emergency surgical debridement
options.B: Hyperbaric oxygen first, then surgery if no better
options.C: IV antibiotics alone, reassessing for surgery tomorrow
options.D: Remove the sutures and pack the wound on the ward
options.E: MRI of the thigh to map the extent before treatment

correct_answer: A. IV antibiotics and emergency surgical debridement
why_correct: A deep, soil- and manure-contaminated wound that was closed, followed by severe pain, bronze skin, haemorrhagic blisters, crepitus, gas in the muscle and shock, is gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis, usually Clostridium perfringens). He needs resuscitation, immediate high-dose IV antibiotics and urgent radical surgical debridement of all dead muscle, with a planned second look and amputation if needed. Empirical antibiotics should follow the local protocol for necrotising soft-tissue infection, which usually means broad-spectrum cover with clindamycin to suppress toxin production, narrowed with microbiology advice once clostridia are confirmed. Source: NHS Lothian antimicrobial guideline Severe soft tissue infection including suspected necrotising fasciitis, 2024; Clostridial myonecrosis review, Infection (Springer), 2024.
why_wrong: B. Hyperbaric oxygen is at most an adjunct and must never delay surgery. C. Antibiotics cannot reach dead, poorly perfused muscle, so delaying surgery allows rapid spread and death. D. Opening the wound on the ward does not remove the dead muscle that is producing toxin. E. The diagnosis is already clear clinically and on X-ray, and further imaging only delays theatre.
pearl: Crepitus, bronze skin and pain out of proportion after a dirty wound = gas gangrene: antibiotics plus theatre, never antibiotics alone.
thinking: Deep manure-contaminated wound closed primarily  ↓  severe pain, bronze skin, dark blisters, crepitus, gas in muscle on X-ray  ↓  shock  ↓  clostridial myonecrosis  ↓  IV antibiotics per local necrotising infection protocol (with clindamycin) + emergency radical debridement
exam_trap: Choosing hyperbaric oxygen or antibiotics alone and putting off surgery.
takeaway: Gas gangrene: IV antibiotics and emergency surgical debridement of all dead muscle.
notes: New vignette: garden-fork puncture into thigh in manure rather than crush injury of calf. Near PLAB DS174/S046/DER007 test necrotising fasciitis in diabetic patients (different scenario and diagnosis); this item's distinguishing point is clostridial myonecrosis after a closed contaminated wound and rejection of hyperbaric oxygen/antibiotics-alone, so not a repeat.

presentation: Sliding hiatus hernia: risk factor
stem:
A 52-year-old woman has an upper GI endoscopy because heartburn and acid coming up into her throat have persisted despite 2 months of a proton pump inhibitor. It shows a 4 cm sliding hiatus hernia with mild oesophagitis and no Barrett oesophagus. She works as a call-centre manager, takes naproxen most days for back pain and drinks about 18 units of alcohol a week. She had H. pylori infection treated successfully 5 years ago and a laparoscopic cholecystectomy 3 years ago. Her BMI is 37 kg/m², and most of her excess weight is carried around her waist.

Which factor has most likely contributed to her hiatus hernia?

options.A: Regular naproxen for back pain
options.B: Central (abdominal) obesity
options.C: Alcohol intake of 18 units a week
options.D: Previous H. pylori infection
options.E: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy

correct_answer: B. Central (abdominal) obesity
why_correct: A sliding hiatus hernia forms when the gastro-oesophageal junction is pushed up through a widened diaphragmatic hiatus, and raised intra-abdominal pressure is one of the main drivers. Obesity, especially central obesity, is a recognised risk factor, along with older age, pregnancy and ascites, which all raise intra-abdominal pressure. Weight loss is also one of the most useful lifestyle measures for her reflux. Source: Hiatus hernia, Patient.info professional reference (updated 2024); Hiatus hernia, NHS website.
why_wrong: A. NSAIDs damage the stomach and duodenal lining and cause ulcers, but they do not widen the hiatus. C. Alcohol can worsen reflux by relaxing the lower oesophageal sphincter but does not cause the hernia itself. D. H. pylori causes gastritis and peptic ulcers and is not a cause of hiatus hernia. E. Gallbladder surgery does not involve the diaphragmatic hiatus; previous surgery around the gastro-oesophageal junction is the relevant surgical risk factor.
pearl: Anything that pushes up from below, such as central obesity, pregnancy or ascites, favours a sliding hiatus hernia.
thinking: Sliding hiatus hernia on endoscopy  ↓  mechanism: widened hiatus + raised intra-abdominal pressure  ↓  BMI 37 with central fat distribution  ↓  NSAIDs, H. pylori and alcohol affect the lining or reflux, not the hiatus  ↓  central obesity
exam_trap: Choosing a factor that worsens reflux or damages the lining (alcohol, NSAIDs, H. pylori) rather than one that raises intra-abdominal pressure.
takeaway: Central obesity raises intra-abdominal pressure and is a key risk factor for sliding hiatus hernia.
notes: New vignette: woman, naproxen, treated H. pylori, cholecystectomy as surgical distractor; waist measurement softened into words (rule 1). No pregnancies mentioned to avoid a second defensible answer. No near PLAB item tests hiatus hernia risk factors.

presentation: Reflux with a known small hiatus hernia
stem:
A 39-year-old woman sees her GP with 2 months of heartburn and a sour taste in her mouth, worse when she bends over, lies down or eats a late evening meal. A CT scan done for suspected appendicitis last year mentioned a small sliding hiatus hernia, and she wants to know if it should be 'fixed'. She has no difficulty swallowing, vomiting, weight loss or signs of bleeding, and a recent blood count was normal. Her BMI is 32 kg/m², she smokes 10 cigarettes a day and drinks several strong coffees daily.

How should she be managed first?

options.A: Refer to upper GI surgery for laparoscopic repair
options.B: Suspected cancer pathway referral for endoscopy
options.C: Barium swallow to assess the hernia size
options.D: Lifestyle advice and a full-dose PPI trial
options.E: Prokinetic domperidone taken regularly with meals

correct_answer: D. Lifestyle advice and a full-dose PPI trial
why_correct: A small sliding hiatus hernia is common and does not need repair in itself; the aim is to treat her reflux symptoms. NICE advises lifestyle advice (weight loss, stopping smoking, avoiding late large meals and trigger foods, raising the head of the bed) and a full-dose proton pump inhibitor for about a month for reflux-type dyspepsia without alarm features. Anti-reflux surgery is considered only later, for confirmed reflux disease that responds to acid suppression when the person does not want or cannot tolerate long-term treatment. Source: NICE CG184 Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and dyspepsia in adults, 2014 (updated 2019).
why_wrong: A. NICE reserves surgery for confirmed reflux disease after a trial of acid suppression, so first-line repair of a small sliding hernia is not appropriate. B. She is young with no dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding or anaemia, so she does not meet suspected cancer pathway criteria. C. Hernia size would not change management, which is guided by symptoms. E. The MHRA restricts domperidone to short-term relief of nausea and vomiting because of cardiac risk, and it has no role in reflux.
pearl: Treat the reflux, not the hernia: a small sliding hiatus hernia is a finding, not an indication for surgery.
thinking: Typical reflux symptoms  ↓  known small sliding hiatus hernia  ↓  no alarm features, age 39  ↓  lifestyle advice + full-dose PPI trial  ↓  surgery only for confirmed reflux that responds to PPI, if long-term treatment unwanted
exam_trap: Assuming a hiatus hernia that causes reflux needs surgical repair before medical treatment has been tried.
takeaway: Sliding hiatus hernia with reflux and no alarm features: lifestyle measures and a PPI first.
notes: New vignette (39-year-old woman, smoker, coffee, CT for suspected appendicitis). Rule 1: '4 weeks' removed from the key and softened to 'about a month' in the explanation; domperidone dose removed. H. pylori test-and-treat kept out of the options as in the source. Near PLAB GAS081 tests uninvestigated dyspepsia without a hernia; this tests whether a known hernia needs repair, so different learning point. NICE CG184 recs 1.4.3/1.6.2 re-checked 8 Oct 2026.

presentation: Incidental para-oesophageal hiatus hernia
stem:
A 59-year-old man who cycles competitively has a CT coronary angiogram for atypical chest pain, which shows normal coronary arteries. The report describes a type II (rolling) para-oesophageal hiatus hernia: part of the gastric fundus has rolled up into the chest alongside the oesophagus, while the gastro-oesophageal junction remains in its normal position below the diaphragm. He has mild bloating after large meals but no heartburn, swallowing difficulty, vomiting or weight loss, and his haemoglobin is normal.

Which statement about his hernia is most accurate?

options.A: It is the most common type of hiatus hernia in adults
options.B: His gastro-oesophageal junction has moved into the chest
options.C: He needs referral only if reflux fails to settle on a PPI
options.D: He needs yearly endoscopy to look for Barrett oesophagus
options.E: Volvulus is more likely than with a sliding hernia

correct_answer: E. Volvulus is more likely than with a sliding hernia
why_correct: Hiatus hernias are classified by where the gastro-oesophageal junction lies: type I (sliding, about 95%) moves the junction up, type II has the fundus rolling up beside a normally placed junction, type III combines both, and type IV contains other organs. In types II to IV (para-oesophageal hernias) the stomach can twist within the chest, so they carry a greater risk of gastric volvulus, obstruction and strangulation than sliding hernias. For this reason even mildly symptomatic para-oesophageal hernias in fit people are referred for a surgical opinion, and patients are told to seek emergency help for sudden severe pain or retching without vomiting. Source: SAGES Guidelines for the Management of Hiatal Hernia, 2013.
why_wrong: A. Sliding (type I) hernias make up the large majority, so a para-oesophageal hernia is the less common type. B. In a type II hernia the junction stays below the diaphragm; it moves up in types I and III. C. A para-oesophageal hernia is judged by its mechanical risk rather than by heartburn, and he has no reflux to treat. D. Barrett oesophagus is linked to long-standing reflux, not hernia type, and a hiatus hernia alone does not justify yearly endoscopy.
pearl: Sliding hernias mainly cause reflux; para-oesophageal hernias can twist: refer and safety-net for volvulus.
thinking: Type II = fundus beside the oesophagus, junction in place  ↓  types II to IV are para-oesophageal  ↓  stomach can rotate in the chest  ↓  risk of volvulus, strangulation, perforation  ↓  surgical opinion + safety-net for sudden pain or unproductive retching
exam_trap: Treating every hiatus hernia like a sliding hernia and judging it only by reflux symptoms.
takeaway: Para-oesophageal hiatus hernias carry a greater risk of volvulus than sliding hernias, so even mildly symptomatic fit patients should be referred for a surgical opinion.
notes: Angle change: type III (AKT) changed to type II (rolling), so the GEJ-position distractor now tests the type II definition (junction stays in place). Same learning point and key (volvulus risk greater than sliding hernia). Prevalence figure (about 95%) kept only in the explanation, not needed to answer. Near PLAB GF016/GF018 test X-ray diagnosis and acute volvulus respectively.

presentation: Refractory iron-deficiency anaemia with a large hiatus hernia
stem:
A 76-year-old man who walks his dog for an hour every day has had recurrent iron-deficiency anaemia for 2 years. He has needed intravenous iron and one blood transfusion despite taking oral iron and a high-dose proton pump inhibitor twice daily throughout. He feels full and short of breath after meals. Gastroscopy shows a large mixed para-oesophageal hiatus hernia, with linear ulcers on the gastric folds where the stomach passes through the diaphragm. His colonoscopy was normal and tests for coeliac disease were negative.

Which is the best course of action now?

options.A: Upper GI surgical referral for hernia repair
options.B: Increase the PPI dose and continue oral iron
options.C: Small bowel capsule endoscopy to find a source
options.D: Repeat colonoscopy with random biopsies
options.E: Lifelong regular intravenous iron infusions

correct_answer: A. Upper GI surgical referral for hernia repair
why_correct: Linear ulcers on the gastric folds at the diaphragmatic pinch of a large hiatus hernia are Cameron lesions, a recognised cause of chronic occult bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia. His anaemia has needed transfusion despite iron and twice-daily PPI, and the hernia is also causing post-meal symptoms, so medical treatment has failed. Symptomatic para-oesophageal and mixed hernias are usually considered for repair, so he should be referred to an upper GI surgeon to assess him for elective laparoscopic repair, with the final decision resting on that assessment and his own choice. Source: SAGES Guidelines for the Management of Hiatal Hernia, 2013; Li et al., Cameron ulcer systematic review, Frontiers in Medicine 2025.
why_wrong: B. He is already on maximal PPI and iron and still needs transfusion, so more of the same has failed. C. Capsule endoscopy is for anaemia with no cause found on gastroscopy and colonoscopy, and a cause has been found here. D. His colonoscopy was normal, and random biopsies look for microscopic colitis in diarrhoea rather than a bleeding source. E. Lifelong IV iron replaces losses without treating the bleeding lesion or his hernia symptoms in a man fit for surgery.
pearl: Iron-deficiency anaemia with a large hiatus hernia: look for Cameron lesions at the diaphragmatic pinch.
thinking: Recurrent IDA despite iron and PPI, needing transfusion  ↓  large mixed hernia + linear ulcers at the diaphragm = Cameron lesions  ↓  colonoscopy and coeliac serology normal  ↓  symptomatic hernia, fit patient  ↓  refer for elective laparoscopic repair
exam_trap: Sending him for capsule endoscopy as if the anaemia were unexplained when gastroscopy has already found the cause.
takeaway: Symptomatic large hiatus hernia with Cameron lesions and refractory anaemia: refer for surgical assessment for elective repair.
notes: New vignette (76-year-old fit man, IV iron plus one transfusion). Rule 1: PPI drug and dose and hernia length removed. Key reworded as referral for repair, consistent with the reviewed source's emphasis that the decision rests on surgical assessment. No near PLAB item covers Cameron lesions.

presentation: Incidental adrenal mass
stem:
A 47-year-old woman has a CT scan of the abdomen to investigate recurrent right upper abdominal pain, which shows gallstones. The scan also shows an incidental 2 cm right adrenal nodule. The radiologist reports that it is smooth, uniform and of low density on the unenhanced images, typical of a benign lipid-rich adenoma, and that no further imaging is needed. She has never had cancer. Her blood pressure and serum potassium are normal, and she has no features of Cushing syndrome.

Which should be arranged next?

options.A: Reassure and discharge with no further tests
options.B: Repeat adrenal CT in one year
options.C: Overnight dexamethasone suppression test
options.D: Image-guided biopsy of the adrenal nodule
options.E: Referral for laparoscopic adrenalectomy

correct_answer: C. Overnight dexamethasone suppression test
why_correct: A small, homogeneous, low-density adrenal mass on unenhanced CT is a benign adenoma and needs no further imaging, but every adrenal incidentaloma still needs assessment for hormone excess. The European guideline recommends an overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test in all patients to look for autonomous cortisol secretion, which is often clinically silent and linked to hypertension, diabetes and fractures. Metanephrines are reserved for masses that do not look benign, and an aldosterone-to-renin ratio for people with hypertension or low potassium. Source: European Society of Endocrinology/ENSAT clinical practice guideline on adrenal incidentalomas, 2023.
why_wrong: A. A benign appearance does not exclude hormone secretion, so she still needs biochemical testing. B. A mass with clearly benign imaging features needs no repeat imaging. D. Adrenal biopsy is not part of routine work-up and is considered only in selected patients with a history of cancer elsewhere, after phaeochromocytoma is excluded. E. Surgery is not indicated for a small benign-looking adenoma unless hormone excess or suspicious features are found.
pearl: Imaging tells you whether an adrenal incidentaloma is benign; only blood tests tell you whether it is working.
thinking: Incidental adrenal nodule  ↓  small, uniform, low density = benign adenoma, no more imaging  ↓  function still needs checking in everyone  ↓  normal BP and potassium  ↓  overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test
exam_trap: Reassuring and discharging because the CT looks benign, forgetting that a benign adenoma can still secrete cortisol.
takeaway: Every adrenal incidentaloma needs an overnight dexamethasone suppression test, even when it looks benign.
notes: New vignette: woman, CT for gallstone pain, right adrenal. Rule 1: Hounsfield unit value and 4 cm/10 HU thresholds softened into words (the radiologist states benign features), so the key does not depend on recalling imaging cut-offs. Metanephrines kept out of the options as in the source. Near PLAB CR054 interprets a failed suppression test (different learning point).

presentation: Incidental high-risk lung nodule
stem:
A 62-year-old man has a CT scan of the chest after a fall in which he broke two ribs. It shows an incidental 14 mm solid nodule with a spiculated edge in the left upper lobe. There is no previous chest imaging to compare with. He has smoked 35 pack-years and still smokes, but is otherwise well and fit for further tests or surgery. The radiologist calculates his Brock model risk of malignancy and reports it as high.

What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: No further follow-up is needed
options.B: Repeat CT chest in three months
options.C: PET-CT scan
options.D: CT-guided biopsy of the nodule
options.E: Repeat CT chest in one year

correct_answer: C. PET-CT scan
why_correct: The BTS pulmonary nodule guideline uses CT surveillance for small or low-risk nodules, but when a solid nodule large enough to assess has a high Brock malignancy risk, the next step is PET-CT. The PET-CT result is fed into the Herder model to decide between biopsy, surgery or continued surveillance, and it also helps stage the disease. A 14 mm spiculated nodule in a current heavy smoker with a high Brock risk should therefore go to PET-CT. Source: British Thoracic Society Guidelines for the Investigation and Management of Pulmonary Nodules, 2015.
why_wrong: A. Only very small nodules, nodules with clearly benign features or nodules shown to be stable can be discharged, and this one is large and spiculated. B. Short-interval CT surveillance is for smaller or low-risk nodules, not one already judged high risk. D. Biopsy usually follows PET-CT and Herder assessment rather than replacing them. E. A 1-year scan is for the smallest nodules and would dangerously delay assessment of a probable cancer.
pearl: High-risk solid nodule on the BTS pathway: PET-CT next, then the Herder model decides biopsy, surgery or surveillance.
thinking: Incidental solid spiculated nodule, 14 mm  ↓  heavy current smoker, fit  ↓  radiologist: high Brock risk  ↓  PET-CT  ↓  Herder model guides biopsy, surgery or surveillance
exam_trap: Choosing CT surveillance or going straight to biopsy instead of PET-CT for a high-risk nodule.
takeaway: Solid lung nodule with a high Brock risk: PET-CT is the next investigation.
notes: Re-angled under rule 2: the AKT key depended on recalling the BTS size bands and the 10% Brock threshold. Here the radiologist states the risk is high and above the BTS threshold for further assessment, so the item tests the principle (high-risk nodule leads to PET-CT, then Herder) without recall of the cut-off; size and Brock thresholds removed from options and explanation. BTS 2015 remains the current UK guideline as far as checked. No near PLAB item tests the nodule pathway.

presentation: Incidental simple renal cyst
stem:
A 63-year-old woman has a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis after a road traffic collision, which shows no injuries. It reports an incidental 4 cm cyst in the lower pole of the left kidney. The cyst contains uniform fluid of water density, has a thin smooth wall, and has no internal septa, calcification, solid component or enhancing tissue. Her blood pressure, renal function and urine dipstick are normal. She is worried and asks whether anything needs to be done about it.

What is the most appropriate management of the cyst?

options.A: Ultrasound scan of the kidney again in one year
options.B: Suspected cancer pathway referral to urology
options.C: MRI of the kidneys for further characterisation
options.D: Radiologically guided aspiration of the cyst
options.E: Reassurance with no further follow-up

correct_answer: E. Reassurance with no further follow-up
why_correct: A renal cyst with uniform water-density fluid, a thin smooth wall and no septa, calcification or enhancing solid tissue on contrast CT is a Bosniak I simple cyst. Simple renal cysts are very common, especially with age, and are benign with no meaningful malignant potential. No imaging follow-up or referral is needed, and she can be reassured. Source: Bosniak classification of cystic renal masses, version 2019 (Silverman et al., Radiology 2019).
why_wrong: A. Interval imaging is used for Bosniak IIF cysts, not for a simple cyst. B. A suspected cancer pathway referral is for solid or complex renal masses, not a simple cyst. C. The contrast CT has already fully characterised the cyst, so MRI adds nothing. D. Aspiration is reserved for large cysts causing symptoms such as pain or obstruction.
pearl: Water density, thin wall, nothing inside: a simple (Bosniak I) renal cyst is benign and needs no follow-up.
thinking: Incidental renal cyst on contrast CT  ↓  water density, thin smooth wall, no septa, calcification or enhancement  ↓  Bosniak I simple cyst  ↓  benign  ↓  reassure, no follow-up
exam_trap: Arranging interval imaging or a urology referral 'to be safe' for a cyst already characterised as simple.
takeaway: Simple (Bosniak I) renal cyst on CT: reassure, no follow-up.
notes: New vignette: woman, CT after road traffic collision, left kidney. Rule 1: Hounsfield unit figure softened to 'water density'. Contrast CT kept because Bosniak is defined on CT/MRI. Near PLAB OG036 (simple ovarian cyst) and DR055 (gallstones) share the reassurance principle but are different organs and scenarios.

presentation: Incidental finding on a report before discharge
stem:
A 58-year-old woman was admitted with chest pain; acute coronary syndrome has been ruled out and a CT pulmonary angiogram showed no pulmonary embolism. On Friday evening, as an FY1 doctor prepares her discharge letter, she reads the final paragraph of the CT report for the first time. It describes an incidental 2.5 cm indeterminate lesion in the upper pole of the right kidney and recommends dedicated renal imaging. Nobody has discussed this with the patient, who has capacity and whose daughter is waiting to drive her home.

What should the FY1 doctor do?

options.A: Explain the finding to her and secure the follow-up plan
options.B: Leave it to the GP to act on the report sent with the letter
options.C: Discharge her and ask the consultant to write next week
options.D: Say nothing so as not to worry her over the weekend
options.E: Tell her daughter first so she can help break the news

correct_answer: A. Explain the finding to her and secure the follow-up plan
why_correct: GMC guidance requires doctors to give patients the information they want or need about their condition, including uncertainty, and to make sure information needed for ongoing care is shared, with a named clinician or team taking responsibility. The FY1 should discuss the finding with a senior, explain it to her honestly and proportionately, and make sure the recommended imaging is requested or clearly handed over, with the plan and who is responsible written in the discharge summary. Incidental findings left only in a report are a well-known cause of missed diagnoses. Source: GMC Good medical practice, 2024 (paragraphs 28 and 65).
why_wrong: B. Relying on the GP to spot a line in a copied report risks the finding being missed and passes on responsibility without a clear handover. C. Discharging her uninformed with only a promise of a future letter is not a safe follow-up plan. D. Withholding information to avoid worry is not justified for a patient with capacity and could delay a cancer diagnosis. E. Telling her daughter before her breaches confidentiality unless she has agreed to it.
pearl: If you find it, you own it until someone else clearly does: tell the patient and close the loop.
thinking: Incidental finding in a report  ↓  patient with capacity has not been told  ↓  GMC: give patients information they need and share it for ongoing care  ↓  involve a senior and tell her  ↓  arrange or hand over follow-up with named responsibility, document it
exam_trap: Assuming the GP will pick up the finding from the copied report, so the hospital need not act.
takeaway: Incidental findings must be explained to the patient and follow-up arranged with clear ownership before discharge.
notes: New vignette: woman, CTPA for chest pain, indeterminate renal lesion, Friday-evening discharge with daughter present. Duty-of-candour framing avoided as in the source (nothing has gone wrong). Near PLAB BX954 tests candour after an error, a different learning point.

presentation: Fluid-refractory septic shock on the ward
stem:
A 58-year-old woman was admitted from the emergency department with acute pyelonephritis and was given intravenous antibiotics within an hour of arrival. Five hours later she is confused. Her blood pressure is 78/40 mmHg, heart rate 128 bpm, respiratory rate 30/min and oxygen saturation 93% on supplemental oxygen, and her catheter bag holds only a few millilitres. She has already received 1 litre of crystalloid in small boluses without improvement, and the medical registrar is now with her. Her creatinine is about three times the value from a routine GP blood test last month, her platelet count is low, her bilirubin is raised and her venous lactate is 5.6 mmol/L. An ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis. Before this illness she lived independently, and no limits on her treatment have been set.

Which step should the registrar take next?

options.A: A further 2 litres of crystalloid given rapidly as boluses
options.B: Critical care referral for vasopressors and organ support
options.C: Switch antibiotics to meropenem and review the next day
options.D: IV hydrocortisone and continued care on the ward
options.E: Platelet transfusion for the thrombocytopenia

correct_answer: B. Critical care referral for vasopressors and organ support
why_correct: She has septic shock with several organs failing: circulation (hypotension despite fluids), kidneys (acute kidney injury and very low urine output), blood (low platelets), liver (raised bilirubin) and brain (confusion), with a high lactate. She has not responded to fluid resuscitation, and NICE advises seeking senior advice once 1 litre has been given without improvement, discussing vasopressors with the critical care team, and referring a high-risk patient who does not respond to treatment to critical care. Source: Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over: recognition, assessment and early management, NICE NG253, 2025 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Large further fluid boluses in fluid-refractory shock risk pulmonary oedema and delay the vasopressors she needs. C. Her antibiotics were appropriate and prompt; changing them does nothing for her failing circulation, and waiting until tomorrow is unsafe. D. Steroids are considered only in shock already needing vasopressors, and she needs critical care rather than ward care. E. The low platelets reflect sepsis-related organ dysfunction, and platelets are not transfused routinely without bleeding or a planned procedure.
pearl: Sepsis with several failing organs that does not respond to fluids is a critical care problem, not a ward problem.
thinking: Pyelonephritis with sepsis  ↓  hypotension despite 1 litre of fluid  ↓  AKI + oliguria, low platelets, raised bilirubin, confusion, high lactate  ↓  septic shock with multi-organ dysfunction, no obstruction to drain  ↓  no ceiling of care: refer to critical care for vasopressors and organ support
exam_trap: Giving more and more fluid on the ward instead of recognising fluid-refractory shock that needs vasopressors.
takeaway: Fluid-refractory sepsis with several failing organs: refer to critical care for organ support.
notes: New vignette: pyelonephritis instead of pneumonia; ultrasound showing no hydronephrosis added so source control is not a competing answer. Rule 1: creatinine, platelet and bilirubin values softened into words; lactate and the 1-litre trigger kept. Near PLAB GF040 and RES007 test the initial escalation call; here the registrar is present and the decision is critical care for fluid-refractory shock. NICE NG253 recs 1.8.11-1.8.12 re-checked 8 Oct 2026.

presentation: Severe acute pancreatitis with persistent organ failure
stem:
A 43-year-old woman is on day 4 of an admission with acute pancreatitis related to heavy alcohol use; ultrasound shows no gallstones and a normal-calibre bile duct, and her bilirubin is normal. Despite intravenous fluids, her systolic blood pressure has stayed in the low 80s for more than 48 hours. She has passed very little urine overnight and her creatinine has more than tripled since admission. She needs 3 L/min oxygen to keep her saturation at 94%. She has no fever. A contrast CT shows necrosis of about a third of the pancreas with no gas in it.

Which is the priority in her management now?

options.A: Prophylactic IV meropenem to protect the necrosis
options.B: Urgent ERCP to clear the bile duct
options.C: Open necrosectomy at an emergency laparotomy
options.D: Admission to critical care for organ support
options.E: Strict nil by mouth with parenteral nutrition

correct_answer: D. Admission to critical care for organ support
why_correct: Organ failure lasting more than 48 hours defines severe acute pancreatitis, and she has persistent circulatory and renal failure. Treatment is supportive, so the priority is admission to critical care for organ support such as vasopressors and renal replacement therapy. Sterile necrosis this early needs no specific intervention. Source: Pancreatitis, NICE NG104, 2018 (updated 2020).
why_wrong: A. NICE advises against prophylactic antimicrobials in acute pancreatitis, and there is no sign of infected necrosis. B. ERCP is for gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis or a blocked bile duct, and this is alcohol-related with a normal bilirubin and duct. C. Early open necrosectomy carries a high mortality, and sterile necrosis is not an indication for surgery. E. NICE advises enteral nutrition for severe pancreatitis, with parenteral nutrition only if enteral feeding fails or is not possible.
pearl: Severe pancreatitis is defined by organ failure lasting over 48 hours, and its treatment is organ support.
thinking: Acute pancreatitis day 4  ↓  hypotension for over 48 hours despite fluids + oliguric AKI  ↓  persistent organ failure = severe pancreatitis  ↓  sterile necrosis, no biliary obstruction  ↓  critical care for organ support
exam_trap: Reaching for antibiotics or a procedure on the pancreas when the failing organs need support first.
takeaway: Persistent organ failure in acute pancreatitis: critical care organ support; no prophylactic antibiotics.
notes: New vignette: woman, day 4, oxygen requirement and creatinine softened into words (rule 1). The 48-hour definition is mentioned in the stem description but the key does not depend on recalling it. Alcohol aetiology retained (with gallstones excluded, per NICE 1.2.1) so ERCP is clearly wrong. Near PLAB DF041 tests ARDS in pancreatitis; this tests circulatory and renal failure and the futility of antibiotics/necrosectomy/ERCP. NICE NG104 recs 1.2.3, 1.2.6, 1.2.7 re-checked 8 Oct 2026.

presentation: Ceiling of care in a frail patient with multi-organ failure
stem:
At 02:00 the critical care outreach nurse phones you, the medical FY2 on nights, about an 86-year-old retired schoolteacher admitted from his care home 4 days ago with sepsis from an infected sacral pressure ulcer. He has advanced vascular dementia, is bed-bound and fully dependent on carers, and his Clinical Frailty Scale score is 8. Despite intravenous antibiotics and fluid boluses: 'his NEWS2 has climbed to 11, his mean arterial pressure is in the low fifties, the catheter bag has been empty since teatime, tonight's kidney function is several times worse than on admission and the venous lactate keeps going up.' He is barely rousable and cannot weigh up choices about his care. His niece, his closest relative, is on the ward. There is no ReSPECT form, no advance decision to refuse treatment and no lasting power of attorney.

What should happen next regarding escalation of his care?

options.A: Ask his niece to choose whether he is ventilated in intensive care
options.B: Request intensive care admission for intubation and vasopressors
options.C: Arrange urgent haemofiltration for his kidney injury
options.D: Keep full treatment and revisit at the morning ward round
options.E: Senior best-interests ceiling of care after consulting his niece

correct_answer: E. Senior best-interests ceiling of care after consulting his niece
why_correct: He has progressive multi-organ failure despite treatment, on a background of advanced dementia and very severe frailty, so a treatment escalation decision is needed tonight. His frailty score informs but does not by itself decide this: the decision must weigh his overall condition, the likely benefits and burdens of intubation, vasopressors and renal support, and what is known of his previous wishes, values and beliefs. He lacks capacity and has no advance decision or lasting power of attorney, so under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 the senior clinician responsible for his care makes the decision in his best interests after consulting his niece about what he would have wanted, and the agreed, documented plan may set a ceiling of care with attention to symptom control. Source: Treatment and care towards the end of life: good practice in decision making, GMC, 2010 (updated 2022); Mental Capacity Act 2005, section 4.
why_wrong: A. Without a lasting power of attorney for health and welfare his niece is not the decision maker, and she must not be given the impression that she is. B. Escalating to invasive ventilation and vasopressors without weighing his frailty, wishes and likely benefit is not in his best interests by default. C. Renal replacement therapy is organ support whose appropriateness must be decided within the ceiling-of-care discussion, not started reflexively. D. He is deteriorating now, and waiting until morning risks an inappropriate emergency escalation or an unplanned death.
pearl: Relatives without a lasting power of attorney are consulted, not asked to decide.
thinking: 86, CFS 8, advanced dementia  ↓  rising NEWS2, hypotension, anuria, worsening kidneys and lactate despite treatment  ↓  weigh likely benefits and burdens of organ support, not the frailty score alone  ↓  lacks capacity, no ADRT or LPA  ↓  senior clinician decides in best interests after consulting niece, documents a ceiling of care
exam_trap: Asking the relative to choose whether he goes to intensive care, as though she were the legal decision maker.
takeaway: Frail patient with progressive multi-organ failure: senior-led ceiling-of-care decision made in his best interests after consulting family.
notes: Reworked for distance from AKT MG020 (stem Jaccard was 0.57): now a 02:00 outreach-nurse phone call to the night FY2, man of 86 with sepsis from a pressure ulcer, niece as closest relative, deterioration given in the nurse's words. Reviewer best-interests wording preserved in full (frailty score informs but does not decide; senior clinician decides after consulting family; ceiling of care with symptom control). ReSPECT is the UK emergency care and treatment plan form. Near PLAB DT017/BX950/ETH016 are different decisions.

presentation: Recognising organ dysfunction in sepsis
stem:
A 52-year-old woman attends the emergency department with 3 days of fever, productive cough and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Her temperature is 39.2°C, heart rate 108 bpm, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min and oxygen saturation 96% on air. She is fully alert. A chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation and she is started on antibiotics. Blood tests taken by her GP for a routine check 6 days ago, before she became ill, showed a normal full blood count and C-reactive protein, and a creatinine of 70 micromol/L.

Which of today's results most strongly suggests that she is developing organ dysfunction?

options.A: C-reactive protein 312 mg/L
options.B: Creatinine 214 micromol/L
options.C: White cell count 23.8 × 10⁹/L
options.D: Neutrophil count 20.9 × 10⁹/L
options.E: ESR 92 mm/hour

correct_answer: B. Creatinine 214 micromol/L
why_correct: Her creatinine has roughly tripled within a week, which is acute kidney injury and a sign that the infection is now causing hypoperfusion and organ dysfunction. NICE sepsis guidance treats acute kidney injury or a raised lactate as evidence of hypoperfusion and advises managing such patients as high risk. The other results show the size of the inflammatory response but say nothing about whether an organ is failing. Source: Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over: recognition, assessment and early management, NICE NG253, 2025 (updated 2026); Acute kidney injury: prevention, detection and management, NICE NG148, 2019.
why_wrong: A. A very high C-reactive protein reflects inflammation, not organ failure. C. A high white cell count is part of the response to infection and is not organ dysfunction. D. Neutrophilia shows a bacterial response but gives no information about organ perfusion. E. A raised ESR is a non-specific inflammatory marker and is not used to judge organ dysfunction.
pearl: Inflammatory markers show the size of the fire; creatinine, lactate, urine output, platelets, bilirubin and conscious level show which organs are burning.
thinking: Pneumonia with suspected sepsis  ↓  which result shows an organ failing, not just inflammation?  ↓  creatinine roughly tripled within a week = acute kidney injury  ↓  renal dysfunction = evidence of hypoperfusion  ↓  treat as high risk and monitor closely
exam_trap: Picking the most dramatic inflammatory number (CRP 312) as the marker of severity.
takeaway: In sepsis, acute kidney injury (or a raised lactate or low urine output) signals organ dysfunction; CRP and white cells do not.
notes: New vignette: pneumonia instead of urosepsis, with normal saturation and alert so no other organ dysfunction competes. Rule 2: the creatinine rise is made unambiguous (about threefold within a week) so the key does not hinge on recalling the exact 50%-within-7-days AKI cut-off. Lactate kept out of the options as in the source. NICE NG148 rec 1.3.1 and NG253 re-checked 8 Oct 2026.

presentation: Pyrexia of unknown origin: definition
stem:
A 31-year-old man has had fevers of 38.5–38.9°C most evenings for 12 days. He has not travelled abroad. His blood count, renal and liver function, urinalysis, urine culture, blood cultures and chest X-ray are all normal. The admitting doctor writes 'PUO' in the notes, and the consultant asks for the definition to be checked.

Which definition must be met before this label can be used?

options.A: Temperature above 37.5°C on several occasions for more than 3 weeks, undiagnosed after investigation
options.B: Temperature above 38.3°C on several occasions for more than 3 weeks, undiagnosed after investigation
options.C: Temperature above 38.3°C on several occasions for more than 1 week, undiagnosed after investigation
options.D: Temperature above 38.3°C for more than 3 weeks, whether or not any investigation has been done
options.E: Continuous temperature above 38.3°C for more than 6 months, undiagnosed after full investigation

correct_answer: B. Temperature above 38.3°C on several occasions for more than 3 weeks, undiagnosed after investigation
why_correct: Classical pyrexia of unknown origin is a temperature above 38.3°C on several occasions, in an illness lasting more than 3 weeks, with no diagnosis after appropriate investigation. His temperatures are high enough, but 12 days is too short, which is why the consultant calls the label premature. The time limit exists because many short fevers are self-limiting viral illnesses. Source: Pyrexia of unknown origin, Patient.info professional reference (reviewed 2024); Investigating and managing pyrexia of unknown origin in adults, BMJ, 2010.
why_wrong: A. A threshold of 37.5°C is too low and would label many minor fevers as PUO. C. One week is too short, and this is the error made by the admitting doctor. D. The definition requires failure to find a cause after appropriate investigation, not just a long fever. E. The fever need not be continuous, and 6 months is far longer than the 3 weeks required.
pearl: PUO = above 38.3°C, more than 3 weeks, still no answer after proper investigation.
thinking: Fever 38.5–38.9°C  ↓  only 12 days  ↓  classical PUO: above 38.3°C on several occasions  ↓  illness lasting more than 3 weeks  ↓  no cause after appropriate investigation  ↓  label premature
exam_trap: Calling any fever without an obvious source after a week 'PUO'.
takeaway: Classical PUO: above 38.3°C on several occasions, for more than 3 weeks, undiagnosed after appropriate investigation.
notes: New vignette (31-year-old man, 12 days, consultant comment); options reworded and reordered, with the 37.5°C distractor now paired with 3 weeks so temperature and duration are tested separately. Rule 2 consideration: the key is a figure-based definition, but it is the long-standing Petersdorf-Beeson definition (unchanged since 1961 in its temperature and duration elements) rather than a movable guideline cut-off, and PLAB relies on it, so it has been kept under the 'keep' tier; the variable investigation element (1 week in hospital versus 3 days/3 visits) is avoided. Reviewer may skip if the PLAB policy treats any definitional number as movable.

presentation: Prolonged fever with weight loss and lymphadenopathy
stem:
A 41-year-old woman has had 5 weeks of fevers up to 38.8°C, drenching night sweats and 6 kg weight loss. Examination shows several small, rubbery, non-tender lymph nodes in the neck and both groins, with no other abnormality. Her lymphocyte count is low, but her other blood count results are normal. Renal and liver function, urinalysis, urine culture, repeated blood cultures and chest X-ray are normal. She has never had an HIV test.

Which test should she be offered next?

options.A: Excision biopsy of a cervical lymph node
options.B: Whole-body FDG-PET-CT scan
options.C: HIV antigen and antibody blood test
options.D: Bone marrow examination
options.E: Temporal artery ultrasound

correct_answer: C. HIV antigen and antibody blood test
why_correct: Unexplained fever is an HIV indicator condition, so an HIV test should be offered early in the work-up of prolonged fever to everyone, whatever their perceived risk. Her fever, night sweats, weight loss, lymphadenopathy and lymphopenia make HIV, and HIV-related infection or lymphoma, important possibilities. A fourth-generation antigen and antibody test is simple, cheap and directs the rest of the investigation. Source: HIV testing: increasing uptake among people who may have undiagnosed HIV, NICE NG60, 2016 (updated 2025); NICE quality standard QS157, statement 3, 2017.
why_wrong: A. A node biopsy may be needed later, but only after simple non-invasive tests such as HIV serology. B. PET-CT is a later-line test and cannot replace a basic HIV test. D. Bone marrow examination is invasive and kept for later, for example unexplained cytopenias once simpler tests are done. E. Temporal artery imaging is for suspected giant cell arteritis, which is very unlikely at 41 with no headache or jaw pain.
pearl: Every patient with prolonged unexplained fever needs an HIV test: early, and without a risk assessment first.
thinking: Several weeks of fever, sweats, weight loss  ↓  lymphadenopathy + lymphopenia  ↓  first-line tests negative  ↓  unexplained fever is an HIV indicator condition  ↓  offer an HIV test now, before invasive tests
exam_trap: Jumping to biopsies or advanced imaging before a simple HIV test.
takeaway: In prolonged unexplained fever, offer an HIV test early to everyone.
notes: New vignette (41-year-old woman, cervical and inguinal nodes); options reworded, temporal artery biopsy changed to temporal artery ultrasound. Lymphocyte count softened to 'low' (rule 1). Near PLAB DR034 (oral candida, HIV test) reaches the same test from a different scenario and indicator condition, so not a repeat.

presentation: Inpatient fever with eosinophilia on new drugs
stem:
A 64-year-old woman is on day 13 of an admission for cellulitis of the leg, which has resolved after a course of flucloxacillin that finished 6 days ago. Three weeks ago, before she came into hospital, her GP started carbamazepine for newly diagnosed trigeminal neuralgia, and during the admission she was also started on lansoprazole without a clear indication. For the past 4 days she has had temperatures of 38.5–38.9°C but feels well, and her pulse is 74 bpm while febrile. There is no rash or mouth ulceration. Her eosinophil count is raised, liver function tests are normal and C-reactive protein is only mildly raised. Chest X-ray is clear, and repeated blood cultures and urine culture are negative. Her cannula sites are clean and she has no diarrhoea.

Which is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: Empirical IV piperacillin with tazobactam
options.B: Start a course of oral prednisolone
options.C: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
options.D: Give regular paracetamol and keep all her medicines going
options.E: Stop the recently started drugs and assess for DRESS

correct_answer: E. Stop the recently started drugs and assess for DRESS
why_correct: A well patient with a new inpatient fever, a relatively slow pulse, eosinophilia and no source on a thorough infection screen suggests a drug reaction; carbamazepine is a well-recognised cause of drug fever and DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms), which typically begins 2 to 8 weeks after starting the drug, as here, and the lansoprazole has no clear indication, so both should be stopped. Fever with eosinophilia can be an early hypersensitivity reaction before a rash appears, so monitoring the temperature alone is not enough: she needs reassessment of skin, mucous membranes, lymph nodes and observations, and repeat blood tests including full blood count and film, liver and renal function, and urinalysis to look for organ involvement. Escalate to a senior and dermatology if a rash, rising eosinophils or organ involvement develop, arrange an alternative for her trigeminal neuralgia, and report the reaction through the Yellow Card scheme. Source: DermNet Drug hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS); BNF carbamazepine (hypersensitivity reactions); Pyrexia of unknown origin, Patient.info professional reference (reviewed 2024).
why_wrong: A. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics in a stable patient with no source of infection obscure the diagnosis and add further drug exposure. B. Steroids can mask the cause and are not started without a diagnosis; specialists consider them if a severe hypersensitivity syndrome such as DRESS is confirmed. C. Bone marrow examination is invasive and premature before the probable culprit drugs have been stopped. D. Treating the fever while continuing the likely culprit leaves the cause in place and risks progression to DRESS.
pearl: Well, febrile, relatively bradycardic and eosinophilic on new drugs: stop what is new and non-essential, and look actively for DRESS.
thinking: Inpatient fever for 4 days  ↓  well, relative bradycardia, eosinophilia  ↓  infection screen negative, cellulitis resolved  ↓  recently started carbamazepine + lansoprazole  ↓  drug fever or early DRESS  ↓  stop new drugs, reassess skin and organs, repeat bloods, escalate if worsening
exam_trap: Starting broad-spectrum antibiotics for every inpatient fever without looking at the drug chart.
takeaway: Unexplained inpatient fever with eosinophilia on new drugs: stop the likely culprits and assess for DRESS and organ involvement, not just the temperature.
notes: New vignette: culprit changed from allopurinol to carbamazepine (started for trigeminal neuralgia), cellulitis instead of pneumonia, lansoprazole as the non-essential drug. Reviewer-requested DRESS assessment wording preserved in the key and explanation (skin, mucosa, nodes, FBC/film, LFT, renal function, urinalysis, escalation, Yellow Card). Carbamazepine as a DRESS cause should be checked against the BNF/MHRA by the reviewer (BNF lists hypersensitivity syndrome/DRESS among its serious reactions; HLA-B*1502/A*3101 warnings relate to SJS/TEN and DRESS). Eosinophil and CRP values softened into words (rule 1). Near PLAB RHE017 (starting allopurinol) is unrelated.

presentation: Pyrexia of unknown origin after negative first-line tests
stem:
The infectious diseases registrar reads you a GP referral letter for a 47-year-old lorry driver: 'Evening temperatures to 38.8°C most days for five weeks, sweats, tiredness and about 4 kg of unintended weight loss. Repeated histories and examinations have not found a source and I hear no murmur.' He is well enough to be seen in clinic and is maintaining his intake. The letter lists his results: mild normocytic anaemia, normal white count and platelets, CRP moderately raised; kidney, liver and thyroid tests normal; urine dip and culture negative; three blood culture sets, HIV and an autoimmune screen negative; chest radiograph and transthoracic echo unremarkable. He has not been abroad and has no contact with animals.

What should be arranged next?

options.A: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis with contrast
options.B: Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone
options.C: A trial of oral prednisolone
options.D: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy with culture
options.E: Laparoscopy with peritoneal sampling

correct_answer: A. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis with contrast
why_correct: He now meets the definition of classical pyrexia of unknown origin, is stable and has raised inflammatory markers. With the history, repeated examination, baseline bloods and microbiology completed and offering no clue to direct a specific test, the most useful next step is cross-sectional imaging of the chest, abdomen and pelvis to look for occult infection such as an abscess, malignancy such as lymphoma, or inflammatory disease, with FDG-PET-CT to follow if CT does not help. Empirical antibiotics and steroids are avoided in stable patients because they can mask the cause and delay diagnosis. Source: Investigating and managing pyrexia of unknown origin in adults, BMJ, 2010; Pyrexia of unknown origin, Patient.info professional reference (reviewed 2024).
why_wrong: B. Empirical antibiotics in a stable, non-neutropenic patient rarely cure PUO and can make cultures negative and delay the diagnosis. C. A steroid trial can mask lymphoma, infection and vasculitis and is discouraged without a diagnosis. D. Bone marrow biopsy is invasive and kept for significant unexplained cytopenias or for when imaging has not found a cause, and his mild normocytic anaemia fits chronic inflammation. E. Surgical exploration is a last resort, not a step before non-invasive imaging.
pearl: In stable PUO, investigate before you treat: CT first, then PET-CT if needed, not empirical antibiotics or steroids.
thinking: Fever above 38.3°C for 5 weeks, stable  ↓  history, repeated examination, bloods, cultures, HIV, autoimmune screen, CXR and echo unrevealing  ↓  raised CRP, mild anaemia, no localising clue  ↓  classical PUO  ↓  CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for occult infection, malignancy or inflammation  ↓  avoid empirical antibiotics or steroids
exam_trap: Starting empirical antibiotics or steroids in a stable patient to 'see if it settles'.
takeaway: Stable PUO with an unrevealing first-line assessment: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis to look for an occult cause, then PET-CT if needed.
notes: Reworked for distance from AKT MG025 (stem Jaccard was 0.52): now a GP referral letter read out by the ID registrar for a 47-year-old lorry driver seen in clinic, results given as the letter's list. Discriminators kept: stable, no focus, no murmur plus normal echo, full first-line microbiology/serology negative, no travel or animal exposure. PET-CT kept out of the options as in the source. Near PLAB GF045 has CT already negative (different decision point).

presentation: Papilloedema with suspected IIH — image before lumbar puncture
stem:
A 30-year-old woman is referred to the acute medical unit by her optometrist, who saw swelling of both optic discs at a routine eye test. For a month she has had a daily headache that is worse when she lies down and when she coughs. She has gained weight over the past year and is otherwise well, with no fever, neck stiffness or focal neurological signs. The medical registrar suspects idiopathic intracranial hypertension (raised brain pressure with no identifiable cause) and suggests a lumbar puncture this afternoon to measure the opening pressure.
