No brain imaging has been done.

What should be the next investigation?

options.A: Lumbar puncture with opening pressure this afternoon
options.B: Urgent same-day brain imaging
options.C: Routine outpatient MRI via the neurology clinic
options.D: Start acetazolamide and review in clinic
options.E: Formal visual fields and optic disc photographs

correct_answer: B. Urgent same-day brain imaging
why_correct: Bilateral optic disc swelling with a headache worse on lying down and coughing is papilloedema from raised intracranial pressure until proven otherwise. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is a diagnosis of exclusion, so she first needs urgent brain imaging the same day, ideally including the venous sinuses, to exclude a mass lesion, hydrocephalus or venous sinus thrombosis. Lumbar puncture comes only after imaging has excluded a space-occupying lesion, because it can precipitate brain herniation. Source: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension consensus guidelines (Mollan et al., JNNP, 2018).
why_wrong: A. Doing a lumbar puncture before imaging risks herniation if a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus is present, even when IIH seems likely. C. Papilloedema with features of raised pressure is an emergency, so a routine outpatient scan is far too slow. D. Acetazolamide treats confirmed IIH; starting it before imaging and lumbar puncture skips the exclusion of dangerous causes. E. Visual fields and disc photographs help monitoring but do not find the cause and should not delay imaging.
pearl: Even when the story shouts IIH, papilloedema means scan the brain first and needle the spine second.
thinking: Daily headache worse lying down and coughing  ↓  bilateral disc swelling = papilloedema  ↓  raised intracranial pressure until proven otherwise  ↓  IIH is a diagnosis of exclusion  ↓  urgent same-day brain imaging (with venous imaging), then lumbar puncture
exam_trap: Going straight to lumbar puncture because the patient fits the typical IIH profile, before any brain imaging.
takeaway: Papilloedema needs urgent same-day brain imaging before any lumbar puncture, even when IIH is suspected.
notes: Re-angled to a patient who fits the IIH profile, where the trap is an early diagnostic lumbar puncture, so it is distinct from NEU095 (CT already normal, LP next) and NEU118 (older patient with a focal deficit, imaging). Same learning point and key as MG026.

presentation: Papilloedema versus optic neuritis — distinguishing features
stem:
A 34-year-old man is referred to the eye clinic because his optician noticed optic disc swelling at a routine sight test. He has had mild headaches for about two months. The ophthalmology registrar needs to decide whether the swelling is more likely to be due to raised intracranial pressure or to inflammation of the optic nerve.

Which examination finding would most favour papilloedema over optic neuritis?

options.A: Aching in the eye when looking to the side
options.B: Reduced perception of the colour red
options.C: A pupil that dilates on the swinging-light test
options.D: Normal visual acuity and colour vision
options.E: A dense central blind area in the visual field

correct_answer: D. Normal visual acuity and colour vision
why_correct: In early papilloedema the optic nerve fibres still conduct normally, so visual acuity, colour vision and pupil reactions are usually preserved and the main field change is an enlarged blind spot. Optic neuritis damages the nerve itself, giving reduced acuity, red desaturation, a central scotoma, a relative afferent pupillary defect and often pain on eye movement. Papilloedema is also usually bilateral, whereas optic neuritis usually affects one eye. Source: GPnotebook, Comparison of papilloedema and papillitis (2025).
why_wrong: A. Pain on eye movement is a typical feature of optic neuritis. B. Red desaturation reflects optic nerve dysfunction, which points to optic neuritis. C. A pupil that dilates on the swinging-light test is a relative afferent pupillary defect, a sign of a damaged optic nerve as in optic neuritis. E. A central scotoma is the classic field defect of optic neuritis; papilloedema enlarges the blind spot instead.
pearl: Swollen discs that still see well suggest papilloedema; a swollen disc that sees badly suggests optic neuritis.
thinking: Optic disc swelling  ↓  is optic nerve function preserved?  ↓  normal acuity, colour vision and pupils  ↓  nerve working despite swelling  ↓  papilloedema (raised intracranial pressure), not optic neuritis
exam_trap: Assuming that swollen discs with good vision cannot be serious — preserved acuity is exactly what early papilloedema looks like.
takeaway: Papilloedema is usually bilateral, with normal acuity, colour vision and pupils early on.
notes: New vignette (man referred to eye clinic by optician). Options reworded as examination findings; the key is now framed as normal acuity and colour vision in each eye, which also signals bilateral preserved function. CKS optic neuritis was not fetchable for the source writer; features carried over from GPnotebook and LITFL.

presentation: Transient visual obscurations — symptom of papilloedema
stem:
A 19-year-old university student who is overweight has had headaches most days for two months. When she bends to pick up books from the floor and then straightens up, the sight in both eyes goes dark for a couple of seconds and then comes back completely. She sees no zigzag lines or flashing lights and has no floaters. Her blood pressure does not fall when she stands, and her visual acuity is normal.

What is the most likely explanation for these episodes?

options.A: Visual aura of migraine affecting both eyes
options.B: Orthostatic hypotension when she stands upright
options.C: Retinal emboli arising from the carotid arteries
options.D: Transient visual obscurations of papilloedema
options.E: Posterior vitreous detachment in both eyes

correct_answer: D. Transient visual obscurations of papilloedema
why_correct: Brief dimming or blacking out of vision lasting seconds, often brought on by bending or changing posture, describes transient visual obscurations. They occur when a swollen optic disc is briefly under-perfused and are a symptom of papilloedema. In a young overweight woman with daily headaches the likely cause is idiopathic intracranial hypertension, and she needs fundoscopy and urgent assessment. Source: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension consensus guidelines (Mollan et al., JNNP, 2018).
why_wrong: A. Migraine aura builds up over minutes, usually with positive features such as zigzags, rather than lasting seconds on posture change. B. Orthostatic hypotension is unlikely because her blood pressure does not fall on standing. C. Retinal emboli (amaurosis fugax) usually affect one eye for minutes in older people with vascular risk factors. E. Posterior vitreous detachment causes floaters and flashes, not seconds-long dimming of both eyes.
pearl: Seconds-long greying of vision on bending or standing means examine the optic discs.
thinking: Seconds-long bilateral dimming of vision  ↓  brought on by bending and straightening  ↓  no postural blood pressure drop  ↓  transient visual obscurations  ↓  papilloedema (likely IIH): urgent fundoscopy
exam_trap: Putting posture-related visual dimming down to low blood pressure without looking at the optic discs.
takeaway: Transient visual obscurations are a red-flag symptom of papilloedema.
notes: New vignette (student, bending to pick up books). BMI figure softened to 'overweight'. Same key and learning point as MG028.

presentation: Fundoscopic features of papilloedema
stem:
A 52-year-old man comes to the emergency department with three weeks of headache that is worse when he bends over or strains, and he vomited once this morning. His vision seems normal to him. The foundation doctor dims the lights and examines both fundi with an ophthalmoscope.

Which fundoscopic appearance would most strongly suggest papilloedema?

options.A: Cupped discs with a thin neuroretinal rim
options.B: Blurred, raised disc margins with peripapillary haemorrhages
options.C: Flat, pale optic discs with crisp margins
options.D: A pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula
options.E: Silver-wiring of arterioles and arteriovenous nipping at crossings

correct_answer: B. Blurred, raised disc margins with peripapillary haemorrhages
why_correct: Papilloedema is swelling of the optic disc caused by raised intracranial pressure. The disc margins become blurred and the disc raised, the retinal veins engorge and flame-shaped haemorrhages may appear around the disc, usually in both eyes. Loss of spontaneous venous pulsation supports the picture but is also seen in some healthy people, so the diagnosis rests on the overall disc appearance in a patient whose symptoms suggest raised pressure. Source: GPnotebook, Papilloedema (2025); Life in the Fast Lane, That optic disc doesn't look right (2025).
why_wrong: A. A large cup with a thin rim is the appearance of glaucoma. C. A pale, flat disc with sharp margins is optic atrophy, which may follow long-standing papilloedema but is not active swelling. D. A cherry-red spot on a pale retina is central retinal artery occlusion, which causes sudden painless loss of vision. E. Silver-wiring and arteriovenous nipping are signs of chronic hypertensive retinopathy, not raised intracranial pressure.
pearl: Blurred, raised margins with haemorrhages around the disc make the case for papilloedema; absent venous pulsation supports it but never proves it alone.
thinking: Headache worse on bending and straining + vomiting  ↓  suspect raised intracranial pressure  ↓  examine the discs  ↓  blurred raised margins, engorged veins, peripapillary haemorrhages  ↓  papilloedema
exam_trap: Mistaking a pale, sharp-edged disc (optic atrophy) for active disc swelling.
takeaway: Papilloedema shows blurred, raised disc margins with engorged veins and haemorrhages around the disc.
notes: Dropped at independent check: Duplicate of live BX184: same scenario (a patient with a raised-ICP picture has fundoscopy) and same learning point (recognising papilloedema: swollen discs with blurred margins), and it even shares the cherry-red spot and pale-disc distractors. With absent venous pulsation correctly dropped from the key, nothing separates it from BX184. No re-angle keeps the source's learning point without repeating it.

presentation: Unilateral tinnitus with asymmetric hearing loss — imaging when MRI is contraindicated
stem:
A 57-year-old woman is seen in the ENT (ear, nose and throat) clinic with eight months of a constant hissing noise in her left ear, muffled hearing on that side and occasional unsteadiness. The tinnitus does not pulse with her heartbeat. Many years ago she had an intracranial aneurysm treated with a metal clip, and neuroradiology have confirmed that the clip is not MRI-safe, so she cannot have an MRI scan. Otoscopy is normal, facial movement is symmetrical, and her audiogram shows a left sensorineural hearing loss that is clearly worse than the right across adjacent frequencies.

As MRI cannot be performed, which investigation should be arranged?

options.A: Non-contrast CT of the head and posterior fossa
options.B: CT of the internal auditory meati with contrast
options.C: Repeat the audiogram in a year before imaging
options.D: Duplex ultrasound of both carotid arteries
options.E: Auditory brainstem response testing instead of imaging

correct_answer: B. CT of the internal auditory meati with contrast
why_correct: Unilateral non-pulsatile tinnitus with an asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss and unsteadiness raises the possibility of a vestibular schwannoma, so the internal auditory meati need imaging. MRI of the internal auditory meati is first-line whenever it can be done. For people who are unable to have MRI, as here because of a non-MRI-safe aneurysm clip, NICE recommends contrast-enhanced CT of the internal auditory meati instead. Source: Tinnitus: assessment and management (NICE NG155, 2020, rec 1.4.6); Hearing loss in adults (NICE NG98, 2018).
why_wrong: A. A non-contrast CT of the head is not designed to show a small tumour inside the internal auditory canal. C. Waiting a year delays the diagnosis of a possible tumour when imaging is already indicated. D. Carotid duplex is relevant to pulsatile tinnitus, and her tinnitus is non-pulsatile. E. Auditory brainstem response testing is less sensitive than imaging for small tumours and does not replace it.
pearl: MRI not possible? Contrast-enhanced CT of the internal auditory meati is the NICE alternative.
thinking: Unilateral non-pulsatile tinnitus + asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss  ↓  possible vestibular schwannoma  ↓  MRI of internal auditory meati is first-line  ↓  MRI contraindicated (non-MRI-safe aneurysm clip)  ↓  contrast-enhanced CT of the internal auditory meati
exam_trap: Picking a plain non-contrast CT head, which can miss a small tumour in the internal auditory canal.
takeaway: Image unilateral tinnitus with asymmetric hearing loss with MRI of the internal auditory meati, or contrast-enhanced CT if MRI is not possible.
notes: New vignette: the MRI contraindication is now a non-MRI-safe intracranial aneurysm clip confirmed by neuroradiology (was a non-conditional pacemaker confirmed by cardiology). MRI-contraindication framing kept explicit in the stem as the reviewer required. The 25 dB figure was softened to 'clearly worse ... across adjacent frequencies'. NG155 1.4.6 wording ('If they are unable to have MRI (IAM), offer contrast-enhanced CT (IAM)') re-checked today. Distinct from DF009 (MRI available).

presentation: Pulsatile tinnitus with headache — check fundi for idiopathic intracranial hypertension
stem:
A 31-year-old woman who has put on a lot of weight over the past year sees her GP. For six weeks she has noticed a rhythmic whooshing, in time with her pulse, mainly in her right ear and loudest when she lies in bed at night. She also has headaches on waking that get worse when she coughs. Her hearing is normal and she has no dizziness or ear discharge. Both eardrums look normal.

Which examination should the GP prioritise at this appointment?

options.A: Listening over the neck for a carotid bruit
options.B: Rinne and Weber tests of both ears
options.C: Dix–Hallpike positional test
options.D: Fundoscopy of both optic discs
options.E: Palpation of both temporal arteries

correct_answer: D. Fundoscopy of both optic discs
why_correct: Pulsatile tinnitus with a headache that is worse on waking and on coughing, in a young woman with recent weight gain, strongly suggests idiopathic intracranial hypertension. The key examination is fundoscopy, because papilloedema confirms raised intracranial pressure and puts her sight at risk. If papilloedema is found she needs same-day referral for brain imaging and specialist assessment. Source: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension consensus guidelines (Mollan et al., JNNP, 2018); Tinnitus: assessment and management (NICE NG155, 2020).
why_wrong: A. Listening for a bruit is reasonable in pulsatile tinnitus, but it does not assess the raised intracranial pressure suggested by her headache. B. Tuning fork tests assess hearing loss, which she does not have. C. The Dix–Hallpike test looks for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, and she has no vertigo. E. Temporal artery palpation is for giant cell arteritis, which is very unlikely at her age.
pearl: Pulsatile tinnitus plus headache in a young woman: look at the optic discs first.
thinking: Pulsatile tinnitus + headache worse on waking and coughing  ↓  young woman with weight gain  ↓  suspect idiopathic intracranial hypertension  ↓  fundoscopy for papilloedema  ↓  if present: same-day referral for imaging
exam_trap: Treating pulsatile tinnitus as purely an ear or vascular problem and forgetting to examine the fundi.
takeaway: In pulsatile tinnitus with headache, always examine the fundi for papilloedema.
notes: New vignette (mainly right-sided pulsatile tinnitus, cough headache). BMI figure removed and replaced with recent weight gain. Same key as MG031; distinct from NEU032/NEU072 (diagnosis after imaging and LP).

presentation: Bilateral tinnitus with gradual hearing loss — audiological assessment
stem:
A 69-year-old retired teacher sees her GP about a buzzing noise in both ears that has been present for about 18 months. Her family say she often mishears them, and she finds it hard to follow conversation in restaurants. The noise is the same on both sides, does not pulse and is not affecting her sleep or mood. She has no dizziness, earache, discharge or neurological symptoms. Both ear canals are free of wax and both eardrums look normal.

What should the GP do next?

options.A: MRI scan of the internal auditory meati
options.B: A trial of betahistine
options.C: Same-day referral to the on-call ENT team
options.D: Reassurance and discharge with no follow-up
options.E: Referral for audiological assessment

correct_answer: E. Referral for audiological assessment
why_correct: Bilateral, symmetrical tinnitus with gradually worsening hearing in an older adult is most likely due to age-related hearing loss. NICE recommends offering an audiological assessment to everyone with tinnitus, and adults with hearing difficulty should have wax and infection excluded and then be referred for audiological assessment. Hearing aids, if needed, often reduce the tinnitus as well as improving communication. Source: Tinnitus: assessment and management (NICE NG155, 2020); Hearing loss in adults (NICE NG98, 2018).
why_wrong: A. MRI of the internal auditory meati is for unilateral or asymmetric tinnitus or hearing loss, or tinnitus with neurological or otological features, none of which she has. B. NICE advises against betahistine for tinnitus. C. Immediate or same-day referral is for red flags such as sudden hearing loss, which she does not have. D. Reassurance alone leaves a hearing loss that is affecting her daily life unassessed and untreated.
pearl: Symmetrical tinnitus with gradual hearing loss needs a hearing test, not a scan.
thinking: Bilateral symmetrical non-pulsatile tinnitus  ↓  gradual hearing difficulty in an older adult  ↓  no red flags, no wax  ↓  likely age-related hearing loss  ↓  audiological assessment (hearing aids if needed)
exam_trap: Requesting an MRI for symmetrical tinnitus with no red flags.
takeaway: Offer an audiological assessment to people with tinnitus; image only when features suggest a structural cause.
notes: New vignette (older woman, restaurants). Option C reworded to same-day ENT referral; the explanation no longer quotes the 30-day sudden-loss window from NG98 (deep reference figure). NG155 1.4.1 re-checked today.

presentation: Cisplatin ototoxicity — new tinnitus and high-frequency hearing loss
stem:
A 23-year-old man with metastatic testicular germ cell cancer is receiving chemotherapy with bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin. Before his third cycle he tells the oncology nurse that he has developed a high-pitched ringing in both ears and struggles to follow conversation in noisy places. An audiogram shows a new high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in both ears compared with his test before treatment. His antiemetics are ondansetron and metoclopramide.

Which drug is the most likely cause?

options.A: Cisplatin
options.B: Bleomycin
options.C: Etoposide
options.D: Ondansetron
options.E: Metoclopramide

correct_answer: A. Cisplatin
why_correct: Cisplatin causes cumulative, dose-related ototoxicity that presents with tinnitus and high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, often in both ears. Audiometry is advised before treatment and when hearing symptoms develop, and significant deterioration may lead to a dose change or stopping the drug. The oncology team must review this before the next cycle is given. Source: Cisplatin 1 mg/ml Sterile Concentrate Summary of Product Characteristics (emc, current).
why_wrong: B. Bleomycin is known for lung fibrosis and skin changes, not hearing loss. C. Etoposide mainly causes bone marrow suppression and hair loss rather than ototoxicity. D. Ondansetron commonly causes headache and constipation but is not ototoxic. E. Metoclopramide can cause extrapyramidal effects, especially in young people, but not sensorineural hearing loss.
pearl: Platinum chemotherapy plus new tinnitus means cisplatin ototoxicity until proven otherwise.
thinking: New bilateral tinnitus + high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss  ↓  during combination chemotherapy  ↓  which drug is ototoxic?  ↓  cisplatin (cumulative, dose-related)  ↓  audiometry and oncology review before the next cycle
exam_trap: Being distracted by bleomycin, the drug most often linked with serious toxicity in this regimen, when its toxicity is in the lungs.
takeaway: Cisplatin is ototoxic: new tinnitus or high-frequency hearing loss needs audiometry and an oncology review.
notes: New vignette: young man on BEP for testicular cancer (was bladder cancer on gemcitabine/cisplatin). Distractors changed to bleomycin, etoposide and metoclopramide. Same key.

presentation: Tinnitus-related distress with high suicide risk — crisis mental health referral
stem:
A 61-year-old widow who lives alone sees her GP about loud tinnitus in her left ear that has troubled her for a year. She says the noise never stops, she barely sleeps and she can no longer face it. On direct questioning she says she has been saving up her amitriptyline tablets, has written letters to her children and intends to take all the tablets tonight. She is calm, not intoxicated, and has no other ear or neurological symptoms.

What should the GP do now?

options.A: Routine referral for tinnitus-focused CBT
options.B: Immediate crisis mental health team referral
options.C: Start mirtazapine and book a review next week
options.D: Urgent ENT appointment within two weeks
options.E: Referral to audiology for sound therapy

correct_answer: B. Immediate crisis mental health team referral
why_correct: She has a specific plan, the means already stored, a set time, final letters written and she lives alone, which together indicate a high risk of suicide. NICE recommends immediate referral to a crisis mental health team for people with tinnitus associated with a high risk of suicide, with a safe place provided while they wait. In practice she should not be left alone while this is arranged, and removing her access to the stored tablets should be discussed and agreed with her (involving family if she consents). Tinnitus care can continue once her immediate safety is secured. Source: Tinnitus: assessment and management (NICE NG155, 2020, rec 1.2.1); Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence (NICE NG225, 2022, safety planning and restricting access to means).
why_wrong: A. Tinnitus-focused CBT helps longer-term distress but cannot manage an immediate risk to her life. C. Starting an antidepressant with a review next week leaves her unsafe tonight, and she is already stockpiling medication. D. An urgent ENT appointment addresses the ear, not the imminent suicide risk. E. Audiology sound therapy does nothing for an immediate threat to her life.
pearl: Tinnitus with a suicide plan is a psychiatric emergency first and an ear problem second.
thinking: Distressing tinnitus  ↓  plan, stored means, set time, letters, lives alone  ↓  high suicide risk  ↓  immediate crisis mental health team referral; keep her safe and restrict means  ↓  continue tinnitus care afterwards
exam_trap: Focusing on treating the tinnitus and referring routinely while missing an imminent suicide risk.
takeaway: Tinnitus with high suicide risk needs immediate referral to a crisis mental health team.
notes: New vignette (widow living alone, stored amitriptyline, letters written). Reviewer-required safety wording kept: not left alone, safe place while waiting, agreed restriction of access to means. NG155 1.2.1 re-checked today.

presentation: Cervical radiculopathy — C6 root
stem:
A physiotherapist writes to the GP about a 29-year-old female indoor rock climber. In her own words: 'Whenever I tip my head back to look up the wall, an electric shock runs from the left of my neck down the outside of my forearm into my thumb, and my thumb and pointer finger are permanently tingly.' The physiotherapist records that Spurling's test reproduces the arm pain on the left. Deltoid power is full. Wrist extensors and elbow flexors are mildly weak on the left. The left biceps and brachioradialis jerks are depressed, while the triceps jerks are normal and equal. There is a patch of reduced pinprick over the left thumb and index finger. Both legs are neurologically normal and she walks normally.

Which spinal root is the physiotherapist most likely to be describing?

options.A: Fifth cervical root (C5)
options.B: Seventh cervical root (C7)
options.C: Eighth cervical root (C8)
options.D: Sixth cervical root (C6)
options.E: First thoracic root (T1)

correct_answer: D. Sixth cervical root (C6)
why_correct: Sensory change in the thumb and index finger, weakness of wrist extension and elbow flexion, and depressed biceps and brachioradialis (supinator) reflexes localise to the C6 root, and a positive Spurling's test supports a cervical radiculopathy. Full deltoid power argues against C5, and a normal triceps jerk argues against C7. Source: Cervical radiculopathy (Clinical Intelligence), British Journal of General Practice, 2018.
why_wrong: A. A C5 lesion weakens shoulder abduction and causes numbness over the lateral upper arm, and her deltoid power is full. B. A C7 lesion weakens elbow extension, depresses the triceps jerk and affects the middle finger. C. A C8 lesion weakens finger flexion and causes numbness of the little finger and medial forearm. E. A T1 lesion weakens the small muscles of the hand and causes numbness over the medial arm.
pearl: C6 is the 'six-shooter' root: thumb and index finger sensation, wrist extension and the supinator jerk.
thinking: Neck extension sends pain into the arm, Spurling positive = radiculopathy  ↓  thumb and index finger tingling  ↓  weak wrist extension and elbow flexion, deltoid full  ↓  biceps and brachioradialis jerks down, triceps normal  ↓  C6 root
exam_trap: Choosing C5 because the biceps jerk is depressed, ignoring the full deltoid power and the thumb symptoms.
takeaway: Thumb tingling, weak wrist extension and a depressed supinator jerk localise to C6.
notes: Reworked for distance from AKT MG035 (stem Jaccard was 0.60): now a physiotherapist's letter about a 29-year-old female climber, with symptoms in her own words and a positive Spurling's test added. Spurling's test (neck extension/rotation with axial load reproducing radicular arm pain) is a standard provocative test for cervical radiculopathy (BJGP 2018; NICE CKS Neck pain - cervical radiculopathy). Same key (C6).

presentation: Foot drop — L5 radiculopathy vs common peroneal palsy
stem:
A 58-year-old man has had three weeks of his left foot slapping on the ground when he walks. He has lost a lot of weight since weight-loss surgery six months ago and often sits with his legs crossed at his desk. He has also had intermittent aching in his lower back. Examination shows weak left ankle dorsiflexion and big toe extension, with reduced sensation over the dorsum of the left foot. The examining doctor wants to decide whether this is an L5 root lesion or a common peroneal nerve palsy at the fibular head.

Which additional examination finding would most strongly favour an L5 root lesion?

options.A: Weakness of ankle eversion
options.B: Tinel's sign over the fibular head
options.C: Numbness only in the first web space
options.D: A preserved ankle reflex
options.E: Weakness of ankle inversion

correct_answer: E. Weakness of ankle inversion
why_correct: Ankle inversion is produced mainly by tibialis posterior, which is supplied by the tibial nerve but shares the L5 root with the dorsiflexors. Weak inversion therefore cannot be explained by a common peroneal nerve palsy and points to the L5 root; weak hip abduction (gluteus medius, superior gluteal nerve) has the same meaning. A common peroneal palsy, made more likely here by weight loss and leg crossing, spares inversion and hip abduction. Source: Mermelstein, Barbosa and Kaski, Neurological gait assessment, Practical Neurology 2024 (with published correction); Foot drop, WikiMSK.
why_wrong: A. Eversion is supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve from L5, so it is weak in both a common peroneal palsy and an L5 lesion. B. Tingling on tapping over the fibular head points to compression of the common peroneal nerve there, not to the L5 root. C. Numbness confined to the first web space is the territory of the deep peroneal nerve and suggests a peripheral nerve lesion rather than a root lesion. D. The ankle reflex (S1) is usually preserved in both an L5 lesion and a common peroneal palsy.
pearl: In foot drop, test inversion and hip abduction: if either is weak, think L5 root rather than the fibular head.
thinking: Foot drop with dorsal foot numbness  ↓  risk factors for both peroneal palsy (weight loss, leg crossing) and L5 (back pain)  ↓  which muscle shares L5 but not the peroneal nerve?  ↓  tibialis posterior (inversion) and gluteus medius (hip abduction)  ↓  weak inversion = L5 root
exam_trap: Choosing eversion weakness, which occurs in both lesions and cannot tell them apart.
takeaway: Foot drop with weak ankle inversion or hip abduction points to L5, not the common peroneal nerve.
notes: Re-angled to avoid duplicating BX1058, which already gives the full L5 picture (foot drop plus weak inversion and hip abduction) and asks for the lesion site. This version gives an ambiguous foot drop with risk factors for both lesions and asks which finding discriminates; the learning point (inversion/hip abduction separate L5 from common peroneal palsy) and the anatomical facts are unchanged from MG036. Power grades removed.

presentation: Cervical radiculopathy without red flags — initial management
stem:
A 38-year-old delivery driver sees his GP with two weeks of right-sided neck pain spreading down the back of his arm, with occasional tingling in his fingers. He feels well otherwise and has had no injury, fever, weight loss or previous cancer. Examination of the arms shows normal power, reflexes and sensation. His hands are not clumsy, his walking is normal and he has no bladder or bowel symptoms. Regular paracetamol and naproxen are easing the pain.

Which is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Analgesia, stay active, review if not settling
options.B: Urgent MRI scan of the cervical spine this week
options.C: Plain radiographs of the cervical spine
options.D: Same-day referral to the on-call spinal surgeons
options.E: A soft collar with rest until the pain has gone

correct_answer: A. Analgesia, stay active, review if not settling
why_correct: This is a likely cervical radiculopathy with no neurological deficit and no red flags, and most cases settle over a few weeks. Initial management is conservative: analgesia, advice to keep active and physiotherapy if needed. He should be safety-netted to return urgently if he develops weakness, numbness, hand clumsiness, difficulty walking, bladder or bowel symptoms, fever or weight loss. Imaging or specialist referral is considered if symptoms persist despite several weeks of conservative care, sooner if there is a neurological deficit, and urgently if there are red flags or features of myelopathy. Source: Cervical radiculopathy (Clinical Intelligence), British Journal of General Practice, 2018.
why_wrong: B. MRI is not needed yet because there are no red flags or deficit, and incidental degenerative changes are common. C. Plain radiographs cannot show nerve root compression and are not recommended for radiculopathy. D. Urgent surgical referral is for suspected myelopathy, progressive deficit or red flags, none of which he has. E. Immobilisation in a collar and prolonged rest are not recommended; staying active helps recovery.
pearl: Radicular arm pain alone usually settles; progressive deficit, myelopathy or red flags are what need urgent action.
thinking: Neck pain with radicular arm symptoms  ↓  normal power, reflexes and sensation  ↓  no red flags or myelopathy features  ↓  good natural history  ↓  conservative care with safety-netting; refer if not settling
exam_trap: Ordering an MRI for every patient with arm pain, even without deficit or red flags.
takeaway: Cervical radiculopathy without deficit or red flags: manage conservatively first and refer if it does not settle.
notes: New vignette (male driver). The 4–6 week review interval was softened to 'review if not settling' (referral timing is a supporting threshold, not the point). Vignette kept free of motor deficit, as in the reviewed source.

presentation: Sciatica — S1 root examination findings
stem:
At handover in the emergency department, your colleague tells you about a 58-year-old taxi driver in cubicle 6: 'Sciatica, left side, ten days, came on lifting a suitcase into the boot. He says his heel and little toe are numb and he can't press the accelerator properly. On the left he manages three single-leg calf raises against fifteen on the right, and I couldn't get the ankle jerk even with reinforcement. Patellar jerks are normal and symmetrical. Tibialis anterior and big-toe extension are full power. Reduced pinprick over the sole and lateral border of the foot. Saddle sensation intact, passing urine normally, no bowel change.'

Which root is most likely to be compressed?

options.A: Fourth lumbar root (L4)
options.B: Fifth lumbar root (L5)
options.C: First sacral root (S1)
options.D: Third lumbar root (L3)
options.E: Both L5 and S1 roots

correct_answer: C. First sacral root (S1)
why_correct: Weak plantar flexion (few calf raises, difficulty pressing a pedal), an absent ankle jerk and numbness over the heel, sole and lateral border of the foot are the classic S1 findings. Full tibialis anterior and big-toe extension power argue against L5, and normal patellar jerks argue against L3 and L4. Source: MSD Manual Professional, Symptoms of common radiculopathies by cord level; Foot drop, WikiMSK.
why_wrong: A. An L4 lesion weakens knee extension, reduces the knee jerk and causes numbness over the medial shin. B. An L5 lesion weakens dorsiflexion and big-toe extension and causes numbness over the dorsum of the foot, with reflexes usually normal. D. An L3 lesion weakens hip flexion and knee extension, with a reduced knee jerk and anterior thigh numbness. E. A combined L5 and S1 lesion would also weaken dorsiflexion and big-toe extension, which are full power here.
pearl: S1: stand on tiptoe, tap the Achilles tendon, touch the sole and little-toe side.
thinking: Radicular leg pain with numb heel and little toe  ↓  weak plantar flexion (calf raises, accelerator)  ↓  absent ankle jerk, patellar jerks normal  ↓  dorsiflexion and big-toe extension full  ↓  S1 root
exam_trap: Choosing L5 because the word 'sciatica' is used, without matching the weakness and reflex to the root.
takeaway: Weak plantar flexion, an absent ankle jerk and lateral foot numbness mean S1.
notes: Reworked for distance from AKT MG038 (stem Jaccard was 0.57): now an ED colleague's handover about a 58-year-old taxi driver, findings as the colleague's spoken summary, with the patient's own complaint (cannot press the accelerator). Cauda equina red flags still explicitly absent. Distinct from BX1021 (asks which sign, not which root) and BX982 (history only). Same key (S1).

presentation: Polyhydramnios with a large fetus — check for gestational diabetes
stem:
A 36-year-old woman in her second pregnancy attends antenatal clinic at 32 weeks. At booking she had no risk factors for gestational diabetes, so no glucose test was arranged. Her fundal height is now well above the expected range for her dates, and a urine dipstick today shows 2+ glucose. An ultrasound scan shows a structurally normal single fetus with an abdominal circumference well above the expected centiles and an increased volume of amniotic fluid (polyhydramnios). Her blood pressure is normal.

Which test should be arranged?

options.A: HbA1c to diagnose diabetes
options.B: Amniocentesis for fetal karyotyping
options.C: Oral glucose tolerance test
options.D: Serology for congenital infection (TORCH)
options.E: Random plasma glucose measurement

correct_answer: C. Oral glucose tolerance test
why_correct: Polyhydramnios with a large, structurally normal fetus and glycosuria strongly suggests gestational diabetes, because fetal hyperglycaemia causes fetal polyuria and overgrowth. The recommended diagnostic test is the 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test, and NICE advises considering further testing for gestational diabetes when routine urinalysis shows significant glycosuria. Source: NICE NG3 Diabetes in pregnancy (2015, updated 2020); Barnsley Hospital NHS FT Polyhydramnios guideline (2024).
why_wrong: A. NICE advises against using HbA1c to assess for gestational diabetes; it is used after diagnosis to look for pre-existing diabetes. B. Amniocentesis is considered when structural anomalies are seen, and this large fetus is structurally normal. D. Congenital infection does not explain a macrosomic fetus with maternal glycosuria. E. NICE advises against using random blood glucose to assess for gestational diabetes.
pearl: Too much fluid plus a big baby: think maternal diabetes and do a glucose tolerance test.
thinking: Large-for-dates fundal height  ↓  polyhydramnios + large abdominal circumference, normal anatomy  ↓  glycosuria on dipstick  ↓  fetal hyperglycaemia causes polyuria and overgrowth  ↓  oral glucose tolerance test
exam_trap: Choosing HbA1c or a random glucose, neither of which NICE uses to test for gestational diabetes.
takeaway: Polyhydramnios with macrosomia: test for gestational diabetes with an oral glucose tolerance test.
notes: New vignette (second pregnancy, 2+ glycosuria once — NG3 1.2.4 re-checked today: 2+ on one occasion or 1+ on two or more). Centile and liquor figures softened to words; '75 g' dropped from the option as the load is not the point. Kleihauer distractor replaced with random plasma glucose (NG3 1.2.3 advises against it). Distinct from GF002/OG003 (risk-factor screening timing).

presentation: Oligohydramnios with an SGA fetus — placental insufficiency
stem:
A 28-year-old woman is 34 weeks pregnant with her second baby; her first baby was born small. Her fundal height is smaller than expected, so she has an ultrasound scan. This shows a severely small-for-gestational-age fetus whose abdominal circumference has fallen across the centiles since the previous scan, a reduced volume of amniotic fluid and normal fetal anatomy. Fetal movements are normal and she has had no fluid leaking from the vagina. Her blood pressure and urine dipstick are normal.

Which investigation should be arranged next?

options.A: Growth scan again in four weeks
options.B: Speculum examination for pooled liquor
options.C: Amniocentesis for fetal chromosomes
options.D: Daily CTG monitoring on its own
options.E: Umbilical artery Doppler assessment

correct_answer: E. Umbilical artery Doppler assessment
why_correct: A severely small fetus with a falling abdominal circumference and reduced liquor, in a woman whose previous baby was small, points to placental insufficiency: the fetus redistributes blood away from its kidneys and makes less urine. Umbilical artery Doppler is the main surveillance test for the small-for-gestational-age fetus and guides how often monitoring is needed and when the baby should be born. Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 31, Small-for-gestational-age fetus and growth restricted fetus (2024).
why_wrong: A. Waiting four weeks for another scan is unsafe in a severely small fetus with reduced fluid. B. She has had no leakage, and growth restriction explains the reduced fluid. C. Karyotyping is offered for severe early-onset growth restriction or structural anomalies, and this fetus is structurally normal at 34 weeks. D. CTG should not be the only form of surveillance for a small-for-gestational-age fetus.
pearl: Low fluid plus a small baby means the placenta is failing until proven otherwise — Doppler the umbilical artery.
thinking: Small fundal height, severely SGA, AC falling  ↓  reduced liquor with no rupture of membranes  ↓  placental insufficiency → less fetal urine  ↓  umbilical artery Doppler is the key surveillance test  ↓  results guide monitoring and timing of birth
exam_trap: Doing a speculum for ruptured membranes when there is no leakage and the small fetus explains the low fluid.
takeaway: Reduced liquor with a small-for-gestational-age fetus: suspect placental insufficiency and do umbilical artery Doppler.
notes: New vignette: risk factor is a previous small baby (was smoking); weight centile, SFH and deepest-pool figures softened to words. Distinct from GF008 (normal growth, ruptured membranes).

presentation: Polyhydramnios — fetal duodenal atresia (double bubble)
stem:
A 25-year-old woman is 29 weeks pregnant with her first baby and says her abdomen has become tight and much bigger over the past fortnight. Her fundal height is larger than expected. Her mid-pregnancy anomaly scan was reported as normal, and a glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks was normal. Ultrasound now shows excess amniotic fluid and normal fetal growth. In the upper fetal abdomen there are two rounded fluid-filled spaces next to each other, with no fluid-filled bowel visible beyond them.

What is the most likely cause of the excess fluid?

options.A: Duodenal atresia
options.B: Oesophageal atresia without a fistula
options.C: Posterior urethral valves
options.D: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
options.E: Gastroschisis

correct_answer: A. Duodenal atresia
why_correct: Two adjacent fluid-filled spaces in the upper abdomen are the 'double bubble' of a dilated stomach and proximal duodenum, which is typical of duodenal atresia. The fetus cannot move swallowed amniotic fluid along the gut to be absorbed, so fluid accumulates, usually becoming obvious in the third trimester. About a third of babies with duodenal atresia have Down syndrome, so this should be discussed with the parents. Source: University Hospital Southampton NHS FT, Duodenal atresia (neonatal surgery); Barnsley Hospital NHS FT Polyhydramnios guideline (2024).
why_wrong: B. Oesophageal atresia also causes polyhydramnios, but the stomach bubble is small or absent rather than a double bubble. C. Posterior urethral valves obstruct fetal urine output and cause reduced fluid with a dilated bladder. D. Pyloric stenosis develops after birth, typically at a few weeks of age, and is not an antenatal cause of polyhydramnios. E. Gastroschisis shows loops of bowel floating outside the abdominal wall, not a double bubble.
pearl: Excess fluid means the baby is not swallowing or absorbing it; too little fluid means the baby is not making urine or the placenta is failing.
thinking: Polyhydramnios in the third trimester  ↓  diabetes excluded, normal growth  ↓  double bubble on scan  ↓  upper gut obstruction → swallowed fluid not absorbed  ↓  duodenal atresia (discuss trisomy 21)
exam_trap: Choosing pyloric stenosis, which appears weeks after birth and does not cause a double bubble or antenatal polyhydramnios.
takeaway: Polyhydramnios with a double bubble on scan means fetal duodenal atresia.
notes: New vignette; deepest-pool and centile figures softened. Bilateral renal agenesis distractor replaced with oesophageal atresia (a plausible polyhydramnios cause with a different scan appearance). Distinct from GF005 (TTTS).

presentation: Anhydramnios at 20 weeks — bilateral renal agenesis and pulmonary hypoplasia
stem:
A 22-year-old woman attends for her mid-pregnancy anomaly scan at 20 weeks. The sonographer finds almost no amniotic fluid around the fetus. Despite prolonged scanning, no fetal bladder can be seen, neither kidney can be identified, and colour Doppler shows no renal arteries. The fetal heart, brain and spine appear normal. A speculum examination shows no pooling of fluid, and fetal medicine confirm the diagnosis.

What is the main reason this condition is usually fatal around the time of birth?

options.A: Neonatal renal failure and hyperkalaemia
options.B: Pulmonary hypoplasia
options.C: Fetal cardiac failure
options.D: Fixed limb contractures
options.E: Non-immune hydrops fetalis

correct_answer: B. Pulmonary hypoplasia
why_correct: No bladder, no kidneys and anhydramnios at 20 weeks mean bilateral renal agenesis. From the second trimester amniotic fluid is mainly fetal urine, and the lungs need this fluid to develop. Without it the lungs are severely underdeveloped, and this pulmonary hypoplasia is the main reason babies with bilateral renal agenesis do not survive after birth. Source: NHS Fetal Anomaly Screening Programme, Bilateral renal agenesis: information for parents (GOV.UK).
why_wrong: A. Absent kidneys would cause renal failure after birth, but the lungs usually fail first, so survival long enough for kidney problems to dominate is exceptional. C. The heart is structurally normal, and renal agenesis does not cause fetal heart failure. D. Limb contractures are part of the Potter sequence but are not what limits survival. E. Hydrops results from fetal anaemia, heart failure or infection and is not a feature of renal agenesis.
pearl: No kidneys, no urine, no fluid, no lung growth: pulmonary hypoplasia is what proves fatal.
thinking: Anhydramnios at 20 weeks, membranes intact  ↓  no bladder, kidneys or renal arteries seen  ↓  bilateral renal agenesis  ↓  amniotic fluid is mainly fetal urine  ↓  lungs need fluid to grow → pulmonary hypoplasia → fatal around birth
exam_trap: Picking kidney failure as the cause of death, when it is the lungs that fail at birth.
takeaway: Bilateral renal agenesis is almost always fatal, mainly because of pulmonary hypoplasia.
notes: New vignette (absent renal arteries on colour Doppler added as a supporting sign; speculum confirms intact membranes). Question reframed as the main reason the condition is fatal; key unchanged. '16 weeks' softened to 'second trimester'. GOV.UK FASP page re-checked today.

presentation: Schizoaffective disorder — mood and psychotic symptoms in the same episode
stem:
A 41-year-old woman with no previous psychiatric history is admitted after ten weeks of profound low mood, guilt, insomnia, weight loss and loss of interest in her family. Within a few days of her mood falling, she began hearing a voice giving a running commentary on everything she does and became convinced that her thoughts were being broadcast to her neighbours. She was treated with an antidepressant and an antipsychotic. For the past five weeks her mood, sleep and appetite have been normal, but the commentary voice and her belief about thought broadcasting are unchanged. She has never been elated or overactive, and she does not use alcohol or drugs.

Using ICD-11, which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Depressive episode with psychotic symptoms
options.B: Schizophrenia
options.C: Bipolar type I disorder
options.D: Schizoaffective disorder
options.E: Delusional disorder

correct_answer: D. Schizoaffective disorder
why_correct: ICD-11, the current WHO classification (ICD-10, still used for NHS coding, is essentially the same), defines schizoaffective disorder as an episode in which the requirements for schizophrenia and for a moderate or severe depressive (or manic or mixed) episode are met in the same episode of illness, at the same time or within a few days, lasting at least one month. She had a severe depressive episode and, within days, two core schizophrenia symptoms (a running-commentary voice and thought broadcasting) for over two months. Her psychotic symptoms then persisted after her mood recovered, which argues against a depressive episode with psychotic symptoms. Source: WHO ICD-11 6A21 Schizoaffective disorder (MMS v2026-01).
why_wrong: A. In a depressive episode with psychotic symptoms, the psychosis is confined to the mood episode and resolves with it. B. ICD-11 does not diagnose schizophrenia when a full moderate or severe mood episode meets its requirements in the same episode as the psychotic symptoms. C. Bipolar type I disorder needs a manic or mixed episode, and she has never had one. E. Delusional disorder involves persistent delusions without prominent hallucinations or other schizophrenia-type symptoms, and she has a commentary voice and a full depressive episode.
pearl: Schizophrenia-type symptoms and a full mood episode in the same episode of illness = schizoaffective disorder; psychosis that outlasts the mood episode points away from psychotic depression.
thinking: Severe depressive episode  ↓  first-rank symptoms (running commentary, thought broadcasting) within days, lasting over a month  ↓  ICD-11: schizophrenia and mood requirements met in the same episode  ↓  psychosis persists after mood recovers; no mania, no substances  ↓  schizoaffective disorder
exam_trap: Labelling it psychotic depression without noticing that the psychosis continues after the mood has recovered.
takeaway: ICD-11: schizophrenia-type symptoms and a moderate or severe mood episode together in the same episode = schizoaffective disorder.
notes: New vignette (woman, running commentary and thought broadcasting). Drug-induced distractor replaced with schizophrenia, which tests the ICD-11 same-episode rule. ICD-11 framework kept as in the reviewed source; DSM-5-TR aside omitted. Distinct from GF028 (manic type) and P062 (mood episodes for most of illness with interepisode psychosis).

presentation: Schizoaffective disorder — persistent psychosis despite two antipsychotics (clozapine)
stem:
At the community mental health team's weekly meeting, a care coordinator presents a 45-year-old former chef with a ten-year history of schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type. 'His mood has been level since the spring on lithium, and every recent level has been in range. The problem is the psychosis: he is still certain the television is sending him coded instructions and he hears a running commentary on everything he does. He had quetiapine at a full dose for long enough, then amisulpride the same way, one after the other, and neither touched it. Supervised dispensing at the pharmacy confirmed he took both. The diagnosis was re-examined last month, he is drug- and alcohol-free, and he finished CBT for psychosis and family work in the summer.'

What medication change should the team recommend?

options.A: Raise the lithium dose toward a higher plasma target
options.B: Start an SSRI antidepressant
options.C: Give quetiapine and amisulpride together over the long term
options.D: Replace lithium with sodium valproate
options.E: Psychiatrist-initiated clozapine with FBC monitoring

correct_answer: E. Psychiatrist-initiated clozapine with FBC monitoring
why_correct: His mood is controlled, so the problem is the persistent psychosis, which has not responded to two adequate, sequential antipsychotic trials (at least one a non-clozapine second-generation drug) with adherence confirmed and other causes of non-response reviewed. This is treatment-resistant psychosis, and clozapine should be offered; there is no NICE guideline specific to schizoaffective disorder, so the schizophrenia guideline is applied to the psychotic component. Clozapine is started and supervised by a specialist, with registration with a monitoring service and frequent (initially weekly) full blood counts because of the risk of agranulocytosis. Combining it with lithium needs specialist oversight, as the clozapine SmPC warns of a possible increased risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome and lithium can mask a falling neutrophil count. Source: NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults (2014, last updated 2026, recs 1.5.7.1–1.5.7.2); Clozaril SmPC (emc, revised February 2026).
why_wrong: A. His mood is stable with lithium in range, and raising it would not treat psychosis but would increase toxicity risk. B. He has no depressive symptoms, and an antidepressant does not treat psychosis and may destabilise mood in the bipolar type. C. Long-term combination of two antipsychotics is not recommended except briefly when switching, and clozapine is the evidence-based option after two failed trials. D. Changing the mood stabiliser does not address the psychosis, and under MHRA rules starting valproate in anyone under 55 needs two specialists to agree.
pearl: In schizoaffective disorder ask which part is uncontrolled: stable mood with persistent psychosis after two antipsychotics means clozapine.
thinking: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type  ↓  mood level on lithium in range  ↓  psychosis persists after two sequential adequate antipsychotic trials (both second-generation), adherence confirmed  ↓  treatment-resistant psychosis  ↓  psychiatrist initiates clozapine with registration and blood monitoring
exam_trap: Adjusting the mood stabiliser because the diagnosis is 'affective', when it is the psychosis that has not responded.
takeaway: Psychosis in schizoaffective disorder that fails two adequate, sequential antipsychotic trials: specialist-initiated clozapine with blood monitoring.
notes: Reworked for distance from AKT MG044 (stem Jaccard was 0.52): now a care coordinator presenting at a CMHT meeting, 45-year-old man (former chef), delusions of reference and running commentary, quetiapine then amisulpride with adherence confirmed by supervised dispensing. Safety content kept: two adequate sequential trials, adherence confirmed, diagnosis and substance use reviewed, psychological therapy completed; clozapine initiated by the specialist with FBC monitoring. Valproate wording: MHRA Jan 2024 two-specialist rule for new starts under 55 still applies to him as a new start; the Feb 2025 MHRA change removed the two-specialist review only for men already taking valproate (checked 8 Oct 2026). NICE CG178 1.5.7.2 re-checked. Distinct from P088, GF028, GF030.

presentation: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type — acute management
stem:
A 24-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, stopped all her medication a month ago. Her sister brings her to the community mental health team because for ten days she has barely slept, has spent large sums of money, talks rapidly and believes she has been chosen to heal the world. She also hears voices praising her. She is not pregnant, is sexually active and uses no contraception. Her physical health and ECG are normal, and she agrees to take medication.

Which is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?

options.A: Sodium valproate started as a mood stabiliser
options.B: An oral antipsychotic such as risperidone
options.C: An SSRI antidepressant such as citalopram
options.D: Lamotrigine started as a mood stabiliser
options.E: Regular oral lorazepam as sole treatment

correct_answer: B. An oral antipsychotic such as risperidone
why_correct: She has a manic episode with psychotic symptoms and is taking no antipsychotic or mood stabiliser, so NICE recommends offering an antipsychotic such as haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone. An antipsychotic treats both the mania and the psychotic symptoms. A mood stabiliser such as lithium may later be added for longer-term control, alongside psychological interventions, family support and care coordination. Source: NICE CG185 Bipolar disorder (2014, last updated 2025, rec 1.5.3); NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults (2014, last updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Valproate is not first-line here: MHRA advice is not to start it in anyone under 55 unless two specialists independently agree there is no other effective or tolerated option, and a woman of childbearing potential must also meet the pregnancy prevention programme requirements. C. Antidepressants can worsen mania and do not treat psychosis. D. Lamotrigine is used to prevent bipolar depression and does not treat acute mania or psychosis. E. A benzodiazepine may help short-term agitation and sleep but does not treat mania or psychosis on its own.
pearl: Acute mania with psychosis in schizoaffective disorder: antipsychotic first, and remember valproate's MHRA restrictions in women.
thinking: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type  ↓  manic relapse with psychotic symptoms  ↓  off all medication  ↓  antipsychotic treats both mania and psychosis  ↓  oral antipsychotic first-line, plus psychosocial support
exam_trap: Starting valproate in a young woman who is sexually active without contraception.
takeaway: Manic relapse in schizoaffective disorder: start an antipsychotic first.
notes: New vignette (grandiose delusion, voices praising her, overspending). Reviewer-required MHRA valproate wording kept in full. CG185 1.5.3 re-checked today.

presentation: Antipsychotic physical health monitoring at 12 weeks
stem:
A 27-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder started quetiapine three months ago and her symptoms are much better. She has noticed her clothes getting tighter and has gained 4 kg. Her father has type 2 diabetes. She takes no other medicines and does not smoke. She attends the community mental health team for her scheduled 12-week physical health review.

Which set of checks should be done at this review?

options.A: Full blood count and neutrophil count only
options.B: Weight, blood pressure, HbA1c and lipids
options.C: Serum lithium level and thyroid function
options.D: Liver function tests and prolactin only
options.E: No tests until her annual review is due

correct_answer: B. Weight, blood pressure, HbA1c and lipids
why_correct: Antipsychotics such as quetiapine can cause weight gain, diabetes and dyslipidaemia, adding to the already high cardiovascular risk in people with psychosis. NICE recommends checking weight, pulse and blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c and lipids at 12 weeks after starting an antipsychotic, then at one year and annually. Her weight gain and family history of diabetes should be acted on now, with a healthy eating and physical activity programme and a review of her antipsychotic choice with her. Source: NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults (2014, last updated 2026, rec 1.3.6.4).
why_wrong: A. Neutrophil monitoring is mandatory for clozapine, not quetiapine. C. Lithium levels and thyroid function are monitored in people taking lithium, which she is not. D. Prolactin is checked before starting an antipsychotic, but liver tests and prolactin alone miss the metabolic risks that matter most at 12 weeks. E. Waiting a year misses the 12-week review recommended by NICE, when early metabolic change can be treated.
pearl: Antipsychotic 12-week check: weight, pulse and blood pressure, HbA1c or fasting glucose, and lipids.
thinking: Schizoaffective disorder on quetiapine  ↓  12-week review, weight gain, family history of diabetes  ↓  antipsychotics cause metabolic syndrome  ↓  NICE: weight, BP/pulse, glucose or HbA1c, lipids at 12 weeks  ↓  act on results now
exam_trap: Choosing the full blood count because of clozapine monitoring, when the key risk with other antipsychotics is metabolic.
takeaway: Check weight, blood pressure, HbA1c and lipids 12 weeks after starting an antipsychotic.
notes: New vignette (woman on quetiapine, family history of diabetes, non-smoker). The detailed weekly-weight schedule omitted as a deep reference figure; the 12-week review is kept because it frames the scenario, and the key does not depend on recalling it. CG178 1.3.6.4 re-checked today.

presentation: Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome after major trauma
stem:
A 27-year-old woman was crushed by farm machinery five days ago, sustaining bilateral femoral fractures and a liver laceration. She needed a laparotomy and a massive transfusion on the day of admission and has had no blood products since that day. In the intensive care unit she remains ventilated, with bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray and poor oxygenation despite high inspired oxygen. She has passed almost no urine for a day, her creatinine has risen sharply, and haemofiltration has been started. She has become jaundiced with a rising bilirubin. Blood and line cultures are negative and no source of infection has been found.

Which term best describes her condition?

options.A: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
options.B: Transfusion-related acute lung injury
options.C: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome
options.D: Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome
options.E: Hepatorenal syndrome

correct_answer: D. Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome
why_correct: Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) is altered function of two or more organ systems in an acutely ill patient, such that homeostasis cannot be maintained without intervention. Her respiratory failure needing ventilation and acute kidney injury needing renal replacement already meet this definition, and her jaundice shows that the liver is also affected. It follows the inflammatory 'second hit' of major trauma, massive transfusion and surgery, and is a recognised cause of late death after major trauma. Source: ACCP/SCCM Consensus Conference definitions for sepsis and organ failure (Bone et al., Chest, 1992).
why_wrong: A. ARDS describes only her lung injury, which is one of three failing organ systems. B. TRALI develops within hours of a transfusion and affects only the lungs, and her last blood products were days ago. C. SIRS describes the systemic inflammatory response (fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea, white cell changes), not failure of several organs needing support. E. Hepatorenal syndrome is kidney failure in advanced liver disease and does not explain her respiratory failure.
pearl: One failing organ is a diagnosis; two or more failing organs needing support is MODS, and mortality rises with each extra organ.
thinking: Major trauma + laparotomy + massive transfusion  ↓  day 5: ventilated with bilateral infiltrates (lungs)  ↓  anuria and rising creatinine needing haemofiltration (kidneys)  ↓  jaundice with rising bilirubin (liver)  ↓  two or more organ systems failing and needing support  ↓  multiple organ dysfunction syndrome
exam_trap: Choosing ARDS because the lung failure is most striking, when the question asks for the term that covers every failing organ.
takeaway: Dysfunction of two or more organ systems needing intervention after major trauma, burns or sepsis is MODS.
notes: New vignette (woman, farm crush injury, liver as third organ instead of clotting). Reviewer-required timing wording kept: massive transfusion on the day of admission and no blood products since, so TRALI is excluded. PaO2/FiO2, urine output and creatinine figures softened to words. DIC distractor replaced with hepatorenal syndrome. Definition carried over from Bone et al. 1992 (no UK guideline defines MODS).

presentation: Schizoaffective disorder — family intervention to prevent relapse
stem:
A 31-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, is reviewed by her community psychiatrist. She has had two relapses needing hospital admission in the past year, each starting after arguments at home. She receives a monthly depot antipsychotic injection, so her adherence is assured, and she is currently well with no mood or psychotic symptoms. She lives with her husband and her mother-in-law, who are often critical of her and frustrated by her illness. She is happy for them to be involved in her care.

Alongside her current medication, which intervention would best reduce her risk of relapse?

options.A: Switch the depot to oral clozapine
options.B: Add a second regular oral antipsychotic
options.C: Diazepam to take on stressful days
options.D: Long-term psychodynamic psychotherapy
options.E: Family intervention with her household

correct_answer: E. Family intervention with her household
why_correct: NICE recommends offering family intervention to the families of people with psychosis, which includes schizoaffective disorder, who live with or are in close contact with them, and it is particularly useful after a recent relapse or when relapse risk is high. It should include the patient where practical, run over several months with a planned course of sessions and include problem solving or crisis management. CBT for psychosis should also be offered alongside medication. Source: NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults (2014, last updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Clozapine is for illness that has not responded to two adequate antipsychotic trials, and she responds to treatment and is currently well. B. Combining regular antipsychotics adds side effects without better relapse prevention, and NICE advises against it except briefly when switching. C. Benzodiazepines do not prevent relapse and carry a risk of dependence. D. NICE recommends CBT for psychosis and family intervention, not psychodynamic psychotherapy, as treatments for psychosis.
pearl: Relapse prevention in psychosis is not a drug-only job: medication plus family intervention plus CBT for psychosis.
thinking: Schizoaffective disorder = psychosis under NICE CG178  ↓  relapses despite assured adherence (depot)  ↓  lives with critical relatives; relapses follow conflict  ↓  offer family intervention  ↓  also offer CBT for psychosis; continue medication
exam_trap: Reaching for clozapine or more drugs when the patient is adherent, currently well and the modifiable factor is family stress.
takeaway: For people with psychosis who live with family, offer family intervention alongside medication to reduce relapse.
notes: New vignette (woman, depressive type, depot antipsychotic, critical in-laws). The session count and 3–12 month duration softened to 'over several months with a planned course of sessions'. CG178 family intervention recommendations re-checked today. Distinct from DS055 (lithium for relapse prevention after first mania).

presentation: Acute bronchitis — evidence-based self-care
stem:
A 36-year-old teacher sees her GP after six days of coughing up yellowish sputum, with an aching chest when she coughs and a slight fever that has now gone. She has no asthma or other long-term conditions and does not smoke. Her observations are normal, and the GP hears a few scattered wheezes but no focal crackles. The GP diagnoses acute bronchitis and she agrees that she does not need an antibiotic. She asks what might help her cough.

What should the GP suggest?

options.A: Honey taken in warm drinks
options.B: A salbutamol inhaler to use as needed
options.C: Carbocisteine capsules to thin the sputum
options.D: A short course of oral prednisolone
options.E: A codeine-based cough linctus

correct_answer: A. Honey taken in warm drinks
why_correct: NICE advises managing acute bronchitis without an antibiotic in people who are not systemically very unwell or at higher risk of complications, with self-care and advice on when to seek help. Honey (in people over 1 year), pelargonium, and over-the-counter cough medicines containing guaifenesin or a non-codeine cough suppressant have limited evidence of some benefit for cough. Source: NICE NG120 Cough (acute): antimicrobial prescribing (2019, rec 1.2.1).
why_wrong: B. NICE advises against bronchodilators for acute bronchitis unless there is underlying airways disease such as asthma. C. NICE advises against mucolytics such as carbocisteine for acute cough with acute bronchitis. D. Oral or inhaled corticosteroids should not be offered for acute bronchitis without underlying airways disease. E. NICE excludes codeine-containing cough suppressants from its self-care advice, and codeine carries harms.
pearl: For acute cough NICE's self-care list is honey, pelargonium, guaifenesin and non-codeine suppressants, not mucolytics, steroids or salbutamol.
thinking: Acute productive cough, no focal signs, systemically well  ↓  no comorbidity, not high risk  ↓  acute bronchitis: no antibiotic  ↓  self-care with limited evidence: honey, pelargonium, guaifenesin, non-codeine suppressants  ↓  avoid mucolytics, steroids, bronchodilators and codeine
exam_trap: Choosing salbutamol because of the wheeze, when NICE advises against bronchodilators in acute bronchitis without asthma or COPD.
takeaway: Acute bronchitis in a well adult: no antibiotic; suggest simple self-care such as honey and explain when to return.
notes: New vignette (female teacher); observations given in words. NG120 1.1.6, 1.1.7 and 1.2.1 re-checked today. Distinct from DF039 (antibiotic request).

presentation: Lower respiratory tract infection — point-of-care CRP
stem:
A 47-year-old man sees his GP with a week of cough productive of green sputum, tiredness and feeling feverish at night. He has no long-term conditions and does not smoke. His temperature is mildly raised but his other observations are normal, he is alert, and there are coarse crackles that clear on coughing with no focal chest signs. After assessment the GP is unsure whether he needs an antibiotic and does a point-of-care C-reactive protein (CRP) test, which is moderately raised.

How should he be managed?

options.A: Immediate course of oral doxycycline
options.B: No antibiotic, self-care advice only
options.C: Back-up doxycycline prescription
options.D: Same-day chest X-ray at the hospital
options.E: Admission for intravenous antibiotics

correct_answer: C. Back-up doxycycline prescription
why_correct: When it is unclear whether someone with a lower respiratory tract infection needs an antibiotic, NICE suggests a point-of-care CRP test and uses three bands: a low result means antibiotics are not routinely offered, a very high result means immediate antibiotics, and a result in between means considering a back-up prescription. A back-up (delayed) prescription is one the patient collects or uses only if symptoms worsen or fail to improve, with clear advice on when to use it. His moderately raised result falls in the middle band, so a back-up prescription with safety-netting is appropriate. Source: NICE NG237 Suspected acute respiratory infection in over 16s (2023, updated 2025, rec 1.3.4).
why_wrong: A. Immediate antibiotics are for a CRP in the top band or a patient who is systemically very unwell, neither of which applies. B. No antibiotic is the default only when the CRP is in the lowest band. D. He has no focal signs or features of pneumonia that would need urgent imaging. E. His observations are reassuring, with no features of sepsis or severe illness to warrant admission.
pearl: Point-of-care CRP in an uncertain chest infection has three tiers: low means no antibiotic, middle means back-up prescription, high means immediate antibiotic.
thinking: Adult with LRTI, systemically well, no pneumonia signs  ↓  clinical doubt about antibiotics  ↓  point-of-care CRP  ↓  result in the middle band  ↓  back-up antibiotic prescription with safety-netting
exam_trap: Treating green sputum or any raised CRP as an automatic trigger for immediate antibiotics.
takeaway: A CRP in the middle band in an uncertain chest infection means a back-up antibiotic prescription, not immediate treatment.
notes: Rule 2 re-angle: the AKT key depended on recalling NICE's CRP cut-offs (currently <20, 20–100, >100 mg/L in NG237 1.3.4), which are movable thresholds. The stem now says only that the CRP is 'moderately raised'; the three-band structure is explained in why_correct. The item tests the three-tier principle (intermediate result = back-up prescription), not the numbers. Edited at reviewer request (band description moved out of the stem).

presentation: Acute bronchitis — natural course and safety-netting
stem:
A 52-year-old man who teaches at a primary school sees his GP with a cough that started 5 days ago, after a cold he caught from his pupils. He is bringing up small amounts of white sputum and feels tired but is still working. He does not smoke, has no lung disease and is not immunosuppressed. He is afebrile and breathing comfortably with normal oxygen saturation, and there are a few scattered wheezes but no focal crackles. The GP diagnoses acute bronchitis, and he is happy to manage without an antibiotic. He wants to know how long the cough will go on and when he should come back.

Which advice is most appropriate?

options.A: Expect it to settle within 7 days; book again if it has not
options.B: Come back for antibiotics as soon as his sputum turns yellow or green
options.C: The cough may persist 3–4 weeks; return if worsening or not settling
options.D: Expect it to last 2–3 months; come back only if he coughs up blood
options.E: It should clear in 5 days; antibiotics are needed if it has not

correct_answer: C. The cough may persist 3–4 weeks; return if worsening or not settling
why_correct: NICE advises that an acute cough is usually self-limiting and gets better within 3 to 4 weeks without antibiotics. Patients should be told this expected course, given self-care advice, and told to seek help if symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly, do not improve after 3 to 4 weeks, or they become systemically very unwell. Realistic expectations reduce unnecessary return visits and antibiotic requests. Source: NICE NG120 Cough (acute): antimicrobial prescribing, 2019.
why_wrong: A. A post-bronchitis cough commonly lasts well beyond a week, so this sets him up to return unnecessarily. B. Sputum colour does not tell bacterial from viral infection and is not a reason to start antibiotics. D. Two to three months is far longer than expected, and limiting safety-netting to haemoptysis misses rapid worsening or systemic illness. E. Five days is too short, and a cough that has not cleared by then is not an indication for antibiotics.
pearl: Tell patients with acute bronchitis at the outset that the cough can last 3–4 weeks, and safety-net for rapid worsening or systemic illness.
thinking: Acute bronchitis in a well adult  ↓  No antibiotic agreed  ↓  Usual course: up to 3–4 weeks  ↓  Return if rapidly or significantly worse, systemically very unwell, or not better by 3–4 weeks
exam_trap: Underestimating the natural course as about a week, or using green sputum as a trigger for antibiotics.
takeaway: Acute bronchitis cough may last 3–4 weeks; advise return if much worse, very unwell or not settling by then.
notes: New vignette (male teacher, 5-day cough, no antibiotic already agreed). Same learning point: expected 3–4 week course and NG120 safety-net. Not a duplicate of DF039 (antibiotic decision) or DF040 (persisting cough at 6 weeks → CXR). The 3–4 week figure is kept as it is the learning point (NG120 1.1.1 wording, rechecked on nice.org.uk 8 Oct 2026).

presentation: Acute stress disorder — marked symptoms within a month of trauma
stem:
A 33-year-old man who runs a convenience shop sees his GP 3 weeks after two men threatened him with a knife during a robbery. He was not hurt. Since the robbery he has relived the moment several times a day, wakes from nightmares most nights, and says he feels numb and as if the world is not real. He jumps at the sound of the shop door and has not been able to go back to work. His sleep and concentration are worse now than in the first week. He has no thoughts of harming himself, drinks little and has never had mental health problems before. A validated trauma symptom questionnaire scores well above the clinical cut-off.

What should the GP offer him now?

options.A: Watchful waiting with GP review in a month
options.B: A group psychological debriefing session this week
options.C: Start sertraline and review in 2 weeks
options.D: A short course of a benzodiazepine at night
options.E: Refer for individual trauma-focused CBT now

correct_answer: E. Refer for individual trauma-focused CBT now
why_correct: Within the first month after trauma, NICE limits active monitoring to people with subthreshold symptoms. Adults with acute stress disorder or clinically important PTSD symptoms within a month of the event should be offered individual trauma-focused CBT, such as cognitive therapy for PTSD or prolonged exposure. His symptoms are marked, getting worse rather than settling, above the clinical threshold and stopping him working, so he should be referred now. Source: NICE NG116 Post-traumatic stress disorder, 2018.
why_wrong: A. Watchful waiting is for subthreshold or settling symptoms; his are marked, worsening and disabling. B. NICE advises against psychologically focused debriefing to prevent or treat PTSD, as it does not help and may cause harm. C. NICE advises against drug treatment to prevent PTSD; an SSRI is considered only for diagnosed PTSD when the person prefers medication. D. Benzodiazepines are specifically not to be offered to prevent PTSD and carry a risk of dependence.
pearl: In the first month after trauma: settling, mild symptoms — monitor; marked or worsening symptoms — individual trauma-focused CBT; never debriefing.
thinking: Knife-point robbery 3 weeks ago  ↓  Re-experiencing, dissociation, hyperarousal, avoidance; worsening; above threshold  ↓  Acute stress disorder / clinically important symptoms within 1 month  ↓  Not suitable for active monitoring  ↓  Refer for individual trauma-focused CBT
exam_trap: Assuming everyone seen within a month of trauma should simply be monitored, whatever the severity.
takeaway: Marked, worsening symptoms in the first month after trauma need individual trauma-focused CBT, not waiting, drugs or debriefing.
notes: New vignette (male shopkeeper, armed robbery, worsening at 3 weeks; numeric questionnaire score softened to 'well above the clinical cut-off'). Same learning point: NG116 1.6.15 (TF-CBT within 1 month for ASD/clinically important symptoms) vs 1.6.4 (active monitoring for subthreshold); 1.6.5 and 1.6.24 as distractors. Not a duplicate of GF032 (subthreshold, improving) or P064 (diagnosis). NG116 1.6.24 wording rechecked on nice.org.uk 8 Oct 2026.

presentation: Acute stress reaction versus PTSD — timing
stem:
A 29-year-old woman sees her GP 3 days after a lorry crashed into the side of her car on the motorway. She was checked in the emergency department and had only bruising. Since the crash she has had flashbacks of the impact, a nightmare each night and a pounding heart whenever she hears brakes screech, and she has avoided driving. She says the first night was the worst and she feels a little calmer each day. She has gone back to her office job and is sleeping at her parents' house for a few nights. She asks whether she has PTSD.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Acute stress reaction
options.B: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
options.C: Adjustment disorder with anxious mood
options.D: Specific phobia of driving
options.E: Panic disorder

correct_answer: A. Acute stress reaction
why_correct: Intrusive memories, nightmares, arousal and avoidance that start straight after an exceptionally threatening event and are already easing while she keeps functioning fit an acute stress reaction: in ICD-11 this is a transient, normal response to an extreme stressor that usually begins to subside within a few days. It is distinct from DSM-5 acute stress disorder, which needs a fuller set of symptoms lasting from 3 days to 1 month and causing significant distress or impairment; her symptoms are improving and she is functioning. PTSD can only be diagnosed when symptoms persist for more than 1 month after the trauma, and NICE frames care in the first month as active monitoring for settling symptoms or early trauma-focused treatment for marked ones. Source: NICE NG116 Post-traumatic stress disorder, 2018; WHO ICD-11 QE84 Acute stress reaction; DSM-5 criteria for acute stress disorder and PTSD.
why_wrong: B. PTSD has the same kinds of symptoms but requires them to persist for more than a month; it is only 3 days. C.
