Adjustment disorder follows a stressful life change rather than an exceptionally threatening event and is not dominated by re-experiencing. D. A specific phobia is a persistent, excessive fear of an object or situation, not a few days of trauma symptoms that are already settling. E. Panic disorder involves recurrent unexpected panic attacks, whereas her palpitations are triggered by reminders of the crash.
pearl: Same symptoms, different clock: settling symptoms in the first days are an acute stress reaction, and PTSD needs more than a month.
thinking: Exceptionally threatening event 3 days ago  ↓  Flashbacks, nightmares, arousal, avoidance  ↓  Began immediately, easing daily, functioning  ↓  Under 1 month — PTSD cannot be diagnosed; not the impairing picture of acute stress disorder  ↓  Acute stress reaction
exam_trap: Diagnosing PTSD because the symptoms look like PTSD, without checking how long ago the trauma was.
takeaway: Trauma symptoms that settle over the first few days are an acute stress reaction; PTSD needs symptoms lasting more than a month.
notes: New vignette (woman, motorway crash, 3 days, settling, back at work). Reviewer framing from MG053 retained: ICD-11 acute stress reaction separated from DSM-5 acute stress disorder (which the stem does not meet). Note for reviewer: existing P064 (5 days, detachment/derealisation, answer acute stress disorder) is a different picture — this stem has no dissociation and symptoms are easing, so the two are consistent. Options reworded so only 2 of 5 match the AKT text.

presentation: Early trauma symptoms — no drug to prevent PTSD
stem:
A 46-year-old woman who drives trains sees her GP 5 days after a man stepped in front of her train and was killed. Since then she has had trouble getting off to sleep, feels on edge, and sometimes pictures the moment of impact during the day. These symptoms are already less intense than in the first two days, she is eating normally, and she has arranged a phased return to work with her employer's support. She has no thoughts of self-harm, drinks alcohol only at weekends and has no previous mental health problems. A friend has told her that a sedative 'stops PTSD setting in', and she asks for a prescription.

How should the GP respond to her request?

options.A: A two-week course of diazepam taken at night
options.B: No drug; sleep advice and review within a month
options.C: Propranolol for 2 weeks to stop PTSD developing
options.D: Sertraline daily, continued for at least 6 months
options.E: Low-dose quetiapine at night until sleep improves

correct_answer: B. No drug; sleep advice and review within a month
why_correct: NICE states that drug treatments, including benzodiazepines, should not be offered to prevent PTSD in adults. Her symptoms are mild, improving and below the threshold for intervention, so active monitoring with follow-up within a month is appropriate, together with an explanation of normal reactions to trauma and practical sleep advice. Trauma-focused psychological treatment is offered if her symptoms become marked or persist. Source: NICE NG116 Post-traumatic stress disorder, 2018.
why_wrong: A. Benzodiazepines are specifically named by NICE as drugs not to offer to prevent PTSD, and they risk dependence. C. Propranolol has been studied for PTSD prevention, but NICE advises against any drug to prevent PTSD in adults. D. An SSRI is considered only for diagnosed PTSD when the person prefers drug treatment, not for early, improving symptoms. E. Antipsychotics are considered only as an add-on for established PTSD with disabling symptoms, and using quetiapine for sleep exposes her to avoidable metabolic and sedative harm.
pearl: No tablet prevents PTSD: after trauma, explain, support, give sleep advice and review — do not prescribe.
thinking: Traumatic event 5 days ago  ↓  Mild, improving sleep problems, tension, occasional intrusions; functioning  ↓  Subthreshold — active monitoring  ↓  No drugs (including benzodiazepines) to prevent PTSD  ↓  Sleep advice + review within 1 month
exam_trap: Giving a short course of a benzodiazepine or propranolol because the patient asks for something to prevent PTSD.
takeaway: Do not prescribe drugs to prevent PTSD; offer support, sleep advice and active monitoring with review within a month.
notes: New vignette (female train driver, person under train, asks for a sedative). Same learning point: NG116 1.6.24 (no drugs including benzodiazepines to prevent PTSD) with 1.6.4 active monitoring; 1.6.25–1.6.26 distractors. Differs from GF032 (debriefing distractor; learning point active monitoring vs debriefing) — here the tested point is refusing preventive drugs. Doses removed from options (not the point). NG116 1.6.24–1.6.26 rechecked on nice.org.uk 8 Oct 2026.

presentation: Borderline personality disorder in crisis — short-term sedation
stem:
A 28-year-old woman with emotionally unstable (borderline) personality disorder is visited at home by the community crisis team. Two days ago she was told she must leave her rented flat, and since then she has burned her forearm with a cigarette lighter several times and has hardly slept. Using her crisis plan, the team talk through what has triggered her distress and agree daily visits; she does not want to go into hospital, has no current intent to end her life and has no depressive or psychotic illness. She drinks alcohol occasionally and takes no other medicines. She asks for something to calm her and help her sleep over the next few nights, and the team agree that brief medication is reasonable.

Which medication plan is most appropriate?

options.A: Zopiclone at night, given as a 28-day supply
options.B: Regular diazepam three times a day for 4 weeks
options.C: Olanzapine at night, continued once the crisis has settled
options.D: Promethazine at night, small supplies, for up to a week
options.E: Sertraline daily, continued for at least 6 months

correct_answer: D. Promethazine at night, small supplies, for up to a week
why_correct: NICE says short-term sedative medication may be considered cautiously for a person with borderline personality disorder in crisis, with agreement among the prescribers involved. It should be a single drug with a low side-effect profile, low addictive potential, minimal potential for misuse and relative safety in overdose; NICE gives a sedative antihistamine as the example, and promethazine is one such option rather than a required choice (it is not licensed for this use, so consent is documented). Because she has recently self-harmed, use the minimum effective dose and prescribe fewer tablets more often, check for alcohol, illicit drugs or other sedatives that would add to its effect, agree the target symptoms and monitoring through the daily visits, and stop it within 1 week, then update the crisis plan. Source: NICE CG78 Borderline personality disorder, 2009 (1.3.5.4, 1.3.7.2–1.3.7.5).
why_wrong: A. A month's supply of a hypnotic carries dependence and overdose risk in someone who is self-harming. B. A month of regular diazepam risks dependence and misuse and is not a short-term crisis option for this group. C. NICE advises that antipsychotics should not be used for the medium- or long-term treatment of borderline personality disorder. E. Drugs should not be used for the personality disorder or its emotional instability; an antidepressant is only for a diagnosed comorbid condition such as depression.
pearl: BPD crisis: one low-risk sedative (for example a sedative antihistamine), small supplies, stopped within a week — then update the crisis plan.
thinking: BPD in crisis with self-harm and poor sleep  ↓  No comorbid depression or psychosis  ↓  Crisis plan used; brief medication agreed  ↓  Single low-risk, low-toxicity sedative in small supplies  ↓  Stop within 1 week; review and update crisis plan
exam_trap: Starting an antipsychotic or antidepressant during a crisis and letting it become long-term treatment for the personality disorder.
takeaway: In a BPD crisis, any drug should be a single low-risk sedative such as an antihistamine, given in small supplies and stopped within a week.
notes: New vignette (eviction trigger, burns, home crisis team). Reviewer safety caveats from MG055 retained (CG78 1.3.7.2–1.3.7.3: minimum dose, fewer tablets more frequently, alcohol/illicit drugs, agreed monitoring; 1.3.7.5 stop within a week; promethazine framed as an example). CG78 1.3.5.2 and 1.3.7.3 rechecked on nice.org.uk 8 Oct 2026. Not a duplicate of DF047 (no drug for BPD itself) or DF048 (psychosocial assessment).

presentation: Antisocial personality disorder — diagnostic criteria
stem:
A 29-year-old man is referred by his probation officer for a psychiatric assessment after a conviction for fraud. Since his late teens he has stolen from employers, used false identities to borrow money he never repaid, been in repeated fights and lost his driving licence for driving at high speed through residential streets. He has walked out of several jobs and left his young son without support. He describes the people he has cheated as 'stupid enough to deserve it'. He has no psychotic symptoms, no mood disorder and is not using drugs or alcohol at present.

Using DSM-5 criteria, which additional finding is required to diagnose antisocial personality disorder?

options.A: A history of ADHD diagnosed in childhood
options.B: A custodial sentence served in adult life
options.C: An IQ below the average range
options.D: A first-degree relative with a criminal record
options.E: Conduct disorder beginning before age 15

correct_answer: E. Conduct disorder beginning before age 15
why_correct: DSM-5 antisocial personality disorder needs a pervasive pattern of disregard for the rights of others since age 15, the person to be at least 18 years old, and evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15. He already shows deceitfulness, impulsivity, aggression, recklessness, irresponsibility and lack of remorse, so the missing piece is the childhood history, which should be sought from family, school or youth justice records. Source: NICE CG77 Antisocial personality disorder, 2009 (Context).
why_wrong: A. ADHD is a common comorbidity and risk factor but is not a diagnostic criterion. B. Imprisonment is not required; repeated acts that are grounds for arrest are enough, whether or not they lead to custody. C. Low IQ is not a criterion, and a learning disability would suggest another explanation for the behaviour. D. Parental or family criminality is a risk factor, not a diagnostic requirement.
pearl: No conduct disorder before 15, no DSM-5 antisocial personality disorder — however antisocial the adult.
thinking: Adult pattern of deceit, aggression, recklessness, irresponsibility, no remorse  ↓  Aged 18 or over  ↓  Not explained by psychosis or mania  ↓  DSM-5 also requires conduct disorder onset before 15  ↓  Seek collateral childhood history
exam_trap: Assuming convictions or prison define the diagnosis rather than the childhood conduct disorder criterion.
takeaway: DSM-5 antisocial personality disorder requires age 18 or over and evidence of conduct disorder starting before age 15.
notes: New vignette (probation referral, fraud, recklessness, irresponsibility to child). Same learning point. Not a duplicate of P066 (which asks for the diagnosis). Age 15 kept as it is the diagnostic criterion itself (stable DSM criterion, not a movable guideline cut-off). Stem specifies DSM-5 because ICD-11 uses a dimensional model.

presentation: Borderline personality disorder — deprescribing a crisis-started antipsychotic
stem:
A 36-year-old man with emotionally unstable (borderline) personality disorder attends his GP for a medication review. Olanzapine was started 18 months ago during a hospital admission after a crisis, and he still takes it every night. He has never had psychotic symptoms, bipolar disorder or depression. He has completed a year of dialectical behaviour therapy, still attends a skills group and has had no self-harm or crises for 9 months. He has put on a lot of weight since starting olanzapine and his latest HbA1c is in the prediabetes range. He wants to know whether he still needs it, but he is anxious about things going wrong without it.

Which is the most appropriate approach to his olanzapine?

options.A: Agree a gradual reduction aiming to stop it
options.B: Continue it long term to prevent further crises
options.C: Stop it today as it has no role in his condition
options.D: Switch to aripiprazole to limit further weight gain
options.E: Continue it and start metformin for his weight

correct_answer: A. Agree a gradual reduction aiming to stop it
why_correct: NICE advises that antipsychotics should not be used for the medium- or long-term treatment of borderline personality disorder, and that people without a comorbid illness who are taking drugs should have them reviewed with the aim of reducing and stopping unnecessary treatment. Psychological therapy is the core treatment and is working for him, so a gradual, agreed reduction with support from his therapy team is appropriate. Source: NICE CG78 Borderline personality disorder, 2009.
why_wrong: B. Antipsychotics should not be used long term for borderline personality disorder and do not prevent crises; psychological treatment does that. C. Stopping a long-term antipsychotic abruptly risks withdrawal effects, rebound insomnia and a crisis, so reduction should be gradual and agreed. D. Switching keeps him on an antipsychotic that has no indication rather than addressing whether he needs one. E. Treating a side effect of an unnecessary drug with another drug adds harm without benefit.
pearl: In BPD without comorbid illness, an antipsychotic started in a crisis is a deprescribing target — taper it, don't keep it.
thinking: BPD, no psychosis, bipolar disorder or depression  ↓  Olanzapine started in a crisis 18 months ago; metabolic harm  ↓  NICE: no medium- or long-term antipsychotic for BPD  ↓  Review aiming to reduce and stop unnecessary drugs  ↓  Gradual, agreed taper alongside psychological therapy
exam_trap: Either leaving a crisis-started antipsychotic in place indefinitely or stopping it abruptly.
takeaway: Review drugs started in a BPD crisis and taper unnecessary antipsychotics gradually while psychological therapy continues.
notes: New vignette (man, olanzapine, DBT, prediabetes; weight figure softened). Same learning point: CG78 1.3.5.2 (no medium/long-term antipsychotic) and review-to-reduce. Gradual taper is standard BNF practice. Distinct from DF047 (request for mood stabiliser → no medication).

presentation: Acute lower limb ischaemia — embolus after anterior myocardial infarction
stem:
A 64-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 2 weeks after she was treated for an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. An echocardiogram before discharge showed a large akinetic area at the left ventricular apex, and she went home on aspirin and ticagrelor. Three hours ago her left leg suddenly became painful. Below the knee the leg is white, cold and mottled, and the popliteal and foot pulses cannot be felt. She has numbness over the foot and toes but can wiggle her toes, and the calf is soft and not tender. Her right leg is warm with normal pulses. Her ECG shows sinus rhythm, and she has never had pain in her legs on walking.

What should be done immediately?

options.A: Outpatient arterial duplex scan and review in clinic
options.B: Low-molecular-weight heparin and review on tomorrow's ward round
options.C: Intravenous heparin and immediate vascular surgical referral
options.D: Aspirin 300 mg and raise the leg on pillows
options.E: Naftidrofuryl and a supervised exercise programme

correct_answer: C. Intravenous heparin and immediate vascular surgical referral
why_correct: A sudden painful, pale, cold, pulseless leg with numbness in someone whose other leg is normal and who has never had claudication is acute limb ischaemia from an embolus, and thrombus forming in the akinetic left ventricular apex after her anterior infarct is the likely source. Sensory loss with preserved movement means the limb is threatened but salvageable, so it needs immediate systemic heparin to stop the clot extending and emergency referral to the on-call vascular team for revascularisation (usually embolectomy) within hours. Imaging such as CT angiography may help planning but must not delay treatment. Source: European Society for Vascular Surgery Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Acute Limb Ischaemia, 2020; RCEMLearning Acute limb ischaemia, Royal College of Emergency Medicine.
why_wrong: A. An outpatient scan wastes the few hours in which a threatened limb can be saved. B. An adjustable intravenous heparin infusion is preferred before likely surgery, and waiting until tomorrow risks irreversible ischaemia. D. Aspirin alone does not stop clot propagation, and raising an ischaemic leg reduces its perfusion further. E. Naftidrofuryl and exercise are for intermittent claudication in chronic peripheral arterial disease, not an acutely threatened limb.
pearl: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, perishing cold, paraesthesia, paralysis: once sensation is lost the limb is threatened and the clock runs in hours.
thinking: Sudden painful, white, cold, pulseless leg  ↓  Other leg normal, no claudication = embolus  ↓  Recent anterior MI with akinetic LV apex = likely mural thrombus source  ↓  Numbness but toes moving = threatened, salvageable  ↓  IV heparin + immediate vascular referral for revascularisation
exam_trap: Treating it as chronic peripheral arterial disease and booking an outpatient duplex scan while the limb dies.
takeaway: Acute limb ischaemia with sensory loss needs immediate heparin and emergency vascular surgical referral.
notes: Dropped after clinical review (reviewer recommendation, accepted): a fourth PLAB question on acute limb ischaemia (S003, CARD053, ACU036 already test recognition and immediate management); the different embolic source is not what the question tests. Kept in drafts. Previous notes: New vignette (woman, readmitted 2 weeks post-STEMI with known LV apical thrombus, sinus rhythm; left leg). Same learning point and answer as MG058. Reviewer should note existing S003, CARD053 and ACU036 teach the same management but all use an AF embolus; this item uses a different embolic source (post-MI LV thrombus, sinus rhythm), so it is a different scenario with the same diagnosis, which the brief allows. If the reviewer judges the overlap too close, this is the item to drop.

presentation: Arterial embolism from new atrial fibrillation — long-term prevention
stem:
A 67-year-old man is recovering on the vascular ward 2 days after an embolectomy for a sudden cold, pulseless left leg. The leg is now warm with good foot pulses and the wound is dry. He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, has never had calf pain on walking, and his other leg has normal pulses. Telemetry shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with no P waves at around 90 beats per minute; he has never been told he has a heart rhythm problem. His kidney function is normal and he has never had a bleed.

Which antithrombotic plan should he be discharged on?

options.A: Lifelong low-dose aspirin
options.B: Lifelong clopidogrel on its own
options.C: A direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban, long term
options.D: Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 3 months, then aspirin alone
options.E: Warfarin for 3 months, then stop once the leg has recovered

correct_answer: C. A direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban, long term
why_correct: Newly found atrial fibrillation in a man with no chronic arterial disease makes left atrial thrombus the likely source of the embolus, and the source must be treated to prevent another. A previous systemic embolism alone puts him at high risk on CHA2DS2-VASc, and his age and diabetes add to it, so NICE recommends long-term anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban or rivaroxaban), taking bleeding risk into account; a vitamin K antagonist is used only if a DOAC is unsuitable. When to start it after the embolectomy is agreed between the vascular and medical teams, once haemostasis is secure and the postoperative bleeding risk allows. Source: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, 2021; European Society for Vascular Surgery Guidelines on Acute Limb Ischaemia, 2020.
why_wrong: A. NICE advises against aspirin alone for stroke and embolism prevention in atrial fibrillation because it is much less effective than anticoagulation. B. Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet and does not adequately prevent clot forming in the left atrium. D. Dual antiplatelet therapy is for atherosclerotic disease and stents, not cardioembolism from atrial fibrillation. E. Removing the embolus does not remove the atrial fibrillation, so the risk of further emboli continues and anticoagulation should be long term.
pearl: An embolus with no history of claudication: look to the heart, and atrial fibrillation is the usual culprit.
thinking: Embolic leg ischaemia, no chronic arterial disease  ↓  New irregularly irregular rhythm, no P waves = AF  ↓  Source: left atrial thrombus  ↓  Systemic embolism = high CHA2DS2-VASc risk  ↓  Long-term DOAC, started when the surgical team judge bleeding risk allows
exam_trap: Choosing antiplatelets because it looks like peripheral arterial disease, or stopping anticoagulation once the clot is out.
takeaway: Embolism from atrial fibrillation needs long-term DOAC anticoagulation, not antiplatelets, started once postoperative bleeding risk allows.
notes: New vignette (man, diabetes, left leg, telemetry). Same learning point. CHA2DS2-VASc arithmetic softened to words (the score is not the point: embolism alone puts him above the anticoagulation threshold, so the key does not hinge on recalling a cut-off). Reviewer timing wording (start once haemostasis allows, agreed with surgical team) retained. Not a duplicate of N9055 (diagnosis only).

presentation: Acute arm ischaemia — brachial embolus mistaken for stroke
stem:
An 81-year-old man with atrial fibrillation had his apixaban paused 5 days ago before a planned hernia repair; the operation was postponed and the apixaban was never restarted. Three hours ago he suddenly developed pain, numbness and weakness of his left hand and forearm. His speech is normal, his face is symmetrical and both legs move normally. The left hand and forearm are pale and cold. The radial and ulnar pulses are absent, and the brachial pulse can be felt in the upper arm but not at the elbow crease. Sensation is reduced across the whole hand and his grip is weak. His right arm is warm with normal pulses.

What should be done next?

options.A: Non-contrast CT head and referral to the stroke team
options.B: Intravenous thrombolysis on the hyperacute stroke pathway
options.C: Restart apixaban and book an outpatient arterial duplex scan
options.D: Nerve conduction studies and a neurology referral
options.E: IV heparin and urgent vascular surgery for embolectomy

correct_answer: E. IV heparin and urgent vascular surgery for embolectomy
why_correct: A pale, cold, painful arm with absent pulses below the elbow is acute upper limb ischaemia from an embolus lodged at the brachial bifurcation, most likely from the left atrium now that his anticoagulant has been stopped. Arm ischaemia is usually embolic because atherosclerosis rarely affects arm arteries. Because he has both sensory loss and weakness, the limb is threatened and needs intravenous heparin and urgent brachial embolectomy, often possible under local anaesthetic; anticoagulation with observation alone is reserved for an arm without neuromuscular deficit. Source: RCEMLearning Acute arm ischaemia, Royal College of Emergency Medicine; European Society for Vascular Surgery Guidelines on Acute Limb Ischaemia, 2020.
why_wrong: A. The deficit is confined to a cold, pulseless limb with normal speech and face, which points to ischaemia of the arm rather than the brain. B. Thrombolysis through the stroke pathway is not the treatment for a peripheral arterial embolus and adds bleeding risk without benefit. C. Restarting apixaban and waiting for an outpatient scan leaves an arm with sensory and motor loss to become non-viable. D. The numbness and weakness come from ischaemic nerves and muscle, and nerve studies would only delay revascularisation.
pearl: Before calling a numb, weak arm a stroke, feel the pulses and the temperature of the hand.
thinking: Sudden pain, numbness and weakness of one arm  ↓  Normal speech and face; arm pale, cold, pulseless  ↓  Brachial pulse lost at the elbow = embolus at brachial bifurcation  ↓  AF with anticoagulant stopped = cardiac source  ↓  Sensorimotor deficit = threatened limb  ↓  IV heparin + urgent brachial embolectomy
exam_trap: Labelling sudden arm weakness and numbness as a stroke and missing the cold, pulseless limb.
takeaway: Acute arm ischaemia with neurological deficit needs heparin and urgent brachial embolectomy.
notes: New vignette (man, apixaban paused peri-operatively and not restarted, left arm). Same learning point. Existing AF-embolus items (S003, CARD053, ACU036) are all lower limb; this tests the arm/stroke-mimic angle.

presentation: Acute ischaemic stroke from carotid dissection — thrombolysis
stem:
You are the medical registrar taking a FAST-positive pre-alert. The paramedic reports: 'A 34-year-old yoga instructor; her partner watched her lose her words and drop her cup with her right hand 50 minutes ago. She has had an ache in the left side of her neck since a rollercoaster ride at a theme park three days ago; no fall or head injury.' In resus she has expressive dysphasia and a weak right arm, a disabling deficit. Observations and capillary glucose are within normal limits. She is on no medication, has had no recent operation or bleeding, and platelets and coagulation are normal. Plain CT brain: no haemorrhage, no established infarct. CT angiogram: tapered narrowing of the cervical left internal carotid in keeping with dissection; intracranial vessels open, no large vessel occlusion.

What is the priority treatment?

options.A: Intravenous alteplase or tenecteplase
options.B: Antiplatelet only, because dissection bars thrombolysis
options.C: Therapeutic-dose intravenous heparin
options.D: Thrombectomy without any thrombolytic
options.E: Urgent stent insertion into the left carotid

correct_answer: A. Intravenous alteplase or tenecteplase
why_correct: She has a disabling acute ischaemic stroke caused by extracranial internal carotid artery dissection, well within the treatment window, with bleeding excluded, no head injury and no other contraindication. UK guidance states that patients with suspected dissection causing acute ischaemic stroke should receive intravenous thrombolysis if otherwise eligible, so dissection itself is not a reason to withhold it; NICE recommends alteplase or tenecteplase, given only within a specialist stroke service once the stroke team has completed the full eligibility and contraindication check. Antiplatelet or anticoagulant treatment for secondary prevention follows later, once post-thrombolysis imaging has excluded bleeding. Source: National Clinical Guideline for Stroke for the UK and Ireland, Intercollegiate Stroke Working Party, 2023 (section 3.8); NICE NG128 Stroke and TIA in over 16s, 2019; NICE TA990 Tenecteplase, 2024.
why_wrong: B. Extracranial dissection is not a contraindication to thrombolysis, so an antiplatelet alone denies an eligible patient the treatment most likely to reduce disability. C. Full-dose heparin in the hyperacute phase does not restore blood flow, increases the risk of bleeding into the infarct and would make her ineligible for thrombolysis. D. Thrombectomy is for a confirmed proximal large vessel occlusion, and her intracranial arteries are open. E. Stenting is reserved for the rare patient with recurrent ischaemia despite medical treatment, not first-line acute care.
pearl: Dissection is a cause of stroke, not a contraindication to thrombolysis.
thinking: Young woman, neck ache after a rollercoaster, no head injury, then sudden dysphasia and right arm weakness  ↓  50 minutes from witnessed onset, disabling deficit  ↓  CT: no bleed; CTA: left ICA dissection, no large vessel occlusion  ↓  dissection does not exclude thrombolysis  ↓  IV alteplase or tenecteplase via the stroke team
exam_trap: Assuming a torn artery wall makes thrombolysis too dangerous and giving an antiplatelet alone.
takeaway: Give intravenous thrombolysis to an otherwise eligible patient whose ischaemic stroke is caused by carotid dissection.
notes: Reworked for distance from AKT MG061 (stem Jaccard was 0.52): now a paramedic pre-alert to the medical registrar, 34-year-old woman, neck ache after a rollercoaster ride (a recognised minor-strain trigger of cervical artery dissection), dysphasia and right arm weakness. Eligibility safeguards kept explicit: witnessed onset 50 minutes, no fall or head injury, normal observations and glucose, no anticoagulant, no recent surgery or bleeding, normal platelets and clotting, CT without haemorrhage. Key does not hinge on recalling the time cut-off. Not a duplicate of DF028 (aspirin at 36 hours) or generic thrombolysis items.

presentation: Carotid dissection with TIA — antithrombotic treatment, not surgery
stem:
A 31-year-old software developer is seen in the TIA clinic. He says: 'Since a chiropractor manipulated my neck last week I've had a pain behind my left eye and down the left side of my neck. Last night my right hand went clumsy and I couldn't type for about twenty minutes, then it came back completely.' His GP gave him aspirin 300 mg at the time and referred him straight to the clinic. On examination his left upper eyelid droops slightly and the left pupil is smaller; there are no other signs. Diffusion-weighted MRI shows no infarct or bleed. CT angiography shows a long, tapering, high-grade narrowing of the left internal carotid beyond the bulb, typical of dissection. He is on no other medicines and has never had a bleed.

What is the most appropriate ongoing treatment?

options.A: Left carotid endarterectomy this week
options.B: Left carotid stent within 48 hours
options.C: Antiplatelet or anticoagulant for 3 months or more
options.D: No antithrombotic drug until a repeat scan at 3 months
options.E: Thrombolysis today, then oral aspirin daily

correct_answer: C. Antiplatelet or anticoagulant for 3 months or more
why_correct: NICE advises aspirin 300 mg immediately for suspected TIA unless contraindicated and specialist assessment within 24 hours, and both have been done; the question is the ongoing plan now that the cause is known. This TIA was caused by extracranial internal carotid artery dissection, and the narrowing is an intramural haematoma rather than atherosclerotic plaque. UK guidance is to treat cervical artery dissection causing stroke or TIA with either an antiplatelet or an anticoagulant for at least 3 months, with no proven advantage of one over the other; dual antiplatelet therapy for the first 21 days followed by a single antiplatelet may be considered. Most dissections heal with medical treatment, so surgery is not indicated. Source: National Clinical Guideline for Stroke for the UK and Ireland, Intercollegiate Stroke Working Party, 2023 (section 3.8); NICE NG128 Stroke and TIA in over 16s, 2019.
why_wrong: A. Endarterectomy is for symptomatic atherosclerotic carotid stenosis, not a dissected artery with an intramural haematoma, which usually heals with medical treatment. B. Stenting is reserved for the rare patient with recurrent ischaemia despite medical treatment. D. Withholding antithrombotic treatment leaves him unprotected in the early period when the stroke risk from dissection is highest. E. Thrombolysis treats acute ischaemic stroke within its time window, and his symptoms resolved overnight with no infarct on MRI.
pearl: A dissected carotid is not an atherosclerotic one: tablets, not the knife.
thinking: Eye and neck pain after neck manipulation + transient right hand weakness  ↓  suspected TIA: aspirin 300 mg at once + specialist assessment within 24 hours  ↓  left partial Horner + tapering ICA narrowing on CTA = dissection  ↓  narrowing is intramural haematoma, not plaque  ↓  antiplatelet or anticoagulant for at least 3 months
exam_trap: Applying the rule for severe symptomatic carotid stenosis and referring for urgent endarterectomy.
takeaway: Carotid dissection causing TIA or stroke is treated with an antiplatelet or anticoagulant for at least 3 months, not surgery.
notes: Reworked for distance from AKT MG062 (stem Jaccard was 0.51): history now in the patient's own words, 31-year-old software developer, dissection after chiropractic neck manipulation (a recognised trigger), left ICA with right hand TIA. Reviewer safety wording retained: stem states immediate aspirin 300 mg and immediate referral to specialist assessment (NG128 1.1.4-1.1.5), restated in why_correct. Not a duplicate of DF028 or DF027.

presentation: Neck pain, headache and focal deficit in a young adult — carotid dissection
stem:
A 41-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after her left arm and the left side of her face suddenly became weak, and she started bumping into things on her left. For 3 days she has had a constant pain in the right side of her neck spreading to her right forehead, which began after a roller-coaster ride. She has never had migraines. On examination she has weakness of the left face and arm, ignores objects on her left side, and has a slightly drooping right upper eyelid with a smaller right pupil. She is afebrile, and her blood pressure and capillary glucose are normal.

Which diagnosis best explains her presentation?

options.A: Hemiplegic migraine
options.B: Cluster headache
options.C: Internal carotid artery dissection
options.D: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
options.E: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST)

correct_answer: C. Internal carotid artery dissection
why_correct: Several days of one-sided neck and head pain after sudden neck movement, followed by sudden deficits in the opposite side of the body and a partial Horner syndrome on the side of the pain, is the classic picture of internal carotid artery dissection. Dissection is a leading cause of stroke in young adults: the right carotid supplies the right hemisphere (left face and arm weakness, left-sided neglect), and the damaged artery wall disrupts the sympathetic fibres to the right eye. She needs urgent CT or MR angiography and management on the stroke pathway. Source: National Clinical Guideline for Stroke for the UK and Ireland, Intercollegiate Stroke Working Party, 2023 (section 3.8).
why_wrong: A. Hemiplegic migraine usually starts in people with a history of migraine aura, the deficit spreads gradually, and it does not explain a Horner syndrome. B. Cluster headache can cause a brief Horner syndrome but gives short attacks of severe eye pain, not constant pain with hemiparesis and neglect. D. Subarachnoid haemorrhage causes a sudden thunderclap headache and does not explain days of neck pain followed by an arterial-territory deficit with Horner syndrome. E. Venous sinus thrombosis causes a progressive headache, seizures and raised-pressure features, not neck pain with a Horner syndrome.
pearl: Young stroke + neck or head pain + Horner on the side of the pain = carotid dissection.
thinking: Young woman, no vascular risk factors  ↓  3 days of right neck and head pain after sudden neck movement  ↓  Sudden left face and arm weakness + left neglect = right carotid territory  ↓  Right ptosis + miosis = partial Horner on the side of the pain  ↓  Right internal carotid artery dissection
exam_trap: Calling it a migraine variant because the patient is young and has a headache.
takeaway: Unilateral neck or head pain, a Horner syndrome on that side and opposite-sided deficits in a young adult suggest carotid dissection.
notes: New vignette (woman, roller-coaster, right ICA, neglect). Same learning point (diagnosis). DF027 is the same condition but tests the confirming investigation (CTA) after a resolved TIA; this item tests recognition of an evolving stroke, so the learning point differs. Migraine with aura replaced by hemiplegic migraine as a fairer distractor for a motor deficit.

presentation: Autonomic dysreflexia — bladder excluded, bowel next
stem:
A 31-year-old man with a complete T3 spinal cord injury from a motorbike crash 8 years ago is an inpatient on the plastic surgery ward with an infected pressure ulcer. He takes codeine for pain. He suddenly develops a throbbing headache and a stuffy nose, and his face and upper chest are flushed and sweating, while his legs are pale and cool. His blood pressure is 146/90 mmHg (his usual is about 90/55 mmHg) and his pulse is 50 beats per minute. The nurse has already sat him up with his legs down and loosened his clothing and leg-bag straps. His suprapubic catheter is draining clear urine freely, and a bladder scan shows almost no residual urine. His bowels have not opened for 3 days.

What should be done next?

options.A: Lie him flat with his legs raised on pillows
options.B: Give oral amlodipine and recheck his blood pressure in 1 hour
options.C: Remove the suprapubic catheter and insert a new one
options.D: Arrange an urgent non-contrast CT scan of his head
options.E: Check his rectum for faecal loading using lidocaine gel

correct_answer: E. Check his rectum for faecal loading using lidocaine gel
why_correct: A sudden headache, flushing and sweating above the injury level, blood pressure well above his usual baseline and a slow pulse in someone with a cord injury at T6 or above is autonomic dysreflexia. After sitting him up and loosening clothing, the priority is to find and remove the trigger below the lesion: the bladder is checked first, and once it is excluded the rectum is gently checked using lidocaine gel and any stool removed. Throughout, he stays upright and his blood pressure is monitored frequently following the local autonomic dysreflexia protocol. If it keeps rising, or stays high once the trigger is dealt with, it is treated promptly with a fast-acting antihypertensive under that protocol rather than continuing to search, with senior and spinal cord injury centre advice if symptoms do not settle quickly. Source: Autonomic dysreflexia guidance, Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital Spinal Cord Injury Centre; Autonomic dysreflexia, British Association of Urological Surgeons.
why_wrong: A. Lying him flat raises the blood pressure further, because sitting upright pools blood in the legs and lowers it. B. Amlodipine acts too slowly for autonomic dysreflexia and a 1-hour gap in monitoring is unsafe; the next step is removing the trigger, with fast-acting treatment if pressure keeps rising. C. The catheter is draining freely and the bladder is empty, so the bladder has already been excluded as the trigger. D. His headache is explained by autonomic dysreflexia, and leaving the ward for a scan delays removal of the trigger while his pressure may keep rising.
pearl: Autonomic dysreflexia: sit up, then bladder, then bowel — check the pressure every few minutes and treat it promptly if it climbs.
thinking: T3 cord injury + sudden headache, flushing above lesion, BP well above baseline, bradycardia  ↓  Autonomic dysreflexia  ↓  Already sat up, clothing loosened  ↓  Catheter draining, bladder empty = bladder excluded  ↓  Constipating codeine, bowels not open for 3 days  ↓  Gentle rectal check with lidocaine gel and remove stool
exam_trap: Changing a catheter that is already draining, or reaching for a slow antihypertensive instead of completing the search for the trigger.
takeaway: In autonomic dysreflexia, once the bladder is excluded, check the bowel using lidocaine gel while monitoring blood pressure closely.
notes: New vignette (man, T3, suprapubic catheter, codeine, plastic surgery ward). Re-angled under rule 2: the AKT nifedipine distractor made the key depend on recalling the local systolic >150 mmHg drug threshold; it is replaced by oral amlodipine with a 1-hour recheck, which is wrong regardless of the threshold, so the key now tests only 'bladder excluded → bowel next'. Reviewer safety wording (RNOH: BP every 2–5 min; systolic >150 mmHg → nifedipine 10 mg or GTN; SCI centre advice) kept in the explanation. Not a duplicate of GF039 (bladder trigger). Protocol detail moved here from why_correct at reviewer request (so the assessed explanation carries no number to memorise): RNOH guidance — blood pressure every 2–5 minutes; if systolic >150 mmHg, nifedipine 10 mg bite-and-swallow or GTN spray; seek spinal cord injury centre advice.

presentation: Central cord syndrome after a hyperextension injury
stem:
A 79-year-old woman falls forwards in her kitchen and hits her chin hard on the edge of the worktop. Paramedics bring her to the emergency department with her spine immobilised. Her hands feel 'on fire' and she cannot grip a cup or hold a pen with either hand, while she can lift both legs off the bed against some resistance. Sensation is patchy in both arms but normal in the legs and around the anus. She has not passed urine since the fall, and a bladder scan shows a large residual volume. CT of the cervical spine shows widespread degenerative changes with no fracture or malalignment.

Which diagnosis best explains her presentation?

options.A: Anterior spinal cord syndrome
options.B: Central cord syndrome
options.C: Brown-Séquard syndrome
options.D: Acute bilateral cervical radiculopathy
options.E: Posterior column (dorsal cord) syndrome

correct_answer: B. Central cord syndrome
why_correct: A blow to the chin or face forces the neck into hyperextension, which pinches a cervical canal already narrowed by degenerative disease and injures the centre of the cord, often without any fracture. Because the fibres to the arms and hands lie more centrally in the cord, the hands and arms are much weaker than the legs, sensory loss is variable, sacral sensation is usually spared and urinary retention is common. MRI is needed to show cord oedema or compression, because a normal CT does not exclude cord injury. Source: Central Cord Syndrome, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), 2026; NICE NG41 Spinal injury: assessment and initial management, 2016.
why_wrong: A. Anterior cord syndrome causes paralysis and loss of pain and temperature that affect the legs at least as much as the arms, with preserved joint position sense. C. Brown-Séquard syndrome causes weakness on one side and loss of pain and temperature on the other, not symmetrical weakness of both hands. D. Radiculopathy causes pain and weakness in a nerve-root distribution and does not explain urinary retention. E. Posterior column injury causes loss of joint position and vibration sense with relatively preserved power.
pearl: Older person + fall onto the face or chin + hands weaker than legs = central cord syndrome, even with a 'normal' CT.
thinking: Older woman with cervical spondylosis  ↓  Chin strike = hyperextension  ↓  Hands and arms much weaker than legs, burning arms, sacral sparing, retention  ↓  No fracture on CT  ↓  Central cord syndrome — needs MRI
exam_trap: Choosing anterior cord syndrome because both sides are weak, without noticing that the legs are relatively spared.
takeaway: Arms and hands weaker than legs after a hyperextension injury in an older person is central cord syndrome.
notes: New vignette (woman, chin on worktop, retention on bladder scan; MRC power grades softened to functional descriptions). Same learning point. Options reworded (only B and C match the AKT text); cauda equina replaced by bilateral cervical radiculopathy as a closer mimic. No near-duplicate in PLAB bank (NEU113 syringomyelia, NEU114 Brown-Séquard are different).

presentation: Spinal trauma with neurological signs and a normal CT — MRI next
stem:
A 45-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after being thrown head first from her horse. She arrives with a cervical collar and head blocks in place. She is fully alert, her observations are stable and she can recall the fall. She has neck pain, pins and needles in both hands, weakness of grip on both sides and reduced pinprick sensation over both hands. A consultant radiologist reports her cervical spine CT as showing no fracture and normal alignment.

What should be done next?

options.A: Remove the collar now that CT has excluded a fracture
options.B: Keep her immobilised and arrange an MRI scan
options.C: Flexion–extension X-rays of the cervical spine
options.D: Repeat the CT of the neck the following day
options.E: Discharge with analgesia and a GP review

correct_answer: B. Keep her immobilised and arrange an MRI scan
why_correct: A fall from a horse is a dangerous mechanism and she has neurological symptoms and signs, so CT was the correct first imaging in an adult. NICE says that if there is a neurological abnormality that could be due to spinal cord injury, MRI should be done after CT, whatever the CT shows, because cord, disc and ligament injury can occur without a fracture. Full in-line immobilisation is kept until the cord injury has been assessed. Source: NICE NG41 Spinal injury: assessment and initial management, 2016 (recs 1.5.6 and 1.5.7).
why_wrong: A. A normal CT does not exclude cord or ligament injury when there are neurological signs, so removing the collar is unsafe. C. Flexion and extension views are dangerous with a possible cord injury and do not show the cord. D. A repeat CT will not show the soft-tissue or cord injury that is the concern, and waiting delays diagnosis. E. A patient with new neurological signs after spinal trauma cannot be discharged before the cord has been imaged.
pearl: Neurological signs after spinal trauma mean MRI after CT, even when the CT is normal.
thinking: Fall from a horse = dangerous mechanism  ↓  Neck pain + bilateral hand weakness and sensory change  ↓  CT cervical spine first in adults: no fracture  ↓  Neurological abnormality still unexplained  ↓  Keep immobilised + MRI (NG41 1.5.7)
exam_trap: Clearing the cervical spine because the CT is normal despite neurological signs.
takeaway: If spinal trauma causes neurological signs, do MRI after CT even when the CT is normal.
notes: New vignette (woman, horse fall, hand signs). Same learning point (NG41 1.5.7, rechecked on nice.org.uk 8 Oct 2026). GF037 (maintain immobilisation on arrival, before imaging) has a similar presentation but a different learning point; this item is about what follows a normal CT.

presentation: Diabetic gastroparesis — first-line dietary management
stem:
A 39-year-old man has had type 1 diabetes since childhood and has diabetic retinopathy, erectile dysfunction and numb feet. He attends the diabetes clinic with 4 months of nausea, bloating, feeling full after a few mouthfuls and vomiting food he ate the evening before. His glucose readings have become unpredictable, often dropping within an hour or two of his meal-time insulin and running high later. He has not lost weight and has no difficulty swallowing or bleeding. Gastroscopy is normal. A gastric emptying study, done while his glucose was within target, confirms slow emptying.

Which is the most appropriate first step in his management?

options.A: Start domperidone and continue it long term
options.B: A high-fibre diet with plenty of raw fruit and vegetables
options.C: Start lansoprazole and repeat the gastroscopy in 2 months
options.D: Small-particle-size diet, e.g. mashed or puréed food
options.E: Refer for a gastric electrical stimulator

correct_answer: D. Small-particle-size diet, e.g. mashed or puréed food
why_correct: Early fullness, bloating and vomiting of food eaten hours earlier, with hypoglycaemia soon after meal-time insulin and later highs, in a man with long-standing type 1 diabetes and other microvascular complications is diabetic gastroparesis from autonomic neuropathy. The diagnosis is confirmed by delayed emptying measured while glucose was in range, because high glucose itself slows gastric emptying. NICE advises a small-particle-size diet (mashed or puréed food) to relieve symptoms; antiemetic or prokinetic drugs are considered for vomiting, and specialist referral is for symptoms that do not respond. Source: NICE NG17 Type 1 diabetes in adults (1.14.23–1.14.28), 2015, updated 2022.
why_wrong: A. MHRA advice restricts domperidone to the lowest dose for the shortest time because of cardiac risk, and NICE reserves it for exceptional circumstances in gastroparesis. B. Fibre and raw fruit and vegetables empty slowly from the stomach and can worsen symptoms or form a bezoar. C. Gastroscopy is already normal, so acid suppression and a repeat scope will not treat slow gastric emptying. E. Gastric electrical stimulation is a specialist option for severe symptoms that fail diet and drugs, not a first step.
pearl: In diabetic gastroparesis food reaches the gut late, so meal-time insulin causes early hypos and later highs.
thinking: Long-standing type 1 diabetes with microvascular and autonomic complications  ↓  Early fullness, vomiting of old food, erratic glucose  ↓  Normal gastroscopy, slow emptying with glucose in range  ↓  Diabetic gastroparesis  ↓  First step: small-particle-size diet; drugs for vomiting; specialist if refractory
exam_trap: Going straight to long-term domperidone, which the MHRA restricts to short courses because of cardiac risk.
takeaway: Diabetic gastroparesis: start with a small-particle-size (mashed or puréed) diet before drugs or specialist procedures.
notes: New vignette (man, erectile dysfunction as autonomic clue). Same learning point (NG17 1.14.23, rechecked on nice.org.uk 8 Oct 2026). Insulin pump (NG17 1.14.25 'consider') deliberately not offered as an option, as in the source. GAS111 asks only for the diagnosis, so not a duplicate.

presentation: Orthostatic hypotension — diabetic autonomic neuropathy and an alpha-blocker
stem:
A 71-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 20 years sees her GP after two falls at home in the past month, both when she got up from a chair after breakfast. She feels light-headed and her vision greys out when she stands. She has diabetic retinopathy and numbness in both feet. Her blood pressure has been hard to control, and doxazosin was added to her lisinopril and amlodipine 2 months ago. Lying, her blood pressure is 158/86 mmHg with a pulse of 76 beats per minute; after 3 minutes standing it is 124/70 mmHg with a pulse of 77 beats per minute. Her ECG, capillary glucose and kidney function are normal.

What should the GP do first?

options.A: Start fludrocortisone and recheck in 4 weeks
options.B: Start midodrine three times a day
options.C: Advise her to cut down on salt and fluids
options.D: Arrange a 24-hour ambulatory ECG
options.E: Stop doxazosin; advise rising slowly

correct_answer: E. Stop doxazosin; advise rising slowly
why_correct: A large fall in systolic pressure on standing with no rise in pulse is orthostatic hypotension, and the unchanged heart rate points to autonomic neuropathy, which fits her long-standing diabetes with other microvascular complications. NICE advises looking for causes, including reviewing medicines, and warns that blood pressure-lowering drugs add to the postural effect of autonomic neuropathy; the recently added alpha-blocker is the obvious culprit. Stopping it, with simple measures such as getting up slowly and keeping up fluid intake, comes first, and her blood pressure targets should then be based on standing readings. Source: NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults, 2019, updated 2026; NICE NG28 Type 2 diabetes in adults (autonomic neuropathy), 2026.
why_wrong: A. Fludrocortisone is considered only if symptoms persist after medicine review and non-drug measures, and it can worsen her lying hypertension. B. Midodrine is used for orthostatic hypotension from autonomic failure only after correctable causes such as offending drugs have been dealt with. C. Cutting salt and fluids would reduce circulating volume and make orthostatic hypotension worse. D. Symptoms only on standing with a reproducible postural drop and a normal ECG point to orthostatic hypotension rather than an arrhythmia.
pearl: A big postural drop with no rise in pulse suggests autonomic failure rather than dehydration.
thinking: Falls and light-headedness on standing  ↓  Large systolic fall, pulse unchanged  ↓  Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (long-standing diabetes, microvascular disease)  ↓  Recently added doxazosin making it worse  ↓  Stop the alpha-blocker + non-drug measures  ↓  Pressor drugs only if symptoms persist
exam_trap: Starting a pressor drug before removing the alpha-blocker that is causing the problem.
takeaway: In diabetic autonomic neuropathy with orthostatic hypotension, stop offending antihypertensives and use non-drug measures first.
notes: New vignette (woman, falls after breakfast, lisinopril + amlodipine + doxazosin). BP and pulse readings kept (needed to show the drop and fixed heart rate); the calculated drop is left in words. Reviewer note: GER015 (generic older patient with OH → review medicines and hydration, rise slowly) teaches a related principle; this item is a different scenario (diabetic autonomic neuropathy, specific alpha-blocker, pressor-drug distractors).

presentation: Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness — autonomic neuropathy and driving
stem:
A 49-year-old woman has had type 1 diabetes for 30 years and has retinopathy, numb feet and autonomic neuropathy causing postural dizziness. She attends the diabetes clinic 2 weeks after colleagues found her confused and sweating at her desk with a very low glucose; an ambulance crew treated her and she did not need admission. It was her first severe low. She says that for several months she has had no warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia and now only knows her glucose is low when her continuous glucose monitor alarms. She holds a car licence and drives her children to school every day.

What should she be told about driving?

options.A: Stop driving and inform the DVLA
options.B: Drive only if her glucose is above 5 mmol/L before each trip
options.C: Drive provided her sensor low alert is always switched on
options.D: Keep driving, as she has had only one severe episode
options.E: Drive if she checks her glucose at least every 2 hours en route

correct_answer: A. Stop driving and inform the DVLA
why_correct: She has impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia: she has lost her warning symptoms and relies on her sensor alarm, and autonomic neuropathy makes loss of the sympathetic warning signs more likely. For Group 1 (car) drivers, the DVLA states that a person with impaired awareness must not drive and must notify the DVLA, and may resume only once a medical report confirms that adequate awareness has returned; sensor alarms supplement, but cannot replace, the driver's own awareness. NICE also advises structured education, strict avoidance of hypoglycaemia and review of insulin doses, which can restore awareness. Source: DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: diabetes mellitus, 2025; NICE NG17 Type 1 diabetes in adults (1.9), 2015, updated 2022.
why_wrong: B. A pre-driving glucose check is routine advice for insulin-treated drivers with normal awareness, but it does not make driving safe or legal when awareness is impaired. C. The DVLA states that a driver who depends on sensor alarms to recognise a low must stop driving and notify the DVLA. D. The number of severe episodes is not the issue here; impaired awareness on its own means she must not drive. E. Regular glucose checks on journeys are a requirement for drivers allowed to drive, not a substitute for adequate awareness.
pearl: For the DVLA, adequate awareness means recognising a low in time to stop the car safely; a sensor alarm does not count.
thinking: Long-standing type 1 diabetes with autonomic neuropathy  ↓  No warning symptoms, relies on CGM alarm, severe hypo  ↓  Impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia  ↓  DVLA Group 1: must not drive, must notify DVLA  ↓  Education and hypo avoidance; resume only after medical report confirms awareness
exam_trap: Counting severe episodes (only one) and missing that impaired awareness alone stops a car driver from driving.
takeaway: Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness means a car driver must stop driving and notify the DVLA until awareness is restored.
notes: New vignette (woman, found at work, school run). Glucose value softened to 'very low'. Key does not hinge on a numeric threshold: the DVLA rule tested is qualitative (impaired awareness / dependence on alarms → stop and notify; wording rechecked on gov.uk 8 Oct 2026). Distractor D explanation avoids the '2 in 12 months' figure. Not a duplicate of END046 (restoring awareness by relaxing targets).

presentation: Ewing sarcoma — diaphyseal lesion with systemic features
stem:
A 13-year-old girl is seen in the paediatric assessment unit with 2 months of pain in her left shin that is getting worse and now keeps her awake. Her parents say she has seemed washed out, has had fevers on and off and her clothes have become loose. She has not injured the leg. She has a low-grade fever, and there is a tender, firm swelling over the middle of the left tibia. Her white cell count, CRP and ESR are all raised. An X-ray shows a poorly defined, 'moth-eaten' destructive lesion in the middle of the tibial shaft, with layers of new bone along its surface like the skin of an onion and a large soft-tissue mass.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Osteosarcoma
options.B: Ewing sarcoma
options.C: Subacute osteomyelitis (Brodie abscess)
options.D: Osteoid osteoma
options.E: Langerhans cell histiocytosis

correct_answer: B. Ewing sarcoma
why_correct: Ewing sarcoma typically affects children and teenagers, often in the shaft (diaphysis) of a long bone or the pelvis, and fever, weight loss and raised inflammatory markers are common, so it can mimic infection. The classic X-ray shows a permeative 'moth-eaten' lytic lesion with a layered 'onion-skin' periosteal reaction and a large soft-tissue mass. She needs very urgent referral to a specialist bone sarcoma service for MRI and biopsy. Source: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (1.11 sarcomas), 2015, updated 2026; CCLG Ewing sarcoma factsheet, 2022.
why_wrong: A. Osteosarcoma usually arises in the metaphysis around the knee and typically shows new bone formation with a 'sunburst' reaction, without prominent systemic upset. C. A Brodie abscess is a small, well-defined metaphyseal lucency with a sclerotic rim, not a destructive lesion with a large soft-tissue mass. D. Osteoid osteoma causes night pain relieved by NSAIDs and shows a small lucent nidus with surrounding sclerosis, with no systemic illness. E. Langerhans cell histiocytosis usually causes punched-out lytic lesions, often in the skull of younger children, without an onion-skin reaction and large soft-tissue mass.
pearl: Child or teenager + diaphyseal lesion + onion-skin periosteal reaction + fever = think Ewing sarcoma, not just infection.
thinking: Teenager with 2 months of worsening night bone pain and swelling  ↓  Fever, weight loss, raised inflammatory markers  ↓  X-ray: permeative mid-shaft lesion, onion-skin periosteum, soft-tissue mass  ↓  Ewing sarcoma  ↓  Very urgent specialist sarcoma referral for MRI and biopsy
exam_trap: Calling it osteomyelitis because of the fever and raised markers, and missing the tumour features on the X-ray.
takeaway: Ewing sarcoma can mimic infection; a diaphyseal permeative lesion with onion-skin periosteal reaction in a young person needs very urgent sarcoma referral.
notes: New vignette (girl, tibial shaft; lab values softened to 'raised'). Same learning point. Options reworded (3 of 5 match AKT text): chondrosarcoma replaced by Langerhans cell histiocytosis (a more plausible paediatric mimic) and osteomyelitis framed as subacute/Brodie abscess. Not a duplicate of RHE049 (osteosarcoma, sunburst).

presentation: Bone metastases — sclerotic lesions from prostate cancer
stem:
A 68-year-old man sees his GP with 6 weeks of pain in his upper back and ribs that wakes him at night. For the past year he has had to wait before his urine starts, and he dribbles afterwards. He has no leg weakness, numbness or problems controlling his bladder or bowels. His alkaline phosphatase is raised, and his calcium and kidney function are normal. X-rays of the spine and ribs show several dense, white (sclerotic) deposits.

Which underlying cancer is most likely?

options.A: Renal cell carcinoma
options.B: Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder
options.C: Multiple myeloma
options.D: Prostate cancer
options.E: Small-cell lung cancer

correct_answer: D. Prostate cancer
why_correct: The cancers that most often spread to bone are prostate, breast, lung, kidney and thyroid, and bone pain that is worse at night is a typical presentation. In an older man with lower urinary tract symptoms, a raised alkaline phosphatase and multiple sclerotic (bone-forming) deposits, prostate cancer is by far the most likely primary. PSA testing and urgent referral should follow, with a low threshold for emergency assessment if any features of spinal cord compression develop. Source: Cancer Research UK, Secondary bone cancer, 2023; NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015, updated 2026.
why_wrong: A. Renal cell carcinoma often spreads to bone but typically causes lytic, often expansile, lesions rather than sclerotic ones. B. Bladder cancer can cause urinary symptoms but spreads to bone less often and does not typically cause sclerotic deposits. C. Myeloma causes punched-out lytic lesions, often with raised calcium, and the alkaline phosphatase is usually normal. E. Lung cancer deposits are mostly lytic, and nothing here points to a lung primary.
pearl: Sclerotic bone metastases in a man: think prostate; in a woman: think breast.
thinking: Older man with night bone pain in spine and ribs  ↓  Hesitancy and terminal dribbling  ↓  Raised ALP, normal calcium, sclerotic deposits  ↓  Osteoblastic metastases  ↓  Prostate primary — PSA and urgent referral; watch for cord compression
exam_trap: Choosing kidney or bladder cancer because of the urinary symptoms, ignoring that the lesions are sclerotic.
takeaway: Sclerotic bone deposits in an older man with urinary symptoms point to prostate cancer.
notes: New vignette (thoracic spine and ribs, hesitancy/dribbling; ALP figure softened to 'raised'). Same learning point. Options reworded (2 of 5 match AKT text): thyroid replaced by multiple myeloma as a commoner lytic mimic. Not a duplicate of BX1023 (known prostate cancer, red-flag feature) or DS094.

presentation: Unexplained bone pain in a child — very urgent direct-access X-ray
stem:
An 11-year-old boy is brought to his GP by his father with 4 weeks of aching in his right lower leg, just below the knee. The ache is there most of the time, is gradually getting worse and has started waking him at night. He plays football but cannot remember any injury. He is otherwise well, with no fever or weight loss. There is mild tenderness over the upper part of the right tibia with no swelling or redness, and the knee and ankle move fully. The left leg is normal.

What should the GP do next?

options.A: Reassure that these are growing pains and review if needed
options.B: Physiotherapy for a probable football strain
options.C: Routine referral to the paediatric orthopaedic clinic
options.D: Suspected cancer pathway referral to the bone sarcoma service
options.E: Very urgent direct-access X-ray of the right tibia

correct_answer: E. Very urgent direct-access X-ray of the right tibia
why_correct: Unexplained, persistent and worsening bone pain that wakes a child at night, with no injury, needs a bone tumour excluded. NICE recommends considering a very urgent (within 48 hours) direct-access X-ray, which the GP can request without a specialist referral, to assess for bone sarcoma in children and young people with unexplained bone pain or swelling. If the X-ray suggests sarcoma, he then needs a very urgent specialist referral. Source: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (1.11.2–1.11.3), 2015, updated 2026.
why_wrong: A. Growing pains are bilateral, come and go, and settle by morning; constant one-sided pain localised to one bone is not growing pains. B. There is no injury to explain the pain, and treating it as a strain risks delaying the diagnosis of a bone tumour. C. A routine referral would delay the X-ray that NICE advises within 48 hours. D. A suspected cancer pathway referral (the fast-track route to a specialist for suspected cancer) follows an X-ray suggesting sarcoma; for children, NICE advises the very urgent X-ray first.
pearl: Unilateral bone pain that wakes a child at night is not 'growing pains' until an X-ray says so.
thinking: Child with persistent, worsening, one-sided bone pain  ↓  Night pain, no injury  ↓  Unexplained bone pain  ↓  NICE NG12: very urgent direct-access X-ray  ↓  X-ray suggests sarcoma → very urgent specialist referral
exam_trap: Labelling one-sided night bone pain as growing pains or a sports strain and delaying imaging.
takeaway: Unexplained bone pain or swelling in a child or young person needs a very urgent direct-access X-ray.
notes: New vignette (boy, proximal tibia). NG12 1.11.2–1.11.3 rechecked on nice.org.uk 8 Oct 2026. The key is the route (very urgent X-ray first vs suspected cancer referral), not the 48-hour figure, which is kept only in the explanation. Not a duplicate of DS094 (adult with known cancer) or DR004 (knee pain → examine hips).

presentation: Soft-tissue lump with uncertain features — ultrasound to characterise
stem:
A 52-year-old man shows his GP a lump on the outer side of his left upper arm that his wife noticed 3 months ago. He thinks it has stayed the same size, and it does not hurt. The GP finds a smooth, rubbery, 3 cm lump that seems to lie just beneath the skin, but it is firmer than a typical lipoma and its edges are difficult to feel clearly. There is no central punctum, the skin over it looks normal and there are no enlarged lymph nodes. He is otherwise well. The GP is not confident whether this is a lipoma or something else.

What should the GP do next?

options.A: Non-urgent ultrasound scan to characterise the lump
options.B: Reassure him that it is a lipoma and discharge
options.C: Remove it at the practice minor surgery session
options.D: Suspected cancer pathway referral to the sarcoma team
options.E: Plain X-ray of the left upper arm

correct_answer: A. Non-urgent ultrasound scan to characterise the lump
why_correct: When a subcutaneous lump cannot be confidently diagnosed clinically, ultrasound is the first-line test: it shows whether the lump is fatty, cystic or solid and whether it lies above or below the fascia. NICE's urgent direct-access ultrasound is for an unexplained lump that is increasing in size, and the British Sarcoma Group red flags are a lump that is growing, larger than 5 cm or painful, with deep lumps more concerning; this lump has none of these, so a suspected cancer referral is not indicated. Because the GP is uncertain, it should not simply be dismissed either, so a non-urgent ultrasound is arranged; if it grows or becomes painful, or the scan is suspicious or uncertain with persisting concern, a suspected cancer pathway referral follows. Source: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (1.11.4–1.11.5), 2015, updated 2026; British Sarcoma Group UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas, 2016; NHS Lipoma.
why_wrong: B. Reassurance alone is only appropriate when the GP is confident the lump is a typical benign lesion, which is not the case here. C. Removing an undiagnosed lump without imaging risks incomplete excision of a deeper or malignant lesion and can compromise later sarcoma surgery. D. He has no sarcoma red flags and no imaging yet, so a fast-track suspected cancer referral is not justified at this stage. E. A plain X-ray shows bone, not soft-tissue detail, so it cannot characterise the lump.
pearl: If you cannot be sure a soft-tissue lump is a lipoma, scan it before you cut it.
thinking: Subcutaneous lump, GP uncertain of diagnosis  ↓  No red flags: stable size, under 5 cm, painless, superficial  ↓  NICE urgent criteria not met; no suspected cancer referral  ↓  Needs characterising, not reassurance: ultrasound  ↓  Growth, pain or suspicious scan → suspected cancer pathway referral
exam_trap: Excising an uncertain lump in minor surgery without imaging, which can compromise management if it turns out to be a sarcoma.
takeaway: A soft-tissue lump with uncertain features but no red flags should be characterised with ultrasound; growth makes it urgent.
notes: New vignette (man, upper arm). Reviewer framing retained: NG12 1.11.4 urgent criteria (increasing size) and BSG red flags explicitly not met, so ultrasound is non-urgent characterisation; option A carries no urgency qualifier and no 'urgent ultrasound' distractor is offered, to avoid an urgency dispute (as in the source). NG12 1.11.4 rechecked on nice.org.uk 8 Oct 2026. Not a duplicate of DF059 (growing deep 6 cm thigh lump → urgent direct-access ultrasound): different scenario and the opposite urgency point. PCDS caveat from source still applies.

presentation: Aspiration lung abscess — likely organisms
stem:
A 40-year-old woman sees her GP with 2 weeks of fever, sweats and a cough bringing up foul-smelling, bad-tasting sputum. A month ago she took an overdose of sleeping tablets and was found drowsy at home the next morning; she was treated in hospital and is now under the community mental health team. Her teeth are in poor condition with inflamed, bleeding gums. Her temperature is 38.2°C and there are coarse crackles at the back of the right lower chest. A chest X-ray shows a thick-walled cavity containing an air-fluid level in the superior segment of the right lower lobe.

Which organisms are the most likely cause?

options.A: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
options.B: Mixed oral anaerobes with streptococci
options.C: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
options.D: Legionella pneumophila and other atypicals
options.E: Pneumocystis jirovecii (PCP)

correct_answer: B. Mixed oral anaerobes with streptococci
why_correct: A period of reduced consciousness plus severe gum disease is the classic set-up for aspiration of oral secretions, which progresses over days to weeks to a lung abscess in a dependent segment (the superior segment of a lower lobe or the posterior segment of an upper lobe). Most such abscesses are polymicrobial, dominated by oral anaerobes (such as Peptostreptococcus, Prevotella, Bacteroides and Fusobacterium) with microaerophilic streptococci, which explains the foul sputum and why antibiotics must cover anaerobes. Source: Lung abscess, Patient.info Professional (UK), 2023; Lung Abscess, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), current edition.
why_wrong: A. Tuberculosis causes upper-lobe cavities that rarely contain an air-fluid level, and the subacute post-aspiration course with putrid sputum points to anaerobes. C. Pseudomonas mainly affects people with structural lung disease, ventilation or immunosuppression, none of which she has. D. Legionella and other atypical organisms cause pneumonia without cavitation in an immunocompetent person and do not produce putrid sputum. E. Pneumocystis causes diffuse bilateral interstitial change in immunosuppressed patients, not a single cavity with a fluid level.
pearl: Foul sputum plus a cavity in a dependent segment after reduced consciousness means anaerobes until proven otherwise.
thinking: Overdose with reduced consciousness + poor dentition  ↓  Aspiration of oral flora  ↓  Necrotising infection in a dependent segment  ↓  Cavity with air-fluid level and foul sputum  ↓  Polymicrobial oral anaerobes with streptococci
exam_trap: Choosing tuberculosis because there is a cavity, ignoring the aspiration history and putrid sputum.
takeaway: Aspiration lung abscess is usually polymicrobial with oral anaerobes, so treatment must cover anaerobes.
notes: New vignette (woman, sedative overdose, superior segment RLL). Same learning point. Avoided alcohol scenarios of DF043/RES038 (management and diagnosis respectively); this item asks for organisms. Options: 3 of 5 match AKT text.

presentation: Lung abscess — persistent cavity in an improving patient
stem:
A 72-year-old woman with Parkinson's disease and swallowing difficulty is on day 12 of intravenous antibiotics for a left lower lobe lung abscess. She has had no fever for 5 days, she is coughing up much less sputum, and her CRP has fallen to a small fraction of its value on admission. She is eating a modified-texture diet, is comfortable on room air and is mobilising with the physiotherapist. A repeat chest X-ray shows the cavity is still there, though its air-fluid level is smaller. Her daughter asks whether the abscess should now be drained.

What should be done next?

options.A: Stop antibiotics now that she has been afebrile for 5 days
options.B: CT-guided percutaneous drainage of the cavity
options.C: Switch to oral antibiotics and repeat chest imaging
options.D: Refer for surgical resection of the left lower lobe
options.E: Escalate to intravenous meropenem

correct_answer: C. Switch to oral antibiotics and repeat chest imaging
why_correct: She is improving clinically and biochemically, so the treatment is working, and most lung abscesses resolve with antibiotics alone. Treatment is prolonged, usually starting intravenously and switching to oral therapy once the patient is afebrile and stable, often for several weeks in total, with the duration guided by clinical response and follow-up imaging. X-ray resolution lags well behind clinical improvement, so a persisting cavity in an improving patient is expected and is not a reason to drain. Source: Lung abscess, Patient.info Professional (UK), 2023; Lung Abscess, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), current edition.
why_wrong: A. Stopping at this point risks relapse, because lung abscess needs a prolonged course well beyond the fever settling. B. Percutaneous drainage is kept for abscesses that fail to respond to antibiotics, not a slowly resolving cavity in an improving patient. D. Lobectomy is reserved for failed medical treatment or complications such as massive haemoptysis. E. Her settling fever and falling CRP show the current antibiotic is effective, so escalation adds harm without benefit.
pearl: Treat the patient, not the X-ray: the cavity lags weeks behind clinical recovery.
thinking: Lung abscess on IV antibiotics  ↓  Afebrile, less sputum, CRP falling  ↓  Responding to treatment  ↓  Cavity persists — expected radiological lag  ↓  Oral step-down, prolonged course, repeat imaging; drain only if failing
exam_trap: Draining or escalating because the cavity is still visible despite clear clinical improvement.
takeaway: Lung abscess needs a prolonged antibiotic course; a persisting cavity in an improving patient is not an indication for drainage.
notes: New vignette (woman, Parkinson's dysphagia, left lower lobe; CRP values softened to words; antibiotic left generic). Same learning point. Total duration deliberately not stated, as sources vary. Not a duplicate of DF043 (initial management) or GF020 (liver abscess failing antibiotics → drain).

presentation: Cavitating lung lesion
stem:
A 57-year-old woman who smoked 30 cigarettes a day until last year is admitted with 10 days of cough, malaise and poor appetite. Her chest X-ray shows a solitary cavity in the right upper lobe. The respiratory registrar is considering a lung abscess, a cavitating lung cancer and pulmonary tuberculosis while sputum results and a CT scan are awaited.

Which further finding would point most towards a lung abscess?

options.A: A thick, irregular cavity wall with a nodular inner lining
options.B: Raised serum calcium with no fever and a normal white count
options.C: Four months of drenching night sweats and weight loss
options.D: A household contact with a long-standing productive cough
options.E: Foul-tasting sputum that began after a recent seizure

correct_answer: E. Foul-tasting sputum that began after a recent seizure
why_correct: Foul-smelling or foul-tasting sputum after a period of reduced consciousness, such as a seizure, suggests aspiration of mouth anaerobes, the classic cause of a lung abscess. An abscess usually causes an acute febrile illness, and the cavity often has an air–fluid level with a fairly smooth inner wall. A thick, irregular wall and no inflammatory response favour carcinoma, while a long constitutional illness or a contact history favours tuberculosis. Source: Lung abscess, Patient.info Professional (UK), 2023; Lung Abscess, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), current edition.
why_wrong: A. A thick, irregular wall with a nodular lining is typical of a cavitating carcinoma. B. High calcium without fever or a raised white count suggests a squamous cell carcinoma secreting PTH-related peptide. C. Months of night sweats and weight loss favour tuberculosis or cancer rather than an acute abscess. D. Close contact with someone who has a chronic productive cough raises the possibility of tuberculosis.
pearl: Aspiration risk plus foul sputum is the clue to a lung abscess, but in a smoker cancer must still be excluded once the infection settles.
thinking: Cavity on chest X-ray  ↓  abscess, cancer or TB?  ↓  aspiration event + foul sputum + acute fever = abscess  ↓  thick irregular wall or high calcium = cancer; long illness or contact = TB
exam_trap: Choosing the long history of night sweats and weight loss as 'infective' when it points to tuberculosis or cancer rather than an abscess.
takeaway: Foul sputum after an episode of reduced consciousness is the strongest pointer to an aspiration lung abscess.
notes: Same learning point as MG078 (features favouring abscess over cancer/TB). New vignette (woman, ex-smoker, seizure as the aspiration event). The 20 mm wall-thickness figure was softened to words (rule 1). RES038 tests the diagnosis of abscess from a classic picture; this item tests the discriminating feature within a cavity differential, so not a repeat. Malignancy should still be excluded in a smoker (pearl).

presentation: Abdominal pain in a child
stem:
A 10-year-old girl is brought to the children's emergency department with a day and a half of pain around the umbilicus and in the lower right abdomen. She has had a runny nose and cough for 4 days, and her temperature is 38.3°C. She is tender in the right lower abdomen without guarding or rebound. Abdominal ultrasound shows several enlarged lymph nodes in the mesentery of the right lower quadrant and a normal-calibre, compressible appendix. After a period of observation with paracetamol, her pain has eased and she has managed a drink and some toast.

Which is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Discharge with regular analgesia and safety-netting
options.B: Oral co-amoxiclav for 7 days, then review by her GP
options.C: CT scan of the abdomen to exclude appendicitis
options.D: Admit for intravenous fluids and keep her nil by mouth
options.E: Laparoscopic appendicectomy on the next list

correct_answer: A. Discharge with regular analgesia and safety-netting
why_correct: Enlarged mesenteric nodes with a normal appendix on ultrasound, after a viral illness, in a child who is improving, fit mesenteric adenitis. It is usually self-limiting, so care is supportive with regular paracetamol or ibuprofen and fluids at home.
