Parents need clear advice to return if the pain worsens or settles in the right lower abdomen, vomiting starts, the fever persists or she stops drinking, because appendicitis can still be missed. Source: Mesenteric lymphadenitis patient information, West Hertfordshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust.
why_wrong: B. Mesenteric adenitis usually follows a viral infection and antibiotics are rarely needed. C. CT adds radiation and is unnecessary when ultrasound has shown a normal appendix and she is improving. D. She is eating and drinking, so intravenous fluids and fasting are not needed. E. A normal appendix on ultrasound with clinical improvement does not justify surgery.
pearl: Mesenteric adenitis is a diagnosis made only after appendicitis is reasonably excluded, so the safety-net matters as much as the reassurance.
thinking: Child with right-sided abdominal pain after a viral illness  ↓  ultrasound: enlarged mesenteric nodes, normal appendix  ↓  improving and eating  ↓  discharge with analgesia and safety-netting
exam_trap: Giving antibiotics 'just in case' or requesting CT in a child who is clearly getting better.
takeaway: An improving child with mesenteric adenitis on ultrasound can go home with simple analgesia and clear return advice.
notes: Same learning point as MG080 (overall management decision after ultrasound). New vignette (girl, ED, coryzal illness). Distinct from GF049 (diagnosis), GF050 (content of safety-net advice) and GF051 (ultrasound as next test). Follows the NHS trust leaflet (antibiotics rarely needed) as in the source.

presentation: Abdominal pain in a child
stem:
A 9-year-old girl was admitted to the children's ward last night for observation. She had a cough and sore throat last week, and an ultrasound on arrival showed enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes but could not visualise the appendix, so a provisional diagnosis of mesenteric adenitis was made. This morning her pain is constant, lies in the right iliac fossa and is made worse by walking or by bumping the bed. She has vomited three times and does not want to eat. Her temperature is 38.6°C and heart rate 130/min, and there is guarding with rebound tenderness in the right iliac fossa.

Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Discharge home with paracetamol and safety-netting advice
options.B: Start oral antibiotics and reassess in the morning
options.C: Urgent assessment by the paediatric surgical team
options.D: Repeat the abdominal ultrasound scan in 2 days
options.E: Increase oral analgesia and continue ward observation

correct_answer: C. Urgent assessment by the paediatric surgical team
why_correct: Mesenteric adenitis can only be accepted once appendicitis has been reasonably excluded, and her appendix was never seen on ultrasound. Constant pain localising to the right iliac fossa with vomiting, anorexia, fever, tachycardia, guarding and rebound now indicates localised peritonism and probable appendicitis. She needs urgent surgical assessment, with IV access, fluids and analgesia, rather than further observation. Source: Mesenteric lymphadenitis patient information, West Hertfordshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust; Appendicectomy without confirmation of appendicitis, Evidence-Based Interventions programme, Academy of Medical Royal Colleges, 2020.
why_wrong: A. She is getting worse and has peritonism, so discharge would be unsafe. B. Oral antibiotics and waiting would delay treatment of probable appendicitis. D. Waiting 2 days for another scan risks perforation. E. More analgesia and observation does not address a likely surgical cause and delays treatment.
pearl: Re-examine a child labelled with mesenteric adenitis; new localised peritonism changes the diagnosis.
thinking: Provisional mesenteric adenitis, appendix not seen  ↓  pain now constant in RIF + vomiting + tachycardia + guarding and rebound  ↓  probable appendicitis  ↓  urgent surgical review
exam_trap: Sticking with the first working diagnosis because the ultrasound showed enlarged nodes.
takeaway: Evolving right iliac fossa peritonism in a child labelled with mesenteric adenitis needs urgent surgical review.
notes: Same learning point as MG081. New vignette (younger girl, admitted overnight). Distinct from S001 (adult classic appendicitis) and GF050 (safety-net content).

presentation: Ear pain / hearing loss after injury
stem:
A 35-year-old man pushed a cotton bud too far into his left ear 3 days ago and felt a sharp pain. His hearing on that side has been dull since. Otoscopy shows a small, dry perforation of the left eardrum with no discharge. He has no dizziness, ringing in the ear or facial weakness, and Weber's test lateralises to the left. He is flying to Spain next week for a conference and hopes to use the hotel pool.

Which advice is most appropriate?

options.A: Postpone the flight until the eardrum has healed
options.B: Swimming is fine if he uses antibiotic ear drops
options.C: Arrange surgical repair of the eardrum before travel
options.D: He may fly but should avoid swimming until healed
options.E: Flying and swimming are both fine as it heals fast

correct_answer: D. He may fly but should avoid swimming until healed
why_correct: Most traumatic perforations heal on their own within weeks to a couple of months, and hearing usually returns to normal. The NHS advises that it is safe to fly with a perforated eardrum; flying is restricted only after surgical repair (myringoplasty) until the surgeon says it is safe. He should avoid swimming and keep water out of the ear until it heals, and should not put cotton buds or drops in the ear unless a doctor advises. Source: Perforated eardrum, NHS website (nhs.uk), accessed 2026; Traumatic tympanic membrane perforation, NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde Right Decisions.
why_wrong: A. Flying is safe with a perforated eardrum; the restriction applies after a myringoplasty. B. The ear should be kept dry, and drops are not used routinely for a dry traumatic perforation. C. A small traumatic perforation usually heals by itself, so immediate repair is not needed. E. Water can enter the middle ear through the hole and cause infection, so swimming should wait until it has healed.
pearl: Perforated eardrum: flying is fine, water is not.
thinking: Small dry traumatic perforation, no red flags  ↓  expect spontaneous healing  ↓  safe to fly  ↓  keep the ear dry and no swimming until healed
exam_trap: Assuming pressure changes in flight are dangerous with a perforation; the flying restriction applies after myringoplasty.
takeaway: With a traumatic eardrum perforation, patients can fly but must keep the ear dry until it heals.
notes: Same learning point as MG082 (flying vs swimming advice). New vignette (man, cotton-bud injury). DF017 tests 'keep dry and review' as overall management; this item tests the flying-versus-water advice, as in the reviewed source. Flying statement re-checked on nhs.uk today ('It's safe to fly if you have a perforated eardrum ... if you've had surgery ... do not fly until you're told it's safe'). Healing time softened to words.

presentation: Ear discharge in a child
stem:
A 5-year-old boy has had a fever and has been pulling at his left ear for 3 days. Overnight his mother noticed creamy discharge on his pillow, and since then he has seemed more comfortable. He is alert, eating and drinking, and his temperature is 37.9°C. The left ear canal is full of pus and the eardrum cannot be seen properly. The skin behind the ear is normal, his face moves symmetrically and he has no known allergies. After discussing the options, his mother and the GP agree to start an antibiotic straight away.

Which is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Lidocaine-phenazone ear drops and oral amoxicillin
options.B: Ear syringing to remove the pus, then review in a week
options.C: Oral decongestant and antihistamine for 7 days
options.D: Oral amoxicillin plus paracetamol or ibuprofen
options.E: Same-day ENT referral for microsuction of the ear

correct_answer: D. Oral amoxicillin plus paracetamol or ibuprofen
why_correct: This is acute otitis media with a perforated eardrum and discharge (otorrhoea) in a child who is not systemically unwell. NICE identifies otorrhoea as a group more likely to benefit from antibiotics, and amoxicillin for 5 to 7 days is first choice when there is no penicillin allergy, with paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain. Anaesthetic-analgesic ear drops (phenazone with lidocaine) should not be used when there is a perforation or otorrhoea. Source: Otitis media (acute): antimicrobial prescribing, NICE NG91, 2018 (updated 2022).
why_wrong: A. Phenazone–lidocaine drops are only for use when the eardrum is intact and there is no discharge. B. Syringing is not appropriate when the eardrum is perforated. C. NICE advises that decongestants and antihistamines do not help the symptoms of acute otitis media. E. There are no complications such as mastoiditis, so same-day ENT referral is not needed.
pearl: Pus in the canal after the pain suddenly eased means the drum has perforated, so no anaesthetic ear drops.
thinking: Earache and fever, then sudden relief with discharge  ↓  acute otitis media with perforation  ↓  antibiotic agreed, no allergy  ↓  oral amoxicillin + oral analgesia; avoid anaesthetic drops
exam_trap: Adding anaesthetic ear drops for comfort when the eardrum has perforated.
takeaway: Acute otitis media with discharge: oral amoxicillin and oral analgesia, never anaesthetic drops through a perforation.
notes: Same learning point as MG083 (first-line amoxicillin plus analgesia; anaesthetic drops contraindicated with perforation). New vignette (5-year-old boy, left ear). DF018 and DT041 test the penicillin-allergy alternative (clarithromycin); this child has no allergy, so not a repeat. NG91 re-checked today (drops 'only if ... there is no eardrum perforation or otorrhoea'; 1.1.6 decongestants/antihistamines do not help). Mother's preference fixed in the stem so immediate antibiotic is clearly best, as in the source.

presentation: Hearing loss after injury
stem:
A 41-year-old man perforated his right eardrum 3 months ago when the side of his head slapped against the water in a fall while water-skiing. He has kept the ear dry as advised. His hearing on the right is still reduced, but he has no pain, discharge, dizziness or ringing. Otoscopy shows a dry central perforation that has not changed in size since it was first seen. Rinne's test is negative on the right and Weber's test lateralises to the right. His facial movements are normal.

Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Routine referral to the ENT clinic
options.B: Reassurance and review again in 6 months
options.C: Ciprofloxacin ear drops for 2 weeks
options.D: Oral amoxicillin and review in 2 weeks
options.E: Emergency same-day ENT admission

correct_answer: A. Routine referral to the ENT clinic
why_correct: Most traumatic perforations heal by themselves within about 6 to 8 weeks. A perforation that is still open well beyond this, especially with ongoing hearing loss, should be referred routinely to ENT for audiometry and consideration of surgical repair (myringoplasty). He has no features needing urgent assessment, such as vertigo, facial weakness or infection. Source: Traumatic tympanic membrane perforation, NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde Right Decisions; Tympanic membrane perforation referral guidance, NHS Lothian RefHelp, 2025.
why_wrong: B. A perforation that has not healed after this long is unlikely to close on its own, and further waiting delays repair. C. There is no infection or discharge to treat with antibiotic drops. D. Oral antibiotics are not indicated for a dry perforation without infection. E. There are no red flags such as vertigo, facial weakness or infection, so emergency admission is not needed.
pearl: A traumatic perforation that has not healed after a couple of months needs a routine ENT referral.
thinking: Traumatic perforation kept dry  ↓  still open months later with conductive loss  ↓  no red flags  ↓  routine ENT referral for audiometry and possible myringoplasty
exam_trap: Continuing to reassure and watch because most perforations heal, after the expected healing time has passed.
takeaway: Refer a non-healing traumatic eardrum perforation to ENT routinely.
notes: Same learning point as MG084 (non-healed traumatic perforation → routine ENT). Re-angled under rule 2: the source key relied on knowing the 6-week cut-off (stem at 7 weeks); this version sets the interval at 3 months so non-healing is unequivocal and no cut-off recall is needed. New mechanism (water-skiing). Distinct from DF017 (acute management).

presentation: Visual field defect
notes: skip: duplicates DR029 (bumping into door frames, bitemporal hemianopia on perimetry, normal acuity and discs → MRI of the pituitary). MG085 has the same scenario and the same learning point (best imaging for a bitemporal hemianopia); no different scenario can test 'MRI pituitary for bitemporal hemianopia' without repeating DR029.

presentation: Visual field defect
stem:
A 66-year-old woman tells her optometrist that for 6 weeks she has been knocking cups off the left side of the table and catching her left shoulder on doorways. Her visual acuity is 6/9 in each eye, her pupils react normally and her fundi appear healthy. On confrontation she may be missing targets in the left half of the field of each eye, but her answers vary and the finding is uncertain. She is referred to the hospital eye service so that any field loss can be mapped precisely and monitored.

Which investigation will most accurately chart any loss of visual field?

options.A: Amsler grid testing of each eye separately
options.B: Ishihara plates to test colour vision
options.C: Repeat confrontation testing with a red pin
options.D: Formal automated visual field perimetry
options.E: Optical coherence tomography of the macula

correct_answer: D. Formal automated visual field perimetry
why_correct: Confrontation is a quick bedside screen but is insensitive and cannot map the shape, depth or edges of a field defect. Formal perimetry, usually standard automated perimetry (for example Humphrey testing), measures sensitivity at fixed points in each eye and produces a reproducible chart showing whether a defect is homonymous and respects the vertical midline, which localises the lesion and allows monitoring. Perimetry defines the defect but does not explain it: if it confirms a homonymous defect, as her symptoms suggest, the lesion lies behind the optic chiasm and she needs timely neuroimaging and a stroke work-up (including checking for atrial fibrillation), and sudden-onset loss or other neurological symptoms would need same-day stroke or emergency assessment. Source: Glaucoma: diagnosis and management, NICE NG81, 2017 (updated 2022); Assessing fitness to drive: visual disorders, DVLA, GOV.UK; Visual field defect, homonymous hemianopia (Community Eyecare Guideline 12.1), NHS Scotland.
why_wrong: A. An Amsler grid tests only the central field for macular distortion. B. Ishihara plates test colour vision, not the extent of the visual field. C. Repeating confrontation, even with a red target, remains a crude screen and cannot map the defect reliably. E. Macular OCT images the retina and does not measure the visual field.
pearl: Confrontation screens; formal perimetry maps.
thinking: Symptoms suggest one-sided field loss  ↓  confrontation uncertain  ↓  formal automated perimetry to define and monitor the defect  ↓  homonymous defect means neuroimaging and stroke work-up
exam_trap: Choosing OCT or an Amsler grid, which look at the macula rather than the whole field.
takeaway: Use formal automated perimetry to define a suspected visual field defect, then investigate its cause.
notes: Same learning point as MG086 (confrontation as screen vs formal automated perimetry). New vignette (woman, left-sided symptoms, optometrist). Source safety wording on neuroimaging, stroke work-up and same-day assessment for sudden loss retained. Not a repeat of DR029/BX667 (pituitary imaging/chiasm localisation).

presentation: Visual field defect
stem:
A 39-year-old man has been referred after a minor car accident in which he did not see a vehicle coming from his upper left. For 3 months he has also had brief spells of a rising feeling in his stomach followed by a smell of something burning, each over within a minute, without loss of awareness. His visual acuity and fundoscopy are normal. Formal perimetry shows a left superior homonymous quadrantanopia.

Which part of the brain is most likely to be affected?

options.A: Optic radiation in the left temporal lobe
options.B: Optic radiation in the right parietal lobe
options.C: Optic chiasm above the pituitary
options.D: Visual cortex of the right occipital lobe
options.E: Optic radiation in the right temporal lobe

correct_answer: E. Optic radiation in the right temporal lobe
why_correct: A homonymous field defect places the lesion behind the optic chiasm on the side opposite the field loss, so a left-sided defect means a right-sided lesion. Fibres carrying the upper half of the opposite visual field loop forward through the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop), so a temporal lobe lesion causes a superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky'). His rising epigastric sensation and olfactory aura are typical of focal seizures arising in the temporal lobe, supporting a right temporal lesion. Source: Visual Field Deficits, Neuroscience 2nd edition (Purves et al.), NCBI Bookshelf.
why_wrong: A. A left temporal lesion would cause a right superior quadrantanopia. B. A parietal lesion affects the lower fibres and causes an inferior quadrantanopia. C. A chiasmal lesion causes a bitemporal, not homonymous, defect. D. An occipital lesion usually causes a homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing, and does not explain temporal lobe seizures.
pearl: Temporal 'pie in the sky', parietal 'pie on the floor'; the lesion is on the side opposite the field loss.
thinking: Homonymous defect  ↓  lesion behind the chiasm, opposite side (right)  ↓  superior quadrant = Meyer's loop in the temporal lobe  ↓  temporal lobe aura confirms: right temporal lobe
exam_trap: Placing the lesion on the same side as the field defect.
takeaway: A superior homonymous quadrantanopia localises to the opposite temporal lobe.
notes: Same learning point as MG087 (Meyer's loop). Mirror-image vignette (left defect, right temporal lesion; epigastric rising aura plus olfactory aura). NEU111 tests the seizure type, not field-defect localisation.

presentation: Booking visit — obesity in pregnancy
stem:
A 27-year-old woman is seen by the community midwife at 11 weeks' gestation. This is her first pregnancy. Her BMI is 41 kg/m², her blood pressure is 112/70 mmHg and her urinalysis is normal. She is otherwise healthy, already takes folic acid and vitamin D supplements, and no one in her family has had pre-eclampsia.

Which additional medicine should be recommended?

options.A: Low-dose aspirin daily from 12 weeks to birth
options.B: Labetalol from 20 weeks to prevent hypertension
options.C: Metformin throughout the pregnancy
options.D: Vitamins C and E to prevent pre-eclampsia
options.E: Oral iron supplements from the booking visit

correct_answer: A. Low-dose aspirin daily from 12 weeks to birth
why_correct: NICE lists a first pregnancy and a BMI of 35 kg/m² or more at the first visit as moderate risk factors for pre-eclampsia. Women with more than one moderate risk factor should be advised to take low-dose aspirin (75–150 mg) daily from 12 weeks until the baby is born. She has two, so aspirin is indicated even though her blood pressure is normal. Source: Hypertension in pregnancy: diagnosis and management (NG133), NICE, 2019 (updated 2023).
why_wrong: B. Her blood pressure is normal, and antihypertensives are not used to prevent pre-eclampsia. C. Metformin is not used in pregnancy without diabetes; her BMI means she should be offered a glucose tolerance test instead. D. NICE advises against vitamin C or E supplements to prevent hypertensive disorders in pregnancy. E. Routine iron supplements are not recommended without evidence of anaemia.
pearl: Count the moderate risk factors for pre-eclampsia: two or more means aspirin from 12 weeks.
thinking: Booking visit  ↓  first pregnancy + obesity = two moderate risk factors  ↓  normal blood pressure does not remove the risk  ↓  low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks until birth
exam_trap: Thinking aspirin is only for women with high blood pressure or a past history of pre-eclampsia.
takeaway: A first pregnancy plus obesity is enough to recommend low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks.
notes: Same learning point as MG088 (aspirin for more than one moderate pre-eclampsia risk factor). Re-angled under rule 2: BMI set clearly above the 35 cut-off (41) so the key does not hinge on exact threshold recall, and dose figures removed from all options. Enoxaparin distractor replaced by vitamins C and E (NG133 1.1.4 'do not use') to avoid any ambiguity with the September 2026 RCOG VTE scoring change. Folic acid kept out of options (NG247/GTG72 conflict noted by source writer). GF006 teaches aspirin for twins; different scenario, permitted. NG133 re-checked today.

presentation: Booking visit — obesity in pregnancy
notes: skip (rule 2, movable threshold): the key depends on recalling that a booking BMI of 50 kg/m² or more now scores 4 points under the RCOG GTG37a position statement of September 2026 (which also brought in the new weight-band dose table). Under the previous GTG37a scoring the same woman would not receive antenatal LMWH from booking, so the answer flips with the threshold. Re-angling to 'BMI 50 or above → LMWH through pregnancy and 6 weeks postpartum' still requires recalling that newly moved BMI cut-off, so no stable principle can be tested without movable-threshold recall.

presentation: Booking visit — obesity in pregnancy
stem:
A 36-year-old woman sees the midwife at 12 weeks' gestation in her third pregnancy; both previous babies were born vaginally without complications. Her BMI is 47 kg/m², her blood pressure is 120/76 mmHg and she has no medical conditions. A glucose tolerance test has been booked for later in pregnancy, and her thrombosis risk has been assessed and documented.

Which further referral should be made because of her weight?

options.A: Dietitian to start a weight-reducing diet in pregnancy
options.B: Bariatric surgeons to assess for weight-loss surgery
options.C: Obstetric anaesthetist for antenatal assessment
options.D: Cardiology for echocardiography before 20 weeks
options.E: Endocrinology to exclude Cushing syndrome

correct_answer: C. Obstetric anaesthetist for antenatal assessment
why_correct: The RCOG advises that pregnant women with a booking BMI of 40 kg/m² or more are referred to an obstetric anaesthetist for consideration of an antenatal assessment. A very high BMI makes cannulation, spinal or epidural anaesthesia, airway management and general anaesthesia more difficult. Planning ahead lets the team agree an analgesia and anaesthetic plan for labour or caesarean birth and arrange suitable equipment. Source: Care of Women with Obesity in Pregnancy (Green-top Guideline No. 72), RCOG, 2018.
why_wrong: A. Weight-reducing diets are not recommended during pregnancy; advice focuses on healthy eating and activity. B. Weight-loss surgery is not performed during pregnancy. D. Obesity alone without cardiac symptoms or signs does not need echocardiography. E. Nothing in her history suggests Cushing syndrome.
pearl: Very high BMI in pregnancy is an anaesthetic problem as much as an obstetric one, so plan early.
thinking: Booking BMI very high  ↓  diabetes screening and VTE assessment already done  ↓  anticipate difficult regional or general anaesthesia  ↓  antenatal obstetric anaesthetic assessment
exam_trap: Referring for dieting in pregnancy, which is not advised.
takeaway: Women with a very high booking BMI should be referred for an antenatal obstetric anaesthetic assessment.
notes: Same learning point as MG090. New vignette (para 2, BMI 47). BMI set well above the 40 cut-off so the key does not hinge on threshold recall (rule 2); the cut-off is mentioned only in the explanation. GF003 tests place of birth at 34 weeks (answer includes anaesthetic review); this item tests the booking referral itself, as judged in the reviewed source.

presentation: Ovarian cyst
notes: skip (rule 2, movable threshold): the key (yearly ultrasound) depends entirely on recalling the RCOG GTG62 size band for simple cysts in premenopausal women (50–70 mm). GTG62 dates from 2011 and a second edition is in development, and the related postmenopausal guideline (GTG34) has already had its size cut-offs amended (Dec 2025), so the band is movable. The stable principle (a simple cyst in a premenopausal woman is almost always benign) is already taught by OG036 (4 cm simple cyst → no follow-up), so re-angling to it would duplicate OG036.

presentation: Ovarian cyst
stem:
A 71-year-old woman saw her GP with 6 weeks of feeling full after small meals and needing to pass urine more often. Her serum CA125 was markedly raised, and an urgent pelvic ultrasound was arranged. In the gynaecology clinic the scan shows an 8 cm right adnexal cyst with several internal septations and a solid component, a normal left ovary and no free fluid. She went through the menopause at 52 and is otherwise well.

What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.A: CT scan and gynaecological oncology MDT referral
options.B: Repeat ultrasound scan and CA125 in 4 to 6 months
options.C: Laparoscopic oophorectomy by the general gynaecology team
options.D: Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the cyst for cytology
options.E: Discharge to her GP with advice to return if worse

correct_answer: A. CT scan and gynaecological oncology MDT referral
why_correct: A postmenopausal woman with a multilocular cyst containing solid tissue and a raised CA125 has a high risk of malignancy index (RMI I, which combines ultrasound features, menopausal status and CA125). For a high RMI the RCOG recommends CT of the abdomen and pelvis and referral to the gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team, so that staging and any surgery are planned by specialists. Follow-up scans, aspiration and surgery in a general unit are only appropriate for low-risk cysts, if at all. Source: Ovarian Cysts in Postmenopausal Women (Green-top Guideline No. 34), RCOG, 2016 (amended 2025); Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (NG12), NICE.
why_wrong: B. Monitoring is reserved for low-risk cysts and would delay treatment of a possible cancer. C. A suspicious mass should be managed by the gynaecological oncology team, not removed in a general gynaecology unit. D. Aspiration is not recommended in postmenopausal women because cytology is unreliable and it risks spilling malignant cells. E. A complex cyst with a raised CA125 needs specialist investigation, not discharge.
pearl: Postmenopausal + complex cyst + raised CA125 = high risk: CT and gynae-oncology MDT.
thinking: Postmenopausal woman with bloating symptoms  ↓  complex multilocular cyst with solid area + raised CA125  ↓  high risk of malignancy  ↓  CT abdomen and pelvis and gynaecological oncology MDT
exam_trap: Arranging laparoscopic removal in the general gynaecology unit, which risks inadequate surgery for an ovarian cancer.
takeaway: A high-risk postmenopausal ovarian mass needs CT and referral to the gynaecological oncology MDT.
notes: Same learning point as MG092 (high-risk postmenopausal complex cyst → CT + gynae-oncology MDT). Re-angled under rule 2: the source key depended on RMI arithmetic (U3 × M3 × CA125 25 = 225) against the 200 cut-off and on the April 2026 NG12 age-specific CA125 thresholds. Here CA125 is described as markedly raised (no number), so the decision rests on the stable principle without threshold recall. CR035 tests the diagnosis of ovarian cancer; this tests the next step.

presentation: Acute pelvic pain — ruptured haemorrhagic ovarian cyst
stem:
You are the gynaecology SHO on call. The emergency department registrar phones a referral: 'A 25-year-old dance teacher, sudden sharp right pelvic pain halfway through a class this afternoon. Regular cycles, about three weeks since her last period started, hCG negative. Obs stable, apyrexial. She needed IV morphine, which has helped, but she is still guarding in the right iliac fossa. Results so far: first haemoglobin normal, the repeat two hours later a little lower. Scan report: right ovarian cyst of about 4 cm with internal echoes in keeping with haemorrhage, moderate free fluid in the pouch of Douglas, ovary not enlarged, Doppler flow present. She is keen to go home.'

What should you advise?

options.A: Home with ibuprofen and a repeat scan in 6 weeks
options.B: Admit for analgesia, observations and serial Hb
options.C: Urgent laparoscopy to detort the right ovary
options.D: Emergency laparotomy and right oophorectomy
options.E: Treat as PID with IV ceftriaxone, doxycycline and metronidazole

correct_answer: B. Admit for analgesia, observations and serial Hb
why_correct: Sudden pain on exertion in the second half of the cycle, a negative pregnancy test, a haemorrhagic cyst and free fluid indicate a ruptured haemorrhagic (corpus luteum) cyst. She is haemodynamically stable and most such women settle without surgery, but she should be admitted because she has a moderate haemoperitoneum, needed IV opioids, still has guarding and her haemoglobin is falling. Admission allows analgesia, regular observations, serial haemoglobin checks and prompt laparoscopy if she becomes unstable, her haemoglobin keeps falling or her pain persists. Source: Kim JH et al., Successful conservative management of ruptured ovarian cysts with hemoperitoneum in healthy women, PLoS One, 2014.
why_wrong: A. Ongoing bleeding has not been excluded, so discharge would be unsafe despite her wish to go home. C. Normal Doppler flow and a normal-sized ovary make torsion less likely, and she has no indication for emergency surgery while stable. D. Laparotomy and oophorectomy are not needed in a stable patient, and any surgery would aim to preserve the ovary. E. Sudden onset during exercise without fever or discharge does not suggest pelvic inflammatory disease.
pearl: A stable ruptured haemorrhagic cyst is managed conservatively, but in hospital until the bleeding has stopped.
thinking: Sudden pain during exercise, luteal phase, hCG negative  ↓  haemorrhagic cyst + free fluid = ruptured cyst  ↓  stable, but moderate haemoperitoneum, IV opioid needed, guarding, falling Hb  ↓  admit, observe, serial Hb; laparoscopy if she deteriorates
exam_trap: Agreeing to discharge a stable patient who wants to go home without weighing the falling haemoglobin and the amount of free fluid.
takeaway: A haemodynamically stable woman with a ruptured haemorrhagic ovarian cyst and haemoperitoneum should be admitted for observation and serial haemoglobin.
notes: Reworked for distance from AKT MG093 (stem Jaccard was 0.54): now an ED-to-gynaecology phone referral, 25-year-old dance teacher, findings as the registrar's results list, patient wanting to go home. All findings that justify admission retained (moderate free fluid, IV opioid needed, persisting guarding, falling haemoglobin). No UK national guideline covers acute cyst rupture (GTG62 excludes it); source evidence carried over. Distinct from N9323 (diagnosis) and OG037/BX095 (torsion).

presentation: Vaginal prolapse
stem:
A 63-year-old woman has a bulge at the vaginal entrance that drags and aches by the evening. Examination shows an anterior vaginal wall prolapse extending beyond the hymen, with good support of the cervix and posterior wall. She has completed a supervised pelvic floor exercise programme without benefit, and both ring and shelf pessaries fell out. She has no urinary leakage or bowel symptoms, has no plans for more children and is fit for an anaesthetic. She now asks for surgery.

Which operation should be offered?

options.A: Transvaginal mesh repair of the anterior vaginal wall
options.B: Another 16 weeks of supervised pelvic floor training
options.C: Vaginal hysterectomy to support the anterior wall
options.D: Anterior vaginal wall repair without mesh
options.E: Anterior repair with a mid-urethral sling added

correct_answer: D. Anterior vaginal wall repair without mesh
why_correct: NICE advises offering surgery to women whose prolapse symptoms have not improved with non-surgical treatment or who decline it. For anterior vaginal wall prolapse, the operation to offer is an anterior repair without mesh, after shared decision-making. Transvaginal mesh for anterior or posterior wall prolapse should be used only in research because of serious safety concerns. Source: Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women: management (NG123), NICE, 2019; Transvaginal mesh repair of anterior or posterior vaginal wall prolapse (IPG599, now HTG456), NICE, 2017.
why_wrong: A. NICE restricts transvaginal mesh for anterior or posterior wall prolapse to research because of serious complications. B. She has already completed a supervised course without benefit and now chooses surgery. C. Her cervix and uterus are well supported, so a hysterectomy would not correct the anterior wall defect. E. She has no urinary leakage, so adding a continence procedure would add risk without a clear benefit.
pearl: Anterior wall prolapse surgery in the UK means native-tissue repair, not mesh.
thinking: Symptomatic anterior wall prolapse  ↓  pelvic floor training and pessaries have failed  ↓  wants surgery and is fit  ↓  anterior repair without mesh
exam_trap: Choosing mesh because it sounds like a stronger repair.
takeaway: After failed conservative treatment, offer anterior repair without mesh for anterior vaginal wall prolapse.
notes: Same learning point as MG094. New vignette (63-year-old, ring and shelf pessaries failed). NG123 1.8.20 re-checked today ('Offer anterior repair without mesh to women with anterior vaginal wall prolapse'). Distinct from DF025 (PFMT first-line) and DF026 (vaginal oestrogen with pessary).

presentation: Vaginal prolapse
stem:
An 87-year-old woman who lives in a nursing home has a symptomatic uterine prolapse that protrudes from the vagina. She has Parkinson's disease, severe COPD on home oxygen and moderate dementia. After discussion with her and her son, a ring pessary has been fitted rather than surgery because of her anaesthetic risk. It is comfortable, stays in place when she stands and coughs, and she can pass urine normally. She cannot remove or reinsert it herself.

What follow-up should be arranged?

options.A: Review only if she reports bleeding or vaginal discharge
options.B: Leave the pessary in place indefinitely if comfortable
options.C: Yearly transvaginal ultrasound scan to check the position
options.D: Care home staff to remove it if it falls out and reinsert
options.E: Planned removal and review in a pessary clinic, 6-monthly

correct_answer: E. Planned removal and review in a pessary clinic, 6-monthly
why_correct: A pessary suits women at high surgical risk, as she is. NICE advises that a pessary should be removed at least once every 6 months to prevent serious complications such as erosion, fistula or impaction. Women who are at risk of complications because a physical or cognitive impairment makes self-management difficult should be offered a pessary clinic appointment every 6 months. Source: Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women: management (NG123), NICE, 2019.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for symptoms risks missing erosion or impaction, and she may not report problems because of her dementia. B. A pessary left in indefinitely can cause erosion, fistula or impaction. C. Ultrasound does not check for vaginal erosion or replace removal and inspection. D. Untrained replacement after it falls out is not planned follow-up and does not include examination of the vagina.
pearl: A pessary needs planned removal and inspection; women who cannot self-manage need a pessary clinic.
thinking: High surgical risk  ↓  ring pessary fitted, cannot self-manage  ↓  risk of erosion, fistula, impaction  ↓  pessary clinic with planned removal and review
exam_trap: Assuming a comfortable pessary can be left alone until problems appear.
takeaway: Women who cannot manage their own pessary should have planned removal and review in a pessary clinic.
notes: Same learning point as MG095 (NG123 1.7.8–1.7.9). Re-angled under rule 2: distractors now differ in kind (no follow-up, indefinite, ultrasound, untrained reinsertion) rather than by interval, so the key does not hinge on recalling the 6-month figure. New vignette (Parkinson's, nursing home). NG123 1.7.8–1.7.9 re-checked today. Distinct from DF026 (vaginal oestrogen).

presentation: Urinary symptoms
stem:
A 59-year-old woman who has had two vaginal births, one by forceps, sees her GP with a year of urinary frequency, a weak stream and a feeling of incomplete emptying, so that she often needs to go again a few minutes later. She has learned to press a soft swelling at the front of the vaginal opening upwards to start passing urine. She has had three urinary tract infections in the past year. The dragging feeling is worse after standing all day. Her bowels open normally without straining or vaginal pressure, and a urine dipstick today is negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Posterior vaginal wall prolapse
options.B: Anterior vaginal wall prolapse
options.C: Vault prolapse with enterocele
options.D: Detrusor overactivity
options.E: Diverticulum of the urethra

correct_answer: B. Anterior vaginal wall prolapse
why_correct: Anterior vaginal wall prolapse (cystocele) causes a vaginal bulge with voiding symptoms: frequency, a slow stream, incomplete emptying and recurrent urinary tract infections from residual urine. Having to push the bulge back to start voiding is typical, because reducing the prolapse straightens the angle between bladder and urethra. Her normal bowel function makes a posterior wall prolapse unlikely. Source: Pelvic organ prolapse patient information, RCOG, 2022; Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women: management (NG123), NICE, 2019.
why_wrong: A. A posterior wall prolapse (rectocele) causes bowel symptoms such as straining or needing to press on the vagina to open the bowels. C. An enterocele is a prolapse of small bowel, usually at the vaginal vault, and does not typically cause these voiding symptoms. D. Detrusor overactivity causes urgency, not a vaginal bulge that must be reduced to void. E. A urethral diverticulum classically causes post-void dribbling, pain and a tender anterior vaginal lump, not a soft reducible bulge.
pearl: Pushing a bulge back to pass urine is the hallmark of a cystocele.
thinking: Vaginal bulge with dragging  ↓  voiding symptoms, incomplete emptying, recurrent UTIs  ↓  must reduce the bulge to void; bowels normal  ↓  anterior wall prolapse (cystocele)
exam_trap: Choosing detrusor overactivity because of frequency, ignoring the bulge and incomplete emptying.
takeaway: A vaginal bulge with incomplete emptying and recurrent UTIs suggests a cystocele.
notes: Same learning point as MG096 (recognising cystocele from voiding symptoms). New vignette. Q16587 diagnoses cystocele from an examination finding; this item gives no examination finding. Uterine prolapse kept out of the options to avoid ambiguity, as in the source.

presentation: Low mood
stem:
A 26-year-old trans man (registered female at birth) attends his GP practice in England. He was referred to an NHS adult gender service 18 months ago and is still waiting for a first appointment. For 2 months he has felt low, has lost interest in playing football and is sleeping badly; his PHQ-9 score falls in the less severe range. He has no thoughts of suicide or self-harm, still works part-time, and takes no medicines or hormones. The GP uses his chosen name and pronouns.

Which is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Wait until the gender service has seen him before treating
options.B: Assess and treat his depression in primary care now
options.C: Start testosterone in primary care to ease his distress
options.D: Refer to psychiatry to confirm his gender identity
options.E: Ask the gender service to expedite his first appointment

correct_answer: B. Assess and treat his depression in primary care now
why_correct: Waits for NHS adult gender services are long, and the GP remains responsible for the patient's general health in the meantime, including co-existing mental health problems. His depression should be assessed in the usual way, including severity and risk of suicide or self-harm, and treated now (for less severe depression, for example NHS Talking Therapies or guided self-help), with safety-netting and review. GMC advice is that GPs should support trans patients while they wait and consider local mental health services if distress or risk increases. Source: GMC ethical hub, Trans healthcare (reviewed 2025); NICE NG222 Depression in adults, 2022.
why_wrong: A. Depression should not be left untreated because specialist gender care has not yet started. C. Gender-affirming hormones are started on specialist advice, not by a GP acting alone. D. Gender identity does not need psychiatric 'confirmation', and his depression can be managed in primary care. E. Contacting the gender service does not treat his current depression, which needs managing now.
pearl: Being on a gender service waiting list does not put the rest of a patient's care on hold.
thinking: Trans patient awaiting gender service  ↓  new low mood, no risk  ↓  assess severity and risk as usual  ↓  treat depression in primary care now, with review
exam_trap: Assuming all of a trans patient's mental health needs belong to the gender service.
takeaway: GPs should assess and treat depression in trans patients while they wait for gender services.
notes: Same learning point as MG097 (GP care while waiting). New vignette (trans man). PHQ-9 number softened to 'less severe range' (rule 1). Not a repeat of DF045 (referral to adult gender services).

presentation: Gender-affirming oestrogen — reducing VTE risk
stem:
A 49-year-old trans woman who drives a delivery van books a telephone appointment with you, her GP in England. Her gender-affirming hormones have been prescribed by the practice under shared care since an NHS gender service discharged her four years ago; she takes estradiol tablets and her last levels were on target. 'I went back to smoking a pack a day when my mum was ill and I'm not ready to quit yet. A friend said smoking on hormone tablets causes clots. Is there a safer way to take them?' She has never had a deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism and no relatives have, and her weight and recent blood pressure are unremarkable.

What change to her oestrogen regimen should you advise?

options.A: Add cyproterone acetate to her estradiol tablets
options.B: Swap to ethinylestradiol tablets at a matched dose
options.C: Swap to transdermal estradiol gel or patches
options.D: Stop oestrogen for good because of her smoking
options.E: Start daily long-term low molecular weight heparin

correct_answer: C. Swap to transdermal estradiol gel or patches
why_correct: Oestrogen therapy increases the risk of venous thromboembolism, and the risk is lower with transdermal estradiol than with oral estradiol because transdermal use avoids the first-pass effect on hepatic clotting factors. UK gender service shared-care guidance recommends offering transdermal preparations to people over 40 and to smokers. She should be switched (with the gender service's advice where needed) while smoking cessation support continues to be offered. Source: Lancashire and South Cumbria MMG trans female prescribing information sheet, 2024; BAGIS Healthcare for Trans Adults: practical guidance for GPs, 2026.
why_wrong: A. Cyproterone adds its own risks and does not reduce the thrombotic effect of oral oestrogen. B. Ethinylestradiol carries a higher risk of thrombosis than estradiol and is not recommended for gender-affirming treatment. D. Smoking is not in itself a reason to stop treatment permanently; the safer step is a transdermal route plus cessation support. E. Long-term anticoagulation is not used as routine prevention in someone with no previous clot.
pearl: Older age or smoking on oestrogen: go transdermal.
thinking: Trans woman on oral estradiol  ↓  over 40 and smokes = higher VTE risk  ↓  transdermal avoids the hepatic first-pass effect  ↓  switch to gel or patches and keep offering cessation support
exam_trap: Stopping hormones altogether, which causes distress and is not required.
takeaway: Switching from oral to transdermal estradiol lowers VTE risk in trans women who are older or smoke.
notes: Reworked for distance from AKT MG098 (stem Jaccard was 0.51): now a GP telephone consultation initiated by the patient, 49-year-old van driver, question in her own words. BMI and BP figures removed. Ethinylestradiol is described as higher-risk and not recommended; no claim of a UK prohibition is made. Not a repeat of DF046.

presentation: Gender distress in a young person
stem:
A 15-year-old registered male at birth attends a GP practice in England with her father. For the past 18 months she has identified as a girl and uses she/her pronouns at home and school. She is becoming very distressed by her deepening voice and facial hair and asks to start puberty blockers. She is attending school and has a supportive group of friends, with no history of self-harm or suicidal thoughts. Her father wants her to get help.

Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Start a GnRH analogue while awaiting specialist review
options.B: Refer straight to the NHS children's gender service
options.C: Suggest a private UK clinic that prescribes blockers
options.D: Reassure that these feelings are a passing phase
options.E: Refer to local NHS paediatrics or CAMHS

correct_answer: E. Refer to local NHS paediatrics or CAMHS
why_correct: Since 1 September 2024, NHS children and young people's gender services in England accept referrals only from NHS paediatric services or NHS children and young people's mental health services (CAMHS), not directly from GPs, so the GP should take her distress seriously, explore it with her and her father, and refer locally for a holistic assessment. Separately, the NHS stopped routine prescribing of puberty blockers for gender incongruence in under-18s in March 2024, and restrictions on new private prescribing and supply to under-18s were made indefinite in December 2024 (with a review due in 2027), with an exemption only for approved clinical research. A GP therefore cannot start them. Source: NHS England, Service specification: referral pathway for the specialist service for children and young people with gender incongruence (PRN01451), 2024; DHSC, Ban on puberty blockers to be made indefinite on experts' advice, December 2024.
why_wrong: A. Puberty blockers are not prescribed routinely for gender incongruence in under-18s and a GP cannot start them. B. The NHS children's gender service no longer accepts referrals directly from GPs. C. New private prescribing and supply of puberty blockers to under-18s is restricted, so directing her there is inappropriate. D. Dismissing persistent distress is unhelpful and fails to arrange the assessment she needs.
pearl: In England, a GP refers a young person with gender distress through paediatrics or CAMHS, not directly to the gender service.
thinking: Young person with persistent gender distress  ↓  take it seriously and explore  ↓  GP cannot refer directly or start blockers  ↓  refer to NHS paediatrics or CAMHS for holistic assessment
exam_trap: Referring directly to the national gender service, which no longer takes GP referrals.
takeaway: In England, refer young people with gender distress to local NHS paediatrics or CAMHS; GPs cannot start puberty blockers.
notes: Same learning point as MG099 (referral route plus puberty blocker restrictions). New vignette (registered male at birth, father attending). England-only policy; carries over the source re-verification of 8 Oct 2026 and makes no PATHWAYS trial-status claim. Recheck before release and at the 2027 review. For PLAB candidates CAMHS is spelt out in the explanation.

presentation: Hypertensive retinopathy
stem:
A 63-year-old woman attends a routine health check, where her clinic blood pressure is 172/102 mmHg. Her vision is normal. On fundoscopy there is arteriovenous nipping in both eyes, together with a few soft, greyish-white patches with feathery margins lying along the vessel arcades. There are no shiny yellow deposits, and both optic discs are sharp.

Which process best explains the soft white patches?

options.A: Ischaemia of the retinal nerve fibre layer
options.B: Lipid leaking from damaged retinal capillaries
options.C: Swelling of the optic disc from raised pressure
options.D: Cholesterol emboli lodged in retinal arterioles
options.E: Deposits beneath the retinal pigment epithelium

correct_answer: A. Ischaemia of the retinal nerve fibre layer
why_correct: Soft white patches with indistinct, feathery edges are cotton-wool spots. They form when arteriolar narrowing causes focal ischaemia of the retinal nerve fibre layer, which interrupts axoplasmic transport in ganglion cell axons so that axonal material builds up. In hypertensive retinopathy they sit in the same severity grade as flame-shaped haemorrhages. Source: StatPearls, Hypertensive Retinopathy (NCBI Bookshelf), 2025; EyeWiki (American Academy of Ophthalmology), Cotton Wool Spots, 2026.
why_wrong: B. Leaked lipid forms hard exudates, which are yellow and sharply defined. C. Optic disc swelling (papilloedema) would blur the disc margins, which are sharp here. D. Cholesterol emboli appear as bright refractile plaques at arteriolar branch points. E. Deposits beneath the retinal pigment epithelium are drusen, seen in age-related macular degeneration.
pearl: Cotton-wool spots are soft and fluffy (nerve fibre ischaemia); hard exudates are yellow and crisp (lipid).
thinking: Fluffy white patches with blurred edges  ↓  cotton-wool spots  ↓  arteriolar narrowing causes nerve fibre layer ischaemia  ↓  axoplasmic flow stops and material accumulates
exam_trap: Mixing up cotton-wool spots with hard exudates.
takeaway: Cotton-wool spots represent ischaemia of the retinal nerve fibre layer.
notes: Same learning point as MG100. New vignette (woman, health check). BP kept below the NICE same-day referral threshold so the item does not overlap DF019. 'Ischaemia' rather than 'infarct' retained as in the reviewed source.

presentation: Suspected hypertension — completing the end-organ work-up
stem:
You are covering the duty doctor list at a GP surgery and pick up a task from the practice nurse: 'Mr K, 63, retired bus driver, came for his NHS Health Check. Seated readings 164/96 and then 170/98. ABPM kit fitted today, he brings it back on Friday. Feels fine. The GP registrar looked at his eyes: silver-wiring and AV nipping, no bleeds or exudates, discs crisp. I have taken bloods for HbA1c, U&Es with eGFR and lipids, and he is booked for an ECG on Tuesday. Is there anything else I should get before he comes back?'

What else should the nurse arrange now?

options.A: Echocardiography to assess the left ventricle
options.B: Spot urine albumin:creatinine ratio
options.C: Ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder
options.D: Duplex scan of the neck arteries
options.E: Twenty-four-hour urine protein measurement

correct_answer: B. Spot urine albumin:creatinine ratio
why_correct: NICE recommends that everyone with hypertension is offered tests for end-organ damage: a urine albumin:creatinine ratio and a urine dipstick for haematuria, HbA1c, electrolytes, creatinine and eGFR, total and HDL cholesterol, examination of the fundi and a 12-lead ECG, and these can start while ambulatory monitoring confirms the diagnosis. The nurse has covered the bloods, his retinae have been examined and the ECG is booked, so the outstanding test is a spot urine albumin:creatinine ratio to look for kidney damage. Source: NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults, 2019 (updated 2026), recommendation 1.3.3.
why_wrong: A. Echocardiography is not part of the routine work-up; the 12-lead ECG is the screen for left ventricular hypertrophy. C. A renal tract ultrasound is not routine in hypertension and is kept for suspected kidney disease or a secondary cause. D. Carotid imaging is not part of the NICE end-organ damage assessment. E. A spot albumin:creatinine ratio has replaced timed urine collections for detecting proteinuria.
pearl: The NICE hypertension work-up is bloods, urine ACR and haematuria dipstick, fundi and ECG, and the urine is the part most often forgotten.
thinking: Raised readings, ABPM under way  ↓  end-organ tests can start before the diagnosis is confirmed  ↓  bloods taken, fundi examined, ECG booked  ↓  still missing: urine  ↓  spot urine albumin:creatinine ratio
exam_trap: Ordering an echocardiogram to look for left ventricular hypertrophy when the ECG is the routine screen and the urine test has been missed.
takeaway: Everyone with suspected or confirmed hypertension needs a urine albumin:creatinine ratio as part of the end-organ assessment.
notes: Reworked for distance from AKT MG101 (stem Jaccard was 0.61): now a nurse-to-doctor task message after an NHS Health Check, man of 63, findings given as the nurse's list. Same key (urine ACR) and same learning point. NG136 1.3.3 re-checked 8 Oct 2026. Haematuria dipstick deliberately not offered, as in the source. Distinct from DF020 (what fundoscopy finding means for treatment).

presentation: Follow-up of hypertensive retinopathy
stem:
A 57-year-old taxi driver returns to his GP surgery. Six months ago a routine sight test by his high-street optometrist found flame-shaped bleeds and cotton-wool spots in both eyes, with crossing changes where the arteries nipped the veins; his discs and acuity were normal. He was seen at the practice the next day with a reading of 172/104, his end-organ tests were completed and he started treatment, which he has taken faithfully. His home readings now average 130/80. He hands you the optometrist's original letter and asks: 'Will my eyes go back to how they were?'

How should you explain what is likely to happen to his retinal findings?

options.A: Laser treatment will be needed to clear the bleeds
options.B: Everything is permanent and his sight will decline
options.C: Bleeds and spots clear; vessel changes may remain
options.D: Injections into the eye are needed to halt progression
options.E: Every finding, including the nipping, clears in weeks

correct_answer: C. Bleeds and spots clear; vessel changes may remain
why_correct: Acute hypertensive changes such as flame-shaped haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and exudates usually resolve over weeks to months once blood pressure is controlled, and vision is generally preserved, whereas chronic arteriolar changes such as narrowing and arteriovenous nipping reflect longstanding sclerosis and often remain. Treatment is blood pressure control, and eye procedures are kept for complications such as macular oedema with visual loss. The haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots were still evidence of target organ damage, needing prompt assessment (NICE's target organ damage tests and a check for same-day referral features such as a clinic blood pressure of 180/120 mmHg or higher with retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema), active treatment rather than reassurance alone, sustained control and repeat fundoscopy. Source: NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults, 2019 (updated 2026); StatPearls, Hypertensive Retinopathy, 2025; MSD Manual Professional, Hypertensive Retinopathy.
why_wrong: A. Laser is not used for hypertensive haemorrhages, which clear with blood pressure control. B. Acute changes are reversible and vision is usually preserved with good control. D. Intravitreal injections are for complications such as macular oedema, not for routine hypertensive retinopathy. E. Arteriovenous nipping reflects chronic vessel wall change and often persists.
pearl: Haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots come and go with blood pressure; nipping stays.
thinking: Hypertensive retinopathy found by the optometrist  ↓  prompt end-organ assessment and treatment  ↓  blood pressure now controlled  ↓  acute changes (haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots) resolve  ↓  chronic arteriolar changes (nipping) may remain
exam_trap: Thinking all retinal changes reverse, including arteriovenous nipping.
takeaway: With good blood pressure control, haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots fade but arteriolar changes may persist.
notes: Reworked for distance from AKT MG102 (stem Jaccard was 0.59): now a 57-year-old taxi driver whose retinopathy was found by a high-street optometrist, prompt GP assessment with end-organ tests, question in his own words. Source safety wording on target-organ damage needing prompt assessment (NG136 tests, same-day referral features) retained in why_correct, and the stem shows that assessment happened. BP at detection below the NG136 same-day threshold, avoiding overlap with DF019.
